div.head: Pottrp.
div.p: Pottrp.

--- AN AUSTRALIAN NATIONAL ANTHEM. Maker of earth and sea, What shall we render Thee? All things are Thine: Ours but from day to day, Still with one heart to pray, "God bless our land alway, This land of Thine." Mighty in brotherhood, Mighty for God and good, = ' Let U 3 be Thine. Here let the nations see. Toil from the curse set free, Labour and Liberty One cause—and Thine. Here let glad Plenty reign, Here let none seek in vain Our help and Thine— No heart for want of friend • . Fail ere the timely end. But level for ever blend Man's:cause and Thine. Here let Thy peace abide; - Never may strife divide This land of Thine. Let us united stand, . One great Australian band, Heart to heart, hand in hand, Heart and hand Thine. Stronz to defend our right, Proud in all nations' sight, Lowly in thine— One in all noble fame, Still be our path the same, - Onward in Freedom's name, Upward in thine. —Centennial Magazine. J. BRUNTON STEPHENS.

The conversation had turned on Mademoiselle Three Stars, who resembles a skeleton, when some one said that she had lately grown quite stout. "You mean," said her best friend, who was present, "that she is less A little girl saw a parrot for the first time in a:con- fectioner's shop, and while she was in the middle of a mouthful of tart, the parrot called out "Hullo!" The child stopped eating, and with half-opened mouth and staring eyes, exclaimed in an awed tone, ",Hullo, -achicken !" "Where are you going this summer?" "I haven't the least idea." "But can't you judge from what you've beard your pa and ma say?" "Well, from the way ma talks, l'd think we were going to Paris, Italy, Switzer- land, and the Rhine. From the way pa talks, I'd think we were going to the poor-house." " Who was that gentleman I just saw you talking with so earnestly ?" " Oh, that was the exiled Nihilist, Mr. At-choo-at-chow-at-chee-at-chiski !" "Why, what a frightful cold you have !" " Not at all ; not at all. I was merely giving you the exact pronunciation of the gentleman's name. It's sneezy enough when you've learned how."

"Do you notice anything peculiar in the movements of these wasps ?" -he asked, as he pointed to a puddle in the middle of the road. "Nothing, except that they seem to come and go," replied one of the boys. The other was less prompt his reply, but he had observed to some purpose. "I 11000 that they fly away in pairs," he said. "One has - , pellet pi mud, the other nothing. Are there a la.- drones am wasps, As among bees?" " Both WEIC alike ti:ig busy, and each 7ent away with a burden," replied the naturalist. "The Coe you thought a 'do-nothing' bad a mouthful of water. They reach their nest together; the one deposits his pellet of mud, and the other ejects the water upon it, which makes it of the consistency of mortar. They then paddle it upon the nest, and fly away for more materials." You see, one boy observed a little, and the other a good deal more, while the naturalist had something to tell them that surprised them very much. Boys, be observant. Cultivate the faculty. Mr. Spurgeon does not like instrumental music in the church. But what of whistling? A man whistled "Nearer, my God, to Thee," with varia- tions, as part of a special service in an Ocean Grove (U.S.) church.

A Zurich correspondent writes apropos of the Ticino Revolution :—lt is a Liberal v. Clerical 'ousi- ness, and has no special social significance. It was beautifully managed, as the other party admit. At a given hour 'the tocsin was rung in Bellinzona, Lugano, Locarno, &c., as a signal, and the anti- clericals assembled in arms, seized the public build- ings, and placed the authorities under lock and key —a wonderfully executed coup de main.

The great and terrible Matterhorn has claimed another offering of victims. A Strasburg gentle- man, roped between two guides, has been found at the bottom of the great arrete. Their fate recalls the fate of the unhappy German tourist who three years ago was frozen high up on the snowy breast of the great mountain, and of the still more terrible calamity of the first ascent by Mr. Whymper and his party, the majority of whom lost their lives in the descent. That was in 1857.

So far from the Australian strike showing any signs of collapse, it looks from this morning's news as though Australia were on the eve of a general strike such as London was threatened with a year ago. The Labour Conference at bydney has decided to call out at once all men connected with the wool trade, and has passed an instruction to all unions in all the colonies to hold themselves in readiness for a strike. This is a pretty clear answer to the programme of the federation of the Australian cap- italists.

A worm that feeds on steel has been discovered by Belgian scientists. It is said to be two centi- meters in length, and about the size of a common knitting needle. It is of a light gray colour, and on the head it carries two little sacs or glands filled with a most powerful corrosive secretion, which is ejected every ten minutes when the worm is lying undisturbed. The liquid, when squirted upon iron, renders that metal soft and spongy and the colour ot rust, when it is easily and greedily devoured by the little insect.

It is likely that the Parnell-O'Shea case will come on about Christmas--either just before or after. It will probably be set down as a special jury case, and may take about three days. A number of letters will be disclosed on either side.

Mr. A. Bruce Joy, the well-known sculptor, has left England en route for America, where he will superintend the placing of the huge lion which is to surmount the sarcophagus of the " Cherry Pic- ton" monument. He joins the Majestic at Queens- town, having in the meantime assisted at the unveiling of the Bishop Berkeley memorial in Cloyne Cathedral, one of the latest works ef his chisel.

Robert Louis Stevenson is back in Australia after a three months' yachting cruise in the South Seas, during which he was accompanied by Mrs. Steven- son. At Noumea, the capital of the French penal settlement of New Caledonia, the novelist spent several days studying convict life and making numerous entries in his notebook for future use. Re is reported to be greatly improved in health.

Mr. J. 11. Wilson, founder and general secretary of the National Amalgamated Sailors and Firemen's Union of Great Britain and Ireland. who is being suggested as the Labour candidate for Deptford, is one of the ablest as well as one of the most popular leaders in the Labour movement. The fact that Mr. Wilson headed the poll in the election of Parliamen- tary Committee at the Liverpool Congress shows the esteem in which he is held by the trade unionists. He is an advanced man, but does not go so far as the Socialist wing of the Congress.

Sir Edwin Arnold finds life very comfortable in Japan. He likes the country, the people, and their ways. He lives in regular Japanese style, and is understood to be a confirmed Buddhist. The Ameri- can newspaptrs have published many articles about Sir Edwin and his life in Tokio, and have stated that he threatens to marry a winsome Japanese lady; but this is asserted to be a pure fabrication.

The most exhilarating thing at Boulogne is the spectacle of Dr. Tanner taking his bath. He is a very powerful swimmer, and he throws the boat- men who mount guard over the bathers into con- stant excitement by disappearing in the direction of the horizon. They tootle at him on their horns, and he defies their authority as if they were so many Speakers. Dr. Tanner may also be seen at the Casino, where he foots it with the best of them.

Preparations are now actively going forward among the Wesleyan Methodists for the celebration of the centenary of Wesley's death, which occurs in March next year. It is proposed by the Committee of Conference to which was deputed the organisa- tion of the celebration to raise £7,000 as a fund to restore City-road Chapel and the adjoining premises, including Wesley's house. The chapel is one hun- dred and ten years old, and is sadly out of repair.

What notice is Mr. Balfour going to take of the charges made by Dr. Moorhead, J.P., against the treatment of Mr. McEnery at Tullamore ? Here is a perfectly unimpeachable witness, with an official ' title to the attention of the Irish Government, who officially records in the journal of the gaol one specific instance of a gross and unprovoked assault on a prisoner, and a general charge against the officials of habitual persecution and misconduct. The case is aggravated by the fact that the prisoner so treated is a political offender and a man of educa- tion and refinement, against whom there is no charge of misconduct. It will be a disgrace to Mr. Balfour personally if this charge is not refuted or the wrong redressed. But it will not be the first disgrace of the kind.

The Sultan of Sokoto has presented the Queen, through the medium of the Royal Niger Company, with a young lion. The lion arrived at Liverpool on Monday, and during his voyage proved to be a very entertaining passenger, He scampered about on deck, and was on "very friendly, even lovable •' terms with his keeper Daniel, who had as little to fear as the other Daniel had when he was in the lion's den. The Sultan of Sokoto is the Arrican potentate who made a present of 250,000 square miles of the most fertile land in Africa to the Royal Niger Company.

The Duke of Clarence and Avondale is to visit Liverpool next month, to open the new Infirmary, and the Finance Committee of the City Council have decided that fifty guineas of the ratepayers' money is to be squandered in providing "an illumin- ated address of welcome," which will be presented to H.R.H. when he enters the city. No doubt this is only the beginning of the profligate extravagance which distinguishes public bodies on such occasions, and we shall presently hear of sums being voted for decorations and refreshments. Let this egregious address of welcome " be suppressed, and the fifty guineas, which is to be wasted on it, might be given to the Infirmary. The Duke of Clarence and Avon- dale is to be the guest of Lord Sefton at Croxteth during his visit to Lancashire.

Some pity used to be expended on the convict who was put to useless labour; but if it was gall and wormwood for him to be engaged on unproduc- tive work, what must it be to labour for the benefit of his natural enemy the policeman, and to help the progress of works for checkmating his Yellow- criminals? At Dartmoor a cruel fate has compel- led the convicts in the last twelve months to quarry and dress hundreds of tons of granite for the Cen- tral Metropolitan Police Office on the Thames Em- bankment ; while at Parkhurst they have been building a studio for taking their own photographs' to be witnesses against themselves should they ever be re-convicted.

Mr. Hyndman pooh-poohs Sir Charles Dilke's and Mr. Sydney Buxton's adherence to an Eight Hours Bill for miners avid the eight hours rule for munici- palities and Government servants, and clamours for an all-round universal obligatory Eight Hours Bill. All very well, Mr. Elyndman, but how will you get Parliament to look at such a measure for years and years to come? "Force it on candidates," is the reply But the working-men delegates are nearly equally divided on the subject of such a bill as Mr. Hyndman proposes. Moreover, does anybody ima- gine that it would be possible to legislate for any branch of industrial workers without their own express consent and co-operation?

M. Jules Simon makes an energetic appeal to his fellow-countrymen to put an end to the generally absurd but sometimes tragic custom of duelling. "1 should like to know," he says, "what a duel proves beyond the fact that so-and-so had a better fencing-master than somebody else, or else that be was in better condition than his adversary on the day of the encounter. When one of the combatants is killed, what must be the reflections of the victor gig he returns home? Of those two men who went out oriiy- a quarter of an hour ago, one is a corpse, the 6' her j Zmurderer. The provocation must have his conscience can reassure itself been very gfeat ever so little. For time. be will have no sleep. a ion; Every day he is liable to /airlv a woman whom he has made a widow, and cbildron ivhom he has made orphans."

-- -- The British Association, in the course of its long I existence, has been made the subject of many severe attacks, but for venom the following tirade, which appears in the last issue of the " World," must be; pronounced unsurpassed. Mr. Edmund Yates sap —"Two-thirds of the members of the British Asso- ciation are simply sorners, cadgers, and 'dead-beats, who travel third-class to and from the town which iS the association's victim for the year, live at free quarters on its inhabitants, insist on gratuitous ex- cursions with luncheon thrown in, and stickle for a nightly conversazione, the buffet of which they sack without ruth or decency. A British Association ticket is the cheapest investment in the known world—this guttling, this free billet on the abori- gines, this posturing as a savant, all for a guinea! N ay, there is yet more ; for, when at last reluctantly compelled to retire into their normal obscurity, does there not still remain to those loafers and bum- mers of science the joy of vituperating with sour snarling acrimony the place which has given them a week's hospitality."

The Bishop of Ballarat, Victoria, has offered an insult to the Y.M.C.A., which nothing but gore will ever wipe out, lie states that he wants to have no connection with that body "if its effects were simply to create young females of the male sex, and though he liked to see the youths put off, as the Scripture said, the old man, he did not wish them to put on the,old woman." The "Sydney Bulletin," which reports this hard saying of the Bishop's, adds :—" The boneless young person with the heavenly smile and the inch of white sock showing between his pants and his shoes is so mad at this that he has risen with his umbrella in one hand and his golosh in the other, and has placed his milk and his bath-bun on the table in front of him, and had asked in a small voice for an explanation. And if he doesn't get it the chances are that he will let his carnal passions loose and inform his mother about it."

The tendency towards classification has extended from cricket to football, and it is proposed that at the meetings of the Rugby Union certain rules shall be adopted for the regulation of the county championship. Briefly the idea is to divide the country for football purposes into four divisions— north-east, north-west, south-east, and south-west; the first district to include Yorkshire, the second Lancashire, the third Middlesex, and the fourth to be made up of Somersetshire, Devonshire, Glouces- tershire, and the Midland Counties Union. Pre- liminary contests between the counties of every one of the four districts are to be played before Christmas each year, and then the four winners, who are to be considered first-class counties, are to play each other for the championship, This scheme is'the result of the deliberations of the Yorkshire County Committee, to whom, when the proposals of the Rugby Union were negatived at the meeting in March, the task of drawing up a set of iules was entrusted. The scheme is not an attractive one. but the Yorkshiremen, who have won the champion- ship during the two previous years, are sure toonake every attempt to carry it into effect.

A correspondent writes to ask, What has become of the glowworm ! "1 have (he says) been about of late a good deal on the roads and lanes ef the southern countries, and often after dusk, but have never once observed the tiny spark which used to be familiar wmy eye on the banks and sides of ditches. On inquiring of cyclists, I have found them, con- firm my impression that this interesting little crea- tnre is getting very scarce. Gilbert White tells us that in his time the glowworms would come into the parlour of his house at Selborne, attracted by the light of the candles. He adds that by observing two specimens whi6 had been brought from a field to the bank in his garden, he discovered that they have the exemplary habit of putting out their lamps between eleven and twelve. Judging from my recent observation I might almost imagine that they had now put them out altogether. I remem- ber often seeing them in considerable numbers on the sides of the upper road between Winchester and Alresford ; and iirmy boyhood, in hot, dry weather, you could always count on finding the little wan- dering light round about llornsey Wood before that picturesque resort of Londoners came under the dominion of Bumble. Where are they now ? "
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER•2O, 1890

out to the East, by the shipwreck of the "Transit in the Malay Straits he lost everything he possessed in the world except the clothes on his back. Mr. Low, his biographer, says this was the first time. but not the last, he lost his things. When the rebels defeated General Windham and burned Cawnpore, Wolseley, and his brother officers lost the second kit they had provided themselves with in Calcutta; among his losses at Cawnpore were his Legion of Honour and Crimean medals, which were afterwards found on the body of a dead "randy." Again during his absence from England on his Ashantee Campaign, Wolseley had the mis- fortune to lose all his furniture and goods which he had warehoused in the Pantechnicon, in a great fire which in a few hours reduced to ashes that vast building. . _

After the loot of Lucknow an officer gave him a valuable cashmere sham; it was stolen. The men of his company presented him with two large sil- ver bowls. They afterwards shared the same fate. A similar malign influence seems to dog his foot- steps when he makes a voyage. His first journey to China was one long series of disasters, culmina- ting in the foundering of the transport in the Straits of Malacca. When he went to Ashantee the steamer behaved so infamously, that the war cor- respondents on board declared that the voyage out was enough to aecoupt for all the mortality of the West Coast; and when he hurried out to Canada, during the Trent affair, his ship took thirty days in crossing the Atlantic. This is the more notable be- cause Lord Wolseley, unlike that great sea captain Nelson, does not suffer from sea sickness. Like General Joubert, he is a very good general on horse- back, but he hates the sea and life on board ship, which makes it all the more trying when storms persue him as if he were a new Jonah.

HAIRBREADTH 'SCAPES. In such warfare there is still ample room and scope enough for the display of individual heroism. Christopher North lamented that battles had ceased to be interesting when they ceased to be the tussle of contending mobs, like those of the Greeks and Trojans in the Iliad, and became mere movements of an immense machine. The battles in which Lord Wolseley has been engaged were more of the an- tique sort. Othello did not tell Desdemona more marvels—baring the trifling detail of the Anthro- pophagi—than those which have actually occurred in Lord Wolseley's own experience. Of hairbreadth escapes he has had enough to furnish even a hero of one of Ouida's novels. In his first serious action in Burmah nothing but the dccident of falling into a covered pit as he was leading a storming party against the Burmese position saved him from des- truction. In the second attempt, he and his,brother officer, who were the first to enter the enemy's works, were both shot down together. Both were struck in the left thigh, each by a large iron-jingall ball. His companion bled to death in a few minutes. Wolseley, although for months he hovered between life and death, recovered, thanks to a magnificent constitution, which has stood him in good stead at every turn in his career. But it was in the Crimea, that charnel-house of death, that he was most severely mauled. Mr. Lowe says of his escape from the perils of the siege ; During its progress Captain Wolseley was Wounded severely on the 30th August, and slightly on the 10th ol April, and the 7th of June. On the 15th of Feb- ruary his coat was pierced by a ball; on the 10th of April a round shot struck the embrasure at which he was working and his trousers were cut; and on the 7th of June a ball passed through his forage cap from the peak to the back, knocking it off his head. It may be said without exaggeration that he bore a charmed life, for at the termination of the siege, of three messes of four members each he was the only remaining officer in the Crimea, all the others having been killed or forced to leave through wounds.

ADVENTURES AT SEBASTOPOL. Men were killed all round him. On one occasion when he was giving orders to two sappers in the trenches, "suddenly a roundshot took off one man's head and drove his jawbone into the other man's face, to which it adhered, bespattering the party with blood." Here is one little episode of his ex- periences in the quarries before Sebastopol : Between the assaults made by the Russians tore- take the work i he busied himself with building tip, on the reverse side of the quarries, a little parapet composed of anything he could lay his hands on, amen; the chief ingredients be;ng the bodies of the fallen friends and foes indiscriminately, the latter thus afford- ing in death the welcome protection they would have denied while living. So overpowered was he with the exertions of the last twenty-four hours, and the strain upon hia faculties, that in the morn- ing when the fighting ended he fell down outside the quarries, and lay there among a number of dead bodies, himself having the appearance of one num- bered with the dead. So thought an officer of his regiment, who, passing by,. found his friend lying on a heap of slain covered with blood. Although he had not reported himself wounded, Wolseley had been hit in the thigh by bullet from a canis- ter shot, which tore his trousereand caused consi- derable loss of blood. "lIE'S A DEAD. trA!" This, however, was a less serious affair than his wound in the advanced sap on the 3fash of August. The Russians made a sortie, .and for a moment, after capturing the advanced saprharli been driven out again, and Wolseley, with two flappers, was busy superintending the repair of the mischief they had done, when suddenly a round *hot dashed into the middle of the group : The round shot had struck the gabionovirich was full of stones, and striking its contents-vvitn terri- fic violence,, instantaneously killed the peer fellows by his side, the heaxl of one being taken' off; while the other was disembowelled. Wolseley wae dandled to the ground;.whe.re he lay' senseless for a time. After a time he rallied and was, able to totter tothe dbetor's hut;-where•he was laid down unconscious. "'He's a derlintietrial the doctor; This roused Wolseley, who, tanning: in his blood said : "1 worth &good marry dead menTet.?' Wolse- ley'S head and body presented a shocking appear- ance. His features were. not distlivuishible as those of a human being, while bloodiffewed from innumerable woundaeausedi by the stones by- which he had been struck. Sharp fragmentt. were' em- bedded all over-his face, and his left cheek had beer' almost cut away:. The•doctor fancied, after/robing the wound, that his jawbone was shattered,. but Wolseley made- him pull cut the substance in his mouth, when a large stone. came away.% The-sur- geon then liftedup and stitched the cheek, Both ,his eyes were completely dosed, and the inktrY 'done to one of them was so serious that- the- sight .has been permanently lost.- Not a sgpare inch of ,his face' but waabattered.and cut about,. whTha his .body was wounded all over, lust as though • he. had ;been peppered with small shot. Ile had. received 'also a severe wound on hie-right leg, so. that both his limbs had now been injured. The 'wound itra the :left thigh received in Blirmali rendered him ertghtly He• passed some weeks inu. cave, as need the sight of both lus-eyes•was too muchinj to subject them to the-light: While he was pent up ha thio gloomy cavern, meditating on the. seia Pros- pect of being totally' blind for the remainder sr his life, news arrived of the fallof Sebastowoh ins antinal. are not a soldier, and have not attemptpd to deal with Lord Worseley from a military point of view. He is more interesting to his countrymen as a picturesque and commanding personality -than as a mere man of the sword, -Yet even the nsoet OUt- and-out Peace man cannot refrain altogether from admiring the caps.city, the resource, the energy, and the intelligence of the man who has.for so many-1 years been the brain of the British army. Nor cut% even the most envious- among hi a detractors deny.' that there is no living general to whom the natiom would so instinctively turn as to Lord Wolseley th [, aver—which Heaven forbid—we were•to be threats- 'cued with invasion or to be seriously involved in European war. If for a year or two he is allowed i to pass into comparative retirement at Dublin, tis anly because in these piping times of peace' the public can afford him leisure to finish his Life of arlhorough. But it is not a very hazardous pre- diction that,, in certain very possible eventualities, Lord Wolseley will return to the Ranger's House at Greenwich, not as Comraander-in-Chief•of ths Aaany in Ireland, but as Commander-inXhief a all the Forces of the Crown.

div.head: LORD WOLSELEY.
div.p: LORD WOLSELEY.
The subject of the character sketch in the "Review of Reviews" for September is Lord Wolseley. We take the following extracts from it :

On the 30th of September Lord Wolseley will cease to be Adjutant-General of the British Army, and on the Ist of October will take over the duties of Commander-in-Chief of Her Majesty's forces in Ireland. Sir Redvers Buller will succeed Lord Wolseley at the War Office. Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar will make room for Lord Wolseley at Dublin. The change is one of more than merely departmental interest for it indicates the conviction that prevails in high places that the peace of the world is secure. Had there been any war clouds ou the horizon, our ablest soldier would not have been relegated to the reapeetable obscurity of the Irish Commandership. No rule of five years' tenure of office would have been allowed to remove from the War Office the officer who for the last twenty years has been the brain of the service.

A FAMOUS RECORD. Look for a moment at the cycle described by Lord Wolseley between the March, 1852, when he left Lis Irish home, a raw ensign, and October, 1800. when he returns to Ireland as Commander-in-Chief of Her Majesty's forces. The mere list of his appointments is more eloquent OMB any rhetoric 185. Second Burmese War—Ensign. 1854. Siege of Sebastopol—Lieut., Captain. 1857. Ordered to China. Wrecked near Singa- pore. 1857. India. Suppression of Mutiny—Lieu.-Col. V.C. 1860. Chinese War. Mission to Nanbin. 1861. Canada. First Assistant, then Deputy, Quartermaster-Master General. 1870. Red River Expedition—K.C. M.G. 1871. Assistant-Adjutant-General at War Office. 3873-4. Ashantee War—Major-General, K.C.B. 1874. Inspector-General Auxiliary Forces. 1875. Governor of Natal. 1878. Governor of Cyprus. 1879. Zulu War—Commander-in-Chief and High Commissioner, South Africa. /882. Egyptian Campaign. Tel-el-Kebiat.. Peer- age. 1884. The War in the Soudan. 1885. Adjutant-General at War-Office. 1890. Commander-in-Chief of Forces in Ireland. What a record ! With the exception of Australia, Lord Wolseley has served in every continent, and faced almost every description of human and natural obstacle. il.or is this career by any means - concluded. Who can say how soon he may not have to complete this universality of his service by la mission to advise the military authorities oZ•1 Federated Australasia? Yet in all this Lord Wolseley is but a type of the British soldier. He is at the too ; Tommy Atkins is at the bottom. Rat they share the same lot, in having the whole wiJe• world as their parade ground, and all mankind as, their next-door neighbour.

LUCK AND ILL-12TX. To write a biography of Lord Wolseley would, be to, write a history of the British Empire for the last forty years. As a commander he has been singu- larly fortunate. His record is unstained by a single reverse in the field. Wherever be went fortune smiled on his flag, and promozion followed as a matter of course. One great misfortune alone darkens the brilliance of his record—a misfortune . for which he was not responsible, and which be did all that lay in mortal power to avert. He -was too late to save Gordon. But the blame in not starting ' in time was not his, but that of those wha, month after month, turned a deaf ear to the urgent repre- sentations which reached them, from the War Office and from the country as to the necessity for action. With that exception, everything which he touched prospered. It is careers like his which lead men to believe in a lucky star. Curiously enough, his luck in the field was I colipled by a persistent ill-luck in other matters. Some men go through the hottest battles without a scratch. Lord Welseley was wounded—sometimes very seriously—in almost every action in which he fought. Still more curious and persistent has been the misfortune which dogged him in the minor matter of the loss of his kit. In this matter some fatality seemed to attend him. When he first went

div.head: EXILED GITARDS.
div.p: THE EXILED GITARDS.

REPORTED INSUBORDINATION.. The Quards in Bermuda seem in every sense of the word to be exiles. According to a private letter of a cor- respondent in the service, the greatest discontent prevails among the men at the way they are treated, and there is every probability of k serious revolt. The correspondent, writing from Bermuda on August 20, says the authorities are very strict with the Guards. They were not per- mitted to leave the Bowling Island, and consequently were confined within an area of half a square mile. Their only recreation has been fishing. They had already got tired of this, and had " nothing in the world else to do." Already eight of the men were in the guard-room for insubordination, and another " kick-out " was not at all unlikely.

CHAPTER XXIIL AFTER. MANY YEARS. Sim 'MUIR gained the victory over the malcon- tents, and was well pleased. It requires little explanation to understand that when the men whc had undermined the viaduct were obliged, by the force of public opinion, to cross it in the first train they held back, and "owned up." Explanations and finally confessionsibrought the matter to a crisis. Indignation fell upon those wha had so barbarously planned such wholesale destrue. tion, and the discovery did more to turn the men to their allegiance than all the offers of Sir Walter. Even in the strike the spirit of fair play obtained with the majority of the men, and when the larder began to be empty and the wives and children clamorous for bread, the workmen remembered that weekly and sure wages were preferable to a sliding scale of eociety's funds. They had come out to please a few agitators—they went in again to please themselves. This danger over, all went smoothly and well. It must not be imagined, however, that all the necessary arrangements were completed in a day or a week, any more than Rome was built in the same space of time. There were interviews, and meetings, and discussions-of a more or less stormy nature, but nothing of such importance to this nar- rative occurred to warrant our describing the various stages of the negociations. The " shops " again were busy, the traffic was re- sumed, and those who stood out with extravagant demands for concessions which were impossible to be obtained, had the satisfaction of Boeing their places filled up by strangers, and with the tacit approval of those who remained underl,Sir Walter's juris- diction. I 'But no more was heard of the strike, and it; passed away into the limbo of forgotten events. Time passed rapidly, and the three young people who will concern us a good deal until the close of the narrative, were growing up more or less to the satisfaction of their parents. We will see how they have:been progressing all this time. It may be remembered that when Sir Walter and Lady Watson were introduced to the reader, they were considering the probability of a union between their little child, Lily. then an infant, with the son and heir of the Thanes, who had also but lately arrived in England, or indeed in the world at all. Sir Walter had looked upon the birth. of an heir to the Deane property as specially intended ,by an over-ruling Providence to match with his daughter, Lily, but like a prudent speculator, and one who did not wish to depend too much upon the interference Of Heaven in mundane affairs, he had a chance in reserve in his son. Edward Watson was a fine youth, and rapidly developing towards manhood. Had Sir William and Lady Deane's child been a girl, Sir Walter would have made the alliance equally possible by bringing forward his second string. As it was, however, the pretty Lily was desti hed to be the bride of the heir of the house of Deane. P.ltThere was, of course, no objection made to this proposal by the Deanes, although both Sir William, then absent in India, and his wife stipulated that the match should never be hinted at before the children. They were to be kept in total ignorance of any such arrangement for their benefit. If affection resulted from intimacy in childhood—well; if not, events must take their own course. Lily Watson was a very taking child. She had brown hair and blueeyes,wasbeautl'ully proportioned, and was really pretty. Her disposition was particu- larly sweet. She was thoroughly unselfish and very willing to assist in anything in which she fancied she could be of use. She was sometimes inclined to have bar own way, but, as a rule, her respect for parental authority quite overcame her own wishes, and she obeyed with every :appearance of willingness and

pleasure. There was another girl with whom Miss Watson had become acquainted, and had she not been the daughter of a person M the lower walks of fife, any casual observer, even, would have pronounced the chid a member of the aristocracy, or, at any rate, of gentle blood. This young gill was the daughttr of Mrs. Lay- ton, who' by favour of Lady Deane, inhabited a small cottage at the outskirts of the village known generally as Watson-town, from the grand per- sonage who' had built the cottages, the church, and the schoolse and was good enough to permit the Pest Office authorities to have an agent in the grocer's shop; tor was not Sir Walter Watson the autocrat of the district? Minnie Layton was a decided contrast to her m.ing neighbour. Lily, as becomes a lily, was fair; me was dark, with beautifully-chiselled fee- trses, pale, and—to some people's ideas—delicate- looking; but the clear' fine skin showed no traces of illness or languor. The bright dark eyes flashed brilliantly, and no symptoras of dulness or lassitude was., observable in the upright carriage and firm' tread of the' pale, and somewhat haughty, beauty of the cottage child, who bore no resem- blance to Mrs. Layton. Minnie, apparently, as, she was really quite un- conscious of her appearance, at the age of fifteen was tte very striking t girl, and when she and Lily met end walked across- the path together, as they -occasionally did, the' cottage-girl had really the advantage of the young lady of the "Towers," 'though' both were beautiful Lily, somewhat shorter than her companion and less robust, with her fair- hair and blue eyes, was a .eempeste contrast, yet in harmony with the rounded -figure and budding womanhood of the stouter Minnieewhose limbs, as-seen under her short, cheap, but always neat, frocks, might have served as models :for a sculptor. Was it any wonder that. Edward Watson fell in love with Minnie Layton,.boy-fashion, at first sight, And carried her presents to, the cottage, until even Luceebegan to think the- lad's visits were getting marked, and preventing her scheme from maturing'? And what was her scheme for which she had planned and toiled and humiliated herself in her own eyes for the sake of revenge upon an absent man.? She knew Sir William Deane's pride and his ladvil haughty temper, and regard to birth. That pridb of ancestry, the creedwhich—above all earthly things at any rate—absoreecl the attention of the proud lady-like wife and the aristocratic husband, was Brian. It was the first- article of Sir William's belief in hiefellow men. To be born in the purple, or at any rate wrapped in.it aa in swaddling clothes, was the prominent idea in his mind, and was re- flected in his wife's. We can then readily conceive how great a blow it would be to their pride if once to find that the heir to the grand estate and the future bearer of an honoured name was not only a very common-place, but an exceedingly unpleasant, lad. Such in truth the heir was. How he picked up such vulgar taste and habits his lady mother could not understand. It was not in conseqpence of his occasional asso- ciation with Edward Watson7s friends—the engine. drivers, for they as a body were, at any rate in his presence, well-spoken men, and by no means vulgar in one sense of the term, They respected themselvbe, and no language of questionable import was heard' when Edward or hisdriend, Marmaduke Deane, were, on the loeomotives.4 Marmadetke, the heir, was not a very aristocratic peyson. He was of dark complexion, and boasted! wiry hair of a bristling habit, a low forehead with thick eyebrows, and the greater developments of the skull were, at the back, partaking more of the animal than of the intellectual attributes of human, nature. He had rather a cruel mouth, but a firm chin. He was short and broadly made; hazel eyes, which in some lights looked grey, but when he smiled his face lighted up very pleasantly, and was attractive till he re ay:eel into his usual halfesullen demeanour. He was not a youth one wealdlancy at first sight, nor one of whom it would be advisable to make ap enemy. - _ Edward Watson was a fine, frank, open-minded lad, rather gushing, wearing his heart toomuch upon his sleeve; very proud, very sensitive; gentle as a woman, deferential to women as a ecldier of the old school, and with an ever-ready sympathy which won kim hosts of friends, and" when he grows up," it was prophesied, would "get him into het water," as an attribute likely to create an interest in female hearts which he could not reciprocate, perhaps. These were the four young people who had growl, up in the neighbourhood while the events we have narrated and many others, which we have not space to relate, were going on around them. Lady Deane had never forgotten the remark of °Edward Watson concerning hlinnie's likeness to het husband; and although as the girl advanced in yeart and assumed the household duties and the positior of respectable poverty, she lost in a measure tha likeness, there was in Edward's eyes a mystery con. nected with this girl, who was as much at home in his society as in Collier's cottage, and she was there very often too,

George Collier on his side was apparently devoted to Minnie, and nothing she wanted was ever denied her by the good-natured inspector, who occasionally, when the service demanded it, 'was as ready as ever to lend a hand in the signal-box, or to superintend a shunting operation as of old. In the country in- specters at the smaller stations are not grandees, nor do they always wear uniform and lace. Collier and Lucy met frequently as one will sup- pose, and gossips said that he was waiting for the widow's consent to crown her happiness. It was whispered that Collier and Lucy had never quite forgotten the old days, and many of the knowing olive smiled and said that Mrs. Layton would be Collier's wife, and the beautiful Minnie become by that marriage what she already might be supposed to be—the signalman's daughter. George Collier had changed too. He was still active and good-humoured as ever, but his hair was grey now, though in years he was young. The cause ot this aged_ appearance will be related in the next chapter.
CHAPTER XXIV.

THE SIGNALMAN'S DAUGHTER.' MRS. LAYTON'S residence was a small white house, surrounded at that spring time by apple trees in full rosy blossom, and amongst the trees the figure of Minnie might often be perceived on the look-out for "Uncle George," as she had been taught to call Collier. On the occasion we have in our minds, the inspee- tor came up the path, and his quick eyes soon detected the little Dryad amongst the trees. Minnie ran forward in her own childish manner—an inno- cent and confiding manner it was, too—and, throw- ing her arms round " Uncle George's" neck, kissed him heartily. The girl was delighted to see her friend, and con- fidingly clutching his arm with both hands, led him lovingly towards the cottage. "May I go with you next time you do any sig- nals Uncle George ?" "Well, deary, we must see what your mother says about it. Don't you get crossin' the motels. That good-for-nothing fellow, Stanley, nearly got killed a couple of days ago." "I was going to say serve him right," said Lucy, who had heard the latter portion of the inspector's speech. "But how did he escape ? " "He didn't deserve to," continued Collier. "He was piloting a party of ladies and gentlemen of an antiquary lot that come down hero for an excursion. And he got them into the little tunnel, declaring no train was due. He was rather "slowed," and they hadn't gone far when a down train approached them. The lines are laid in separate arches, as you know." "I know," said Lucy, thoughtfully. "Well, to make a long story short, the people saw the train, and cut back as fast as they could. The driver he whistled and screamed, and there was a bit of a to-do. But all the ladies and gentlemen got out just in time. Stanley didn't." "How did he escape then?" asked Minnie. " He laid down between the railsT for tipsy as he was he had sense enough to know he couldn't get out as-quick as the rest, so he lay flat between the metals, and the train passed over him." "And wasn't he hurt, uncle ? " asked the girl, who took quite an interest in the narrative—which by the way is perfectly true. "Well, not to say hurt. The engine in passing over him dropped a fine live coal upon his back and spoilt hi Sunday sit-upons; " said Collier, laugh- ing. "He must have had a nice time with that cinder. If he had moved he:would have been killed." Poor man," said the sympathetic Minnie. Her mother and the inspector laughed heartily at her sympathy. "A good job," said Collier. "But it has, he says,. cured him of liquor. If so, a very good job, I say.. But I came up for a cup o' tea; can ye give us a cup, Lucy ? " "Why, of course, George. Are you going on thg old service this evening?" "Well, between you and me, I am. I can't altogether give it up; and now Tom is away, I've volunteered to work his time. There's a something about that signal-cabin that will never lose its charms. Ah, Lucy, I often think of the old days and the times there was—" "What happened then?" inquired Minnie. "Any accidents ? " "Hush, child, it was afore you were born," said Mrs. Layton, sharply. "Get the tea ready." Minnie, accustomed to obey without questions,. retired to look after the evening meal. "I think we needn't rake up all the old times, George," said Lucy, after a ,pause. "You know that it cannot be altered now.' "Why cant it?" said Collier. "Igit bec,ause I don't alter? Is it because I'Ve loved ye ever since I first knew ye, and I am now nigh on forty years of age, and you are—" "Never mind what I am,"'replied Lucy. "Age don't count much with me. But how can I tell? George, look here. You musn't be coming up here so much. People will talk." "Let them talk. Ye know what I want," replied Collier, doggedly. "Now, is.it to be, or is it not ? Will you marry me in a year if ye don't hear that Layton is alive? It's—let ma-see—it's more than sixteen years since ye ran off with him, and nigh broke my heart." "Oh, George, don't; please don't." "And here ye come to sit right down afore my face for reasons of your own, I suppose." "Yes, I have reasons—strong reasons," said Lucy, firmly. "-Afore my face, and expect me to keep at the other end of the parish. Why it isn't in human nature. And now, Lucy, if he don't turn up in a year from now, will ye give me an answer proper?" "-I will, George," she replied; "will that content you?' Next spring you shall have adecided answer." A. "yes," mind. None of your playin' round. You're as clever as a cat, and as-wary." "That's not very love-like, at fall events," retorted Mrs. Layton, laughing. " Oh,..George Collier !" "This is, then," said Collier,. catching her in his arms, and before she was aware of it he had kissed her once, twice, thrice on the cheeks and rosy lips. "flat is, and very consoling into th 3 bargain," he added, Lucy felt herself flushed and angry. , "If you attempt such liberties again, Mr. Collier,' she said; " I'll just tell you " "Tea's ready," said Mimed° at this juncture, and the tame termination to her 'mother's sentence, half assumed in its anger, made them laugh, and the stornuwas over. "I'll go down and see you this evening, uncle. Mother is going up to the Hall.about some needle- work.'" "Mind howyou come theree" said Collier; "don't. trip over the wires and get run over." "-Stanley wasn't, so why should I be ?" said; the girl, upon whose mind the incident in the tunnel. had apparently made a great' impression. " come as soon as I can, and we wilLhave a nice talk. You can tell me the story about the runaway engine and. young Mr. Watson. "You like that, do your said George, as. ho patted her head. ' "Yes, uncle, I think he is such a nice young man. —so kind-looking and, brave' I'm sure. Hespoke to me the other day, and asked how I was getting. on at; school." "Did he?" said the inspector. "Was that all?" "Oh, no! Bat he didn't say meek more to, me because mother came in, but we shook hands, after. T,hat was all." "Very well,, and, now you wan4-.to temeinto the signal-box because you think Mr, Watson;willdrive an engine past it?' , "Nonsense, Uncle George. 11l want- to, see you and the trains in.the avening—just for an hour. I Me the railway so much." "All right; come along if you,like. She'll be all right, Lucy.," he called out. Come along." They walked along in the gathering gloom, and Collier's thoughts carried him, back to the days when he had wandered first uith Lucy Raymond as quickly and innocently as he was now with Minnie; but what a change had come over the scene since then, and what a change had come over. lacy, too! He stepped nes the ladder and entered the box. Minnie, with childish glee, running' up and down and, even ocross the rails in the darkness, like a restless fairy. Then she would come and tease bet, uncle, pretending to pull over the levers or tap the signal instruments, laughing and chattering merrily all the time. She dared him to a game at last, and he, mere te 'watch her than for her amusement, came out on the ladder, when she jumped quickly down and ran into the little bit of garden by the line. "Comae and catch me if you can, uncle," she cried. Ile (bated after her, but she eluded him, and ran into the railway behind a lamp, which, put low down for the points, dazzled Collier, and hid her in the shadows, its light, by contrast, making them deeper than usual, apparently. "Minnie, I won't have any more of this. Como up stairs. Remember the train is nearly due." "it passed up long ago," said the girl. "You catch me, and I will come then." "But there's the parliamentary 'to shunt at the sheds below for the special for the boat train to- night. Don't be silly. It's a pretty quick train, and you are not far from the points." "I'll take care," cried Minnie, in tha distance. "Now, don't be afraid. lam coining." - -

To the signalman's horrii,-the " gni-tins" of the bell in the cabin then announced the approach of the train, and he calling to Minnie, ran up, and not daring to " check " the train, gave "all clear." He hurried out of the box and told her the train was coming. She laughed, and farther off than ever she stood in the darkness. Then suddenly, aware of the danger, she came running back. The lamps of the approaching train which was to be shunted shone upon her, and Collier was in a terrible state of mind. If he let the train pass into , the coal siding close by he would possibly sacrifice , several lives, for the driver did not expect to stop till he reached the sheds half a mile farther on. What was he to do—to save the girl standing in the way of the train, or cause a fearful loss of life? He shouted to Minnie, put up a prayer for help and guidance, and let the " parly " go. On it came thundering, the two headdights gleaming along the track, the child at the points feel- ing quite safe as the train, she thought, would pass her by, and recklessly daring the near approach, for the satisfaction of seeing it turn away. But it didn't. A loud shriek of the whistle' and then, before she had time to run away, it bore down upon her, the towering engine quite enveloping her in a halo of light and steam. The train passed on in safety, the passengers little thinking of the nairow escape the wretched, heartbroken signalman had given them at the ex- pense of his life's happiness. The pulling of a lever would have saved his child, as he had learned to call her, but would have wrecked the train. Duty had won the day; but oh at what a price what an awful price! There was in Collier's mind a feeling, then npper- most, that ill luck pursued him with relentless energy. Nearly every year, since he had been entrusted with the signals some dread catastroplu. had happened, or only just been escaped. Abnost his first trial in the box had resulted in an accident, and Lucy Raymond was mixed up in it all—until no, Minnie, the child ho loved so dearly, had been

killed! What would Lucy say? What story could he tell? He could only blame himself for her logs, and yet had he acted otherwise and turned the train lot° the siding, he would probably have had a train full of dead and wounded men and women with children all as dear to their parents and friends as Minnie was to her mother and to him. Yes, he had acted rightly, but he was to blame, Indefensibly to blame,. for letting the girl run about the line. Yet how could he have anticipated her? Stupefied, almost unconscious, caring nothing for train warnings, Collier stood grasping the lever, by. means of which he had guided the train aright, ana wrecked his own peace of mind for ever. "Better had died myself, than let that innocen! be killed. Oh, Lord,. help me to bear tbjs stroke' he murmured. Suddenly a voice close beside him said laughingly "So, you see,:you didnit catch me after all, 'Uncle George!" Gracious Heavens—had his prayer been beard! He scarcely dared to' breathe. He feared to turn 1111 head till the laughter broke out again, and he lookea round, holding tightly to the lever. • Yes there was Minnie, dusty and flushed and a dis- hevelled but bright and loving as ever, as she rushe into his arms, and sobbing, begged his when she saw the appearance of her kind " who fell half fainting against the dosk, poi° '- trembling. "Did you think I was killed, dear uncle? Indee4 lam sorry I went away. lam quite safe." "Thank God, my darling. Thank God. better now; but yew gave me a terrible Minnie. I thought ye were killed and torn to flow in in Heaven's name did ye escape?" "l did as Stanley did," replied the girl. I saw the train wastrel going on the siding, laY - •
down !" It was true. She had thrown herself flat on the permanent way, and the train had passed over her' be had not received a scratch, and was none the
worse. But when George Collier got up next mornin. g Ile perceived that his hair had turned quite greY—t/1 result of the terrible tension of mind the previoul evening. (To be continued.)

ST. HELENS REVISION COURT.

The revision of the lists of voters for the borough f St. Helens was resumed before Mr. .J. T. Foard, re- Vising barrister, at the Town Hall, on Friday. Messrs. J. P. Mearns and J. Bain again represented the Liberals, and Messrs. J. 0. Swift and W. Lamb 'oPpeared for the Conservatives. A QUESTION OF DISTANCE. Mr. Robert C. Goldsmith claimed a vote in respect to 411 office in Hardshaw-st., and was objected to by the Liberals. He said he lived at Edge-lane, Liverpool, and ' tbe seven miles radius from the borough boundary had been measured to a point 300 yards beyond his house.— Mr. Mearns said a surveyor had measured it on the ordnance map and found it was out of the boundary. He remarked that there was a difference as to the dis- tance, and he asked the revising barrister to allow the matter to stand over until a measurement was made,— Mr. Swift said the objection to Mr. Goldsmith had been That of incorrect description and he did not think the question of distance could be gene into. A few hours later the question was again brought forward. It was nederstood that the map had been measured in the mean- , bine and that the residence was found to be over seven miles. Mr. Swift, however, raised an objection to the Vote being struck off on the ground that the issued objec- tion against Mr. Goldsmith was that of incorrect descrip- and the question of distance could not be gone into. --His Honour said it was provided by the statute that he should not enter anybody on the register who was not ' qualified to be on the register as a voter on the 15th July. Mr. Goldsmith was not qualified on that date as he re- , aided beyond the seven miles, and therefore the vote must be struck off.—Mr. Swift: Will your honour give roe a case on that point ?—The Revising Barrister: No. I am quite right.—Mr. Swift: My contention is purely • a technical one. lam bound to admit, for the purpose Of this argument, that Mr. Goldsmith is not entitled to be registered. He lives beyond seven miles, but what- ' ever the words of the Act of Parliament may be it does Cot, in my opinion make the slightest difference. My contention in contesting the correctness of your honour's decision is that it does not depend upon that at all. I !ay that under the section to which I did refer your honour is not entitled to take notice of any grounds of objection other than those stated in the formal notice, • and the only other power you have is that given you ender the sub-section.—The Revising Barrister (inter- rupting) : I have also power enforced upon me by another statute to act with respect to persons not duly ' qnalified.—Mr. Swift said he was bound to give his honour notice of appeal.—The Revising Barrister informed ,Mr. Swift that he could raise the question on the follow- ing day if he wished.—Mr. Swift said he would then ' leave it over. .

THE CURATE OF SUTTON. •The Rev. Granville B. Thurston,cara.te of St. Nicholas's Church, Sutton, claimed a lodger's vote for two furnished rooms upstairs and one room downstairs, at 43, Ditch- hillock. He said he had lodged there for 15 months and Paid 15s. per week for the apartments.—Mr. Mearns naked what the house was assessed at, and the assistant everseer (Mr. J. Kitchen) replied that it was assessed at £1.5 10s.—Mr. Mearns remarked that it did not seem a 'iery big assessment for furnished apartments at 15s. per Week.—me Revising Barrister said everything appeared to be right, and allowed to vote. A CONSERVATIVE COMPLAINT. div.head: TURKISH OUTRAGES IN ARMENIA
div.p: THE TURKISH OUTRAGES IN ARMENIA
A PRIEST SHOT IN A CATHEDRAL.

A Constantinople telegram says that at the Armenian Cathedral of Boum Kapon on Saturday a priest was shot and severely wounded. It is believed the outrage was committed by the author of the previous Tuesday's tragedy.
GERMAN PRINCELETS AND THEIR CREDITORS.

Prince Albrecht of Waldeck Pyrmont, cousin of the Duchess of Albany, has made an offer to his creditors to pay them 30 per cent, of their claims. The Princess Albrecht has offered the same compromise to her per- sonal creditors. Both the Prince and Princess owe £20,000.

div.head: TWO MEN SCALDED TO DEATH.
div.p: TWO MEN SCALDED TO DEATH.

On Saturday afternoon a frightful accident occurred down a coal mine at Hebburn-on-Tyne. Two black- smiths, named respectively William Gates and Thomas Rawlings, were mending a pumping engine, when there was asudden outrush of steam from a valve, and they were both immediately scalded to death,

div.head: ANOTHER APPEAL BY MR. W. O'BRIEN.
div.p: ANOTHER APPEAL BY MR. W. O'BRIEN.

r Mr. Rime, of Bedford Row House, 'solicitor to Mr. William O'Brien, M.P.' has, it is said, served on Messrs. Nicholson and Co., of Parliament-st., solicitors to the Marquis of Salisbury,the petition of appeal by Mr. O'Brien to the House of Lords against the decision of the Court of Appeal in the action brought by Mr. O'Brien at Man- chester claiming damages for slander in a speech made by theaaoble Marquis at Watford.

div.head: SMOKE NUISANCE.
div.p: THE SMOKE NUISANCE.

At the Royton Police Court, on Wednesday, the Butter Green Spinning Company and four other companies were summoned for permitting a smoke nuisance. After evidence had been given it was agreed to take the de- cision in the first case as applying to the others. The magistrates were of opinion that black smoke had been emitted from the defendants' chimneys in such a quan- tity as to be a nuisance, and they made an order that the nuisance should be abated within two months. Dr. Patterson, medical officer for Chadderton, who was the complainant, asked the Bench to allow four months, and they consented.

div.head: 'THE O'SHEA. DIVORCE SUIT.
div.p: 'THE O'SHEA. DIVORCE SUIT.

The" Irish Times" London correspondent says r—Mr. John Dillon, M.P., is to be subpcenaed to give evidence by Messrs. Wontner, the solicitors acting for Captain O'Shea in the divorce suit he brought against Mrs. O'Shea, and in which the hon. member for Mayo's leader, Mr. Parnell, figures as co-respondent. This, it is anticipated, will prevent Mr. Dillon from political touring in the States, in company with Mr. William O'Brien. The startling subpcena will throw the whole arrangements into con- fusion. Mrs. O'Shea has made the disclosure ordered by the court -ef certain documents, and has thus avoided a committal for contempt which was threatened by Mr. Justice Dannen.

div.head: 'SHOCKING FATALITY AT LEEDS.
div.p: 'SHOCKING FATALITY AT LEEDS.

A domestic servant employed at the Hope and Anchor Inn. Call-lane, Leeds, has died from revolver shots fired at her by the nephew of her employer. The latter, Mr. Webb, had recently bought a revolver, and was showing it to the company. He put in a cartridge to show the easy working, and forgot to take it out. He then handed it to Fred Fiddler, his nephew, aged 18, employed as a tapster, with instructions to take it upstairs. He was going to do so when he met the deceased, and playfully pointing the revolver said " Get my dinner, or I'll shoot you." The revolver went off, and she was shot in the head. She was removed to the Infirmary, where she died. She is only known as " Eliza," having only been in Leeds three weeks. Fiddler is in custody.

div.head: TERRIBLE MINING DISASTER.
div.p: TERRIBLE MINING DISASTER.
LOSS OF TWENTY-FOUR LIVES.

COLOGNE, TIIESDAY.—The " Koelnische Yolks Zeitung " reports that a serious miningdisaster has occurred at the IMaybach Pit, near St. Wendel. Of 400 men who des- cended the shaft about 150 are said to be missing. SLARBRTJOK, TIIESDAY.-1 most sericus explosion of fire damp occurred yesterc.lay afternoon in the Maybach Pit, near St. Wendel. Up to the present twenty-three bodies have been brought to the surface. One miner is still missing. The explosion took plase in the second gallery of the eastern main workings. LATER.—Another body has been recovered by the relief parties who descended the Maybach Mine, making a total of twenty-four deaths. Although 350 men were in the pit, nobody else was injured. The disaster is now attributed to a premature explosion during blasting operations.

div.head: SERIOUS RIOT AMONGST NAVVIES.
div.p: SERIOUS RIOT AMONGST NAVVIES.

A serious riot among the navvies engaged on the Thirlmere Water Works took place at Lupton. on Mon- day. The navvies had been drinking at the Plough Inn, near the pipe tank, when, owing to some dispute upon Irish topics, they divided themselves into sides of Eng- lish and Irish and had a desperate fight. There were about sixty en each side. Several navvies received seri- ous wounds, and one Irishman is not expected to recover. Information has reached Keudal that the disturbances between the English and Irish navvies were resumed on Tuesday. The English contingent had been joined by quarrymen at Hutton Roof, and according to the latest reports the Englishmen, 300 strong, armed with all kinds of weapons, were drivingthe Irish before them. It was stated that mans' of the combatants had received seri- ous injuries. All the available police at Kendal have been despatched to the scene.

div.head: QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.
div.p: THE QUEEN OF ROUMANIA.

Her Majesty the Queen of Roumania arrived on Mon- day at Penrhyn Castle, Bangor, on a visit to Lord and Lady Penrhyn. In the course of the day she proceeded to Carnarvon, and was received by the Mayor (Mr. Issard Davies), who, on behalf of the Town Council, pre- sented her with an address. In the evening the Eisteddfod &Mr, under the conductorship of Dr. Roland Roger, organist of Bangor Cathedral, sang by command before her Majesty at Penrhyn Castle. Her Majesty the Queen of Roumania, accompanied by Lord and Lady Penrhyn, on Tuesday drove from Penrhyn Castle, Bangor, to Bethesda, six miles distant, where she paid a visit to the extensive slate quarries owned by Lord Penrhyn. She was conducted over the workings by Mr. Young, the chief manager, and watched with interest the various processes of converting the rock into saleable slate. . _

The Queen of Roumania arrived at Kingstown from Holehead on Thursday evening, and proceeded thence to Bray, where she had a hearty welcome and was pre- sented with an address by the Town Commissioners.

div.head: DUKE OF CLA.RENCE IN WALES.
div.p: THE DUKE OF CLA.RENCE IN WALES.

The Duke of Clarence and Avondale visited Cardiff to opert the new Grangetown bridge, which has tben built at a cost of £50,000. The streets, which were elaborately decorated, were crowded with spectators, from whom his Royal Highness met with a veil, hearty reception. Following the ceremony at the bridge, which passed off very successfully, the Duke was present at a luncheon at Park Hall, where he proposed the toast of " Prosperity to Cardiff," and referred to the rapid growth of the town in recent years, and to its excellent system of docks, which he had had an opportunity of Inspecting. His Royal Highness afterwards received the freedom of the borough at the hands of the Mayor, and then left for Crickhowell. _ _ _

The Duke of Clarence and Avondale on Thursday laid the foundation-stone of a new Public Hall at Crickho- I well. In reply to an address of welcome, he alluded to the interest which had been displayed in the welfare of all classes ot her Majestys subjects during the Queen's reign, and expressed the pleasure it gave him to lay the foundation stone of a building which would be of such lio the inhabitants. He took his leave of Wales WWI the conviction that nowhere throughout her Majesty's dominions had the Queen more loyal or devoted subjects. His Royal Highness left Glauusk last night for Wirnoral.

div.head: REPORTED ASSAULT ON PRINCE
div.p: THE REPORTED ASSAULT ON PRINCE
GEORGE OF WALES.
"AN IMPUDENT INVENTION."

NEW YORK, TUF.SDAY.—A despatch from Montreal states that a correspondent of some New York news- papers, Richard O'Brien by name, has been arrested for concocting and sending to his employers the story re- transmitted to England on Saturday concerning an assault by roughs on Prince George of Wales and the subsequent arrest of the Prince under misapprehension. Several citizens of Montreal having satisfied themselves that the whole narrative was an impudent invention. have started a subscription to pay for the prosecution of the offender.

div.head: FIRE AT THE SPANISH ALHAMBRA.
div.p: FIRE AT THE SPANISH ALHAMBRA.
GREAT DESTRUCTION.

MADRID, TUESDAY AFTERNOON.—Late last night the guards at the famous Alhambra Palace at Granada gave an alarm of fire, mid immediately afterwards urgent nae.s- sages were sent in all directions for assistance. The fire- engines from the palace and from the town were got to work after some delay, but for a considerable time it looked as though the superb historical pile would be des- troyed. The fire broke out in the well-known Court of Myrtles, otherwise known as the Court of Ponds, which, with its wealth of exquisite carvings, and ita almost priceless contents, were completely consumed. A similar fate befell, in the course of a few hours, the Court of Ships and the beautiful hall, but the remainder of the palace was saved, although the conflagration was not completely mastered until eight o'clock this morning. The firemen worked with great bravery and energy, and great praise is due to them. Five of them were disabled by burns or wounds inflicted by falling beams and masonry, and two are in a serious condition. GRANADA, TUBSDAY.—The fire at the Alhambra Palace was finally extinguished this morning, after doing , damage which is irreparable, although less extensive than was at first feared. The flames were first noticed at ten o'clock last night, and the authorities at once requisi- tioned the services of the troops, at the same time sum- moning the ordinary firemen. On the news of the ,1 outbreak reaching this city thousands of people at once flocked to the scene, to find on arriving that the whole of the upper part of the gallery on the right side of the Arrazanes Court was ablaze. To prevent the conflagra- tion spreading, a successful attempt was made to isolate the burning portion. Hundreds of people, including several ladies, assisted the firemen in coping with the flames. Water was obtained from the tanks and foun- tains in the various courts. After several hours' incessant work the fire was subdued, and at length ex- tinguished ha the early hours of the morning. The por- tion burnt comprised the magnificent Sala de la Bares and the right wing of the Arrazanes Court. The remain- der of the buildings were saved. Eight persons were slightly injured. The cause of the outbreak has not yet been ascertained, but suspicions are entertained that it was the work of an incendiary. The judicial authorities have opened an inquiry.

div.head: DESCRIPTION OF THE ALFIAMBRA.•
div.p: DESCRIPTION OF THE ALFIAMBRA.•

The Alhambra is the name given to the remains of the palace of the Moorish kings of Granada. It stands on the highest part of a lofty hill which adjoins and overlooks the city of Granada, in Spain, and is enclosed by a wall forty feet high and six feet thick, flanked with towers, I dating probably from 1019. The palace was begun in 1248. It was considered the finest existing specimen of Arabic architecture in the world. The name Alhambra seems to have been derived from the red appearance of the original walls and towers ("Kasaba-al-Ilambra the red enclosure "). Nothing can be more severe, plain, and unattractive than the exterior of the Alhambra. The interior, on the contrary, when in its perfect state, was probably the most gorgeous specimen of Moorish archi- tecture and decoration that has ever existed. It was Injured to some extent during the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella by the purification and whitewashing of the monks; but the work of destruction was not commenced till Charles V. pulled down a large part of it in order to erect a palace for himself on the site ; and he made many alterations for the worse in the portion which remained. It seems afterwards to have suffered no material injury, except from neglect and decay, till Sebastiani obtained possession of Granada in January, 1810, and oocupied it with his troops. The Moorish palace is entered from the Plaza de Los Algibes by a small doorway of Spaiish construction. The palace consists of courts, colonnades, halls, saloons, and various smaller apartments, paved with marble, and formerly supplied with fountains and baths. The walls are beautifully wrought in arabesques intermingled with inscriptions, and richly painted and gilt. Most of the ceilings are formed in compartments with raised mouldings or in small cupolas with innumerable pendant ornaments; others are of carved timber. Yusuf I. who was stabbed by an assassin in 1832, repainted and regilt the whole palace, which must then have realised the splendours of Arabian fiction.

The Brazilian elections give the Government of the Republic a majority in the Constituent Assembly. The report that the Austrian warship Taurus has been lost proves to have been erroneous. A railway collision occurred on Tuesday near Pontarlier (France), in which four persens were killed and several others injured.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

- MURDER, OF A FARMER. A shocking murder waakommitted on Saturday even- ing at Ballingarry, ten miles fromthere, the victim being James M'Grath, and the reasen„for the crime being, it is suggested, that he had given the shelter of a house to a man named Martin Maher,' who had been evicted from an adjoining farm by the owner, a magistrate named Llangley. Recently coal mining operations had been commenced on the farm, and Maher contended that the colliers in working for Mr. Llangley were violating the principles of the National League. The colliers showed their resentment of this by objecting to WGrath giving shelter to Maher. and so recently as Sunday week threw stones at M'Grath' s children and at night attacked his house. On Saturday evening M'Grath walked down the yard in front of his house, bordering on the public road, when he was attacked by two colliers. According to the evidence of Kate Egan, a servant in the employment of M'Grath, the men knocked him down, and when he got up one of them stabbed him with a penknife. When , Mrs. M'Grath took him in her arms they flung stones at the body. A collier named Heffey has been arrested, and remanded on the charge of wilful murder. He was identified by the girl Egan as one of the two men. The second man has not yet been apprehended. I.l•Grath was a.man in comfortable circumsemets. He leaves a widow and six sons, the eldest of wbom is about 15 years of age. EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF ISLANDERS. _. . _

Dr. Hudson has complained to the Dingle Guar- dians that the people on the Blashet Island, South of Ireland, where a fever epidemic prevails, refused to take him in a boat from the mainland to the island. The islanders were denounced by one of the guardians as savages, and another advocated that doctors, nurses, and every other relief during the epidemic should be taken from them. Dr. Hudson disclaimed all responsi- bility.

div.head: MEMORIAL TO BISHOP BERKELEY.
div.p: MEMORIAL TO BISHOP BERKELEY.

An altar tomb of alabaster' executed by Mr. Bruce Joy, in memory of Dr. Berkeley, Bishop of Cloyne was unveiled in Cloyne Cathedral on Tuesday. Mr. Balfour, Mr. Gladstone, the Lord Chancellor of Ireland, and the Duke of Devonshire are among the subscribers to the memorial. _ _

div.head: SAD STORY,
div.p: A SAD STORY,

A coroner's inquest has been held in Clones, County Monaghan, on the body of H. M. Wilson, cashier in the branch establishment of the Ulster Bank in that town, who committed suicide by hanging himself on the handle of the safe. The police found the following letter in his pocket :—" During the past fortnight I have been in very bad health, and as I felt myself steadily worse, I became very depressed at the prospect of my being laid up for a considerable period, attended as that would be by so much expense, which I could ill afford. Every- thing had been a trouble to me lately. My daily work, which used to be so pleasant to me, has become a matter pf great difficulty for me, and I feel as if I would never , be able to work again as I once was. I have hid my I illness from my friends, so that I think no one but the housekeeper knew of it. Everything in connection with', my post in the bank is in order, and I am not in debt to anyone. I have a list of a few accounts since my last settlement in an envelope in my desk, with ample money to Meet them, and which I trust Mr. Green will attend to for me. May God, who has sent this trouble, afflic- tion of ill-health upon me, forgive me. But the prospect 'of my health broken up maddened me. How I feel the breaking of my:friends' hearts, especially those who have been so very kitid to me ; but then I can live on only in the end to become a burden to them. I hope all will look with compassion on me, as before this I always tried to be a good and true friend." The remains have been brought to Lisburn, near Belfast, and interred.

BOATING ACCIDENT IN DUBLIN BAY. Two young gentlemen, out rowing in Dublin Bay on Monday, stopped at the pier at Kingstown, and took on board two servant girls. They proceeded out in the harbour, when the boat capsized, and the two young women were drowned. The others were rescued in an exhausted state. The deceased are quite unknown. HORRIBLE MUTIL ATION OF A HORSE. . _ . _

intelligence has been received from Ennis of another savage outrage iu the western district. The horse of a boycotted farmer named Kett, at Corbelly Farm, was found on Monday night stabbed In several places and with its tongue cut out. MR. JOHN MORLEY IN IRELAND. ' •

On Monday morning, Mr. John Morley, M.P., arrived at Kingstown from London, and drove to the Royal Marine Hotel, Bray. It is stated that he intends seeing some of the Nationalist leadeis and visiting some of the districts in the south and west, where potato disease is apprehended. This year the area in Ireland under potato cultivation is 780,800 acres, being 6,430 acres less than last year. SENTENCES FOR INTIMIDATION. -

At CorirTll-I;:tier on strike was sentenced to four months' and another to six weeks' imprisonment for assaults on constables and an imported baker, who were met by a crowd. At Bandon' a woman was sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment for striking a girl who dealt with a boycotted baker. • GUARDIANS ANO BOYCOTTING.

The Guardians of Glin and Klimanook Unions have adopted the rasolutionpassed at the Croom board approv- ing of boycotting and the Plan of Campaign on the lines laid down by Mr. John Dillon, as having proved the safe- guards of the Irish tenant farmers.
