SCENE IN PORTUGUESE PARLIAMENr.

Extraordinary scenes were witnessed in the Portuguese Cortes on Monday, consequent on the Minister for Foreign affairs rising to move the adoption of the Anglo- Portuguese Convention. In the midst of the tumult Major Serpa Pinto shouted to the Progressist minority, "Hold your tongues," and was vehemently set upon by a Progressist deputy—a priest named Brands°. The major defended himself with his fists, and a regular hand to hand struggle ensued, the disturbance reaching such a pitch that the President declared the sitting sus- pended. On the House re-assembling a number of modi- fications to the Convention were submitted. RESIGNATION OF THE PORTUGUESE MINISTRY. A Lisbon telegram says Major Serpa Pinto, in his speech in the Cortes on Monday, declared himself a staunch Monarchist and Conservative, but stated that he would do his utmost to oppose the Anglo-Portuguese Convention. Some rioting occu.tred on Monday night, in the course of which a police station was mobbed, and several prisoners set free. A later Lisbon telegram says the Ministry has resigned. Senhor Abren has been entrusted with the formation of a new Cabinet. It is reported that Senhor Navarro has been offered a portfolio, but he is expected to decline it, as the new Government will probably only be a transi- tory one. The arrival of an English man-of-war in the Tagus was followed by a tumult among the population. Some officers and sailors who landed were obliged to re- embark, the people pursuing them while on shore with hisses and insulting remarks. A telegram from Lisbon speaks °Attie probability of a Coalition Ministry being formed, so composed as to con- ciliate all parties.

div.head: SERIES OF FIRES.
div.p: A SERIES OF FIRES.
PAPER WORKS DESTROYED.

On Monday afternoon the extensive mills of the West Fliuttlepool Paper Pulp Works Company at Stranton, West Ilartlepool, caught lire, and the flames, fanned by a strong south-west wind, soon enveloped the entire building. In two hours the place was a complete wreck, and the loss is expected to reach £30,000. Over one hundred hands will be thrown out of employment.

div.head: FIRE AT REATH.
div.p: FIRE AT REATH.

Damage to the extent- a-12.57000 Was caused by a fire which raged for several hours on Monday afternoon, at the Briton Ferry Chemical Works, at Neath. Two sets, containing six acid chambers, were completely destroyed, together with the great acid towers attached. The fire originated in the stores under the chambers, in which were stocked 250 tons of nitre cake and 100 tons of sulphate of copper. There were about 1,000 tons of acid in the chambers. FIRE IN AN IRONWORKS.

A tremendo;;'fi-;:e--breke out at Messrs. Fielding and Platt's Ironworks, Gloucester, shortly before nine o'clock on Monday night. The fire is supposed to have origin- ated in the pattern shop, and from the time of the out- break had a complete hold of the building, which was gutted in an hour or so. The supply of water seemed very inadequate, and the efforts of the fire brigade were from the first directed to saving the surrounding property. About a dozen dwelling-houses were in imminent danger, as the wind blew the flames towards them. A church in the vicinity was also in danger. The damage is estimated at about £20,000.

div.head: FIRE ON THE METROPOLITAN RAILWAY. A BRIDGE COLLAPSING.
div.p: FIRE ON THE METROPOLITAN RAILWAY. A BRIDGE COLLAPSING.

I Early on Monday morning fire broke out in a store- house for naphtha, situated on the Metropolitan Railway, under the bridge between Clerkenwell Green and Far- rington-road. Great damage was caused before the fire was extinguished the girders of the bridgehaving bulged to such a degree that the roadway has given way three or four feet in the middle, so that all traffic over it has been prohibited. It is said that the bridge will have to be taken down and rebuilt. From inquiries it seems that one of the company's men went to the storehouse, taking with him a light, and that instantly the vapour from the the naphtha caught alight, and this was followed by an explosion, and the whole storehouse, with its inflammable contents, was soon on ore.

div.head: FUNERAL OF CANON LIDDON.
div.p: FUNERAL OF CANON LIDDON.

The remains of the late Canon Liddon were ?aid to rest on Tuesday in the crypt of St. Paul's Cathedral There was a large gathering of the public, prominent among whom were Mr. Ritchie, the Baroness Burdett-Coutts, Mr. George Russell, Lord Halifax, and eight bishops. Canons Gregory and Scott Holland and Dean Church read the funeral service. Mr. John Liddon, Dr. Liddon, and Mr. W. Liddon, brothers of the deceased, were the chief mourners. Wreaths were sent by Lord Salisbury, Mr. Gladstone, and many others. The Crypt of St. Paul's Cathedral was on Wednesday thronged with people anxious to look upon the grave in which Canon Liddon was on Tuesday laid. As a matter of fact it is impossible to see the slabs which cover the grave on account of the wealth of floral wreaths which are laid upon them. Not only so, but the temporary rails by which the grave is surrounded are hung with wreaths, the total number of which is about 100. rer- haps the finest floral tributes are those sent by the Duchess of Newcastle and the Baroness Burdett-Coutts, and the most interesting those forwarded by the Mar- quis and Marchioness of Salisbury and Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. The latter two lie side by side at the head of the grave, eloquent, if mute, evidence to the readi- ness with which Canon Liddon, had he so cared, might have received a bishopric from either leader of the two great political parties. In sympathy with the Premier, Lady Salisbury had a great regard for Dr. Liddon, as a preacher, and it is said that she attended the very last sermon he preached in St. Paul's.

General Boulanger left Jersey on Thursday morning for Guernsey, with a lady companion. He sailed in the London and South-Western Railway Co.'s steamer Frederica, being the last passenger to go on Board. A receiving order has been made in the London Bank- ruptcy Court, against Mr. Abercrombie Castle, the pro- prietor of the National Conservative Club, Pall Mall, and the principal shareholder in the Club Owners Corporation, Limited, to whom St. George's Club, Hanover-square, belongs. The amount of the liabilities did not trans- pire.

div.head: LICENSING QUESTION AND "TIED HOUSES."
div.p: THE LICENSING QUESTION AND "TIED HOUSES."

LABOUR AND CAPITAL. THE NORTHUMBERLAND MINERS' DEMAND. The miners of Northumberland are seeking a further advance of wages, and formal application has been made by tha officials of their association requesting the masters to receive a deputation to consider the demands of the men.

div.head: DOCKERS' UNION.
div.p: THE DOCKERS' UNION.

The Executive Council of the Dockers' Union state that owing to "the heavy drain upon our funds through the many disputes having reduced our balance," it has been decided" that a levy of one shilling per member be imposed on all members, the same to be paid by the 27th instant, or to be added to the member's arrears." Further, it has been resolved that in future "no branch secretary shall be allowed t draw commission on the contributions of more than 500 members.

SCOTCH MINERS. At a meeting on Monday, in Glasgow, of miners' dele- gates from all Scotland, it was agreed by a majority to demand an advance of one shilling per day. An amend- ment which was lost was for sixpence a day.

THE STRIKE IN AUSTRALIA. A number of men paraded the principal thoroughfares of the southern district of West Ham on Saturday after- noon, in support of the Australian strikers. The total amount collected in the boxes at the demonstration was £s2Bs. 3d., and in addition a fairly good sum was secured by canvassers who visited the shops and houses. At the labour conference, on Monday at Sydney, a proposal was submitted to immediately call out the shearers, wool shed labourers, and carriers. A resolution was adopted instructing the Strike Committees in the various colonies to order all men affiliated to the Labour Union to hold themselves in readiness to strike. It is thought probable that all the affiliated trades will be called out, a step which it is estimated would affect 8,000 men. Mr. Fitzgerald, labour delegate, has started for England on board the Cuzco, in order to lay the strikers case before the British public. The crew of the steamer at Newcastle who were ar- rested for refusing to work have been discharged from custody on a legal point. The miners at West Wallsend Collieries have struck because non-union men are employed in loading coal. THE MINERS' FEDERATION AND THE EIGHT HOURS QUESTION.

_ The President of the Miners' Federation of Great Britain speaking at a mass meeting of the miners held on Monday at the Attercliffe Vestry Hall, Sheffield. said there were members of Parliament who had received the votes of workingmen and who had pledged themselves to go to the House of Commons to look after the interests of the miners. They were telling the miners that they had no right to combine with the object of pressing upon members of Parliament to pass into law an Eight Hours Bill for miners, or for anyone else. In choosing a candidate they should select a genuine convert, a real workingman representative, a man who would carry out by voice and vote in the House of Commons what he had prmnised at the hustings. The following resolutions were passed :—" That this meeting of miners regrets that the Government should decline to give facilities for the discussion of the Eight Hours Bill, and hereby pledges itself to support a general stand in the mining industry at any time that shall be arranged by the forth- coming conference in order to obtain the same,' That this meeting fails to see the utility pf any Employers' Liability Act that does not de,ia with the question of t0:541M employment, or allow any facilities for contract- ineout of the same, and this meeting urges the labour and other members to oppose the passing into law of any Bills that do not legislate on these important sub- jects."

div.head: END OF THE SOUTHAMPTON DISPUTE._
div.p: END OF THE SOUTHAMPTON DISPUTE._

- The dispute terminated peaceably all round at South- ampton on Tuesday. At the Royal Mail Company's fac- tory there was great eagerness on the part of the men to be re-admitted. The men belonging to ths Union Com- pany's steamer Moor came ashore on Tuesday after having signed articles, the assigned reason being that the boat- swain was a non-unionist. It is expected that the difficulty will be settled. Mr. Welsh, secretary of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union, addressed a meeting on Tuesday afternoon, and congratulated the men on their victory. All the companies except the South-western had treated them very fairly, and had not only cOCO.-ed their demands, but had promised them Midler rise when freights increased. The South-wfistern would be given a few days longer, and it tney did not then give way, demands would be gads which at present were little dreamt of. Fifteen men were committed on Tuesday for trial at the alaifes for taking part in the strike disturb- ances' ar.d the charges against some other defendants wcre adjourned.

TERMINATION OF A STRIKE. As the result of the confereace, on Wednesday, between the representatives of the masters sad the men, the strike in the Manchester rivetted boot and shoe trade has terminated. With the exception of some additions for extras, the men's new list is accepted by the em- ployers. THE LONDON BOOTMAKERS. The London bootmakers on strike, met on Tuesday night, and considered the offer of the masters to submit their case to arbitration. They refused to do so, as a similar offer on the part of the men last week was re- fused by the trnployers. The men believe the masters will give way. SETTLEMENT OP TrIE NORTHWICH JOINERS' STRIKE. The strike of 'carpenters and joiners at Northwich has been settled by compromise. The masters' offer of id. per hour increase in wages, with the privilege of leaving work on Saturday at noon, has been accepted, and the mess have returned to work. THE STRIKE OF FLATMEN AT ELLES:VRE PORT. ' The members of the Upper Mersey Watermen and Quay Porters' Association still remain out on strike at ED.es- mere Fort. The men have recently received aid from other unions, including £4O from the Mersey Flatrnen's Association and £5O from the Winsford flatmen. A strong determination is expressed by the members of the union not to resume work until their demands are con- ceded. The strike has now lasted several weeks. THE DEMANDS OF SCOTCH IRONWORKERS. At the meeting at Glasgow of the Scottish ironmasters, on Wednesday, representing seventy-three furnaces, it was decided to take united action to resist the demands of the men and extinguish the furnaces if necessary.

Mr. Secretary Blaine has written a letter in which he says he regards the opposition of the Free-traders to reciprocity as an evident and specific reason for it, as they know that it will seriously affect the Free Trade enactment.
WARRINGTON REVISION 'COURT.
CONDOLING WITH THE CONSERVATIVIC AGENT.

On Monday the adjourned court for the revisioia of the Warrington voters' lists was held in the Mayor's parlour at the Town Hall. Mr. J. T. Foard was the revising barrister. Mr. A. Browne and Mr. Clayton (agent) represented the Liberal party, and Mr. Hampson appeared for the Conservatives. fhe main business of the court was the reading over of the lists, and in the course of this Mr. Hampson objected to the nctice of objection sent by the Liberals to a declaration made by a Conserva- tive claimant. The objection, it appeared, was signed ;by Patrick James Donohue who said that he was an occupier on number 8 list. This, how- ever, was an error as Donohue was on the number 9 list. It was argued by Mr. Hampson that the ob- jection was invalid inasmuch as the person objected to would not find the objecting person's name on the list specified.—Mr. Browne said that the objection was only to a declaration made after a valid original objection. The statute did not provide a form of objection to a declaration, and the notice that had been given was not likely to mislead the person ob- jected to.—The Revising Barrister overruled Mr. Rampson's objection. The work of revision having been finished. Mr. Hanapson referred to the courtesy with which the Revising Barrister had conducted the Court, and he also alluded to the excellent way the overseers had done their work. He regretted that, owing to a mistake,fitty-six of his objections had been invalid, but he should take care it did not occur again. Fortunately, it was not a very great matter.—Xl.r. Clayton endorsed what Mr. Hampson had said with regard to the Revising Barrister, and added that, personally, he sympathised very much with 11.. Hampson with regard to the mistake that had been made. As to the overseers' lists he thought they would be about the best in England. He had never known better lists, the mistakes that were in being generally printers' errors.—The Revising Barrister said that was so, but there were bound to be printers' errors swing to the short amount of time there was to get the lists out. Ile was sorry be had had to declare Mr. Hampson's objections invalid as he thought it was a hardship, but the law was very strict and left him no option in the matter. If the mistake had been one of form and not of substance he would have amended the objections.

div.head: STRUGGLE IN TIPPERna.
div.p: THE STRUGGLE IN TIPPERna.

MESSRS. O'BRIEN AND DILLON ARRESTED. OT9.ER M.P.'S SUMMONED. The recent proceedings in connection with the institu- tion of the Plan of Campaign on the estate of Mr. A. H. Smith-Barry, M.P., at Tipperary, have engaged the I attention of the Irish Executive at Dublin Castle during the past few months, and the nature of the reports received from the Constabulary officials on the spot has induced the representatives of the Crown to take the de- cisive step of instituting proceedings under the Coercion Act against those who are deemed responsible for the con- duct of the agitation amongst Mr. Smith-Barry's tenants. The evidence accumulated in the hands of the police at Tipperary applies to no fewer than 12 persons, five of whom are members of Parliament, and against these the Irish Executive determined to proceed simultaneously— not, as has been the case on previous occasions of the kind, by summons, as regards two of them at least, but by warrant. The information upon which the warrant was issued by the resident magistrate was based on the information of District Inspector Rafter, of Tipperary. ,He charges Mr. W. O'Brien M.P., Mr. John Dillon, M.P., Mr. T. .L Condon, M.P., Air. David Sheehy, M.P., Mr. Patrick O'Brien, M.P., the Rev. David Humphreys, of Tipperary, Mr. Thomas Walsh, Mr. J. E. O'Mahony, Mr. John Cullinane, Mr. Patrick Mackie, Mr. M. 0. Dalton, and Mr. Daniel Kelly with conspir- ing to prevent the payment of rent on Mr. Smith- Barry's estate between the months of March and Sep- tember last, and with other offences arising out of it. Upon Mr. Rafter's information a warrant was issued on Tuesday last by Mr. Irwin' R.M., empowering the Tip- perary police to forthwith arrest the two first-named defendants, Mr. William O'Brien and Mr. John Dillon. The warrant was executed upon the person of each simultaneously, although Mr. O'Brien was staying with his wife at Glengariff, county Cork, and Mr. Dillon was ,in Dublin. The warrant was issued in duplicate, and Head Constable Cary, of the Royal Irish Constabulary depot, was entrusted with the execution of the one upon the person of Mr. Dillon. The officer proceeded shortly after seven o'clock on Thursday morning to a house at I3allybrack, near Kings- town, where Mr. John Dillon was on a short visit. Mr. Dillon had not breakfasted at the time, but he immedi- ately assented to the request of the Head Constable to accompany him to Tipperary. He was given time, how- ever, to partake of a meal and to telegraph the fact of his arrest to the headquarters of the Irish National League in Dublin.

div.head: MR. O'BRIEN'S JOURNEY TO TIPPERARY. CHEERING THE PRISONER.
div.p: MR. O'BRIEN'S JOURNEY TO TIPPERARY. CHEERING THE PRISONER.

Mr. O'Brien's arrest was made at Roche's Hotel, Glen- gariff, between ten and eleven o'clock on Thursday morning, by District Inspector Smith. of Maeroom. There was a large force of police mustered near the hotel, under District Inspectors Sullivan, of Bantry, and Greene, of Bandon. The police left Bantry early in the morning for Glengariff, twelve miles away. When the arrest was reported the peasantry and people of the dis- trict crowded into Glengariff and cheered lustily for Mr. O'Brien when he made his appearance in custody. Both Mr. O'Brien and his wife were conveyed from Glengariff to Bantry in a closed carriage, in which also rode District Inspector Smith. A large police escort accompanied the party. Mr. O'Brien and his escort, consisting of 50 police- men, arrived at Bantry soon after one o'clock. After a short dekey at the police barrdcks, the hon. member was conveyed to the railway terminus. An immense crowd followed the carriage, cheering for Mr. O'Brien, and at the railway station the cheering was renewed. Both Mr. and Mrs. O'Brien acknowledged the warmth of their reception by the 'Bantry people, and until the start- ing of the train the hon. gentleman was besieged by friends anxious to shake hands with him and Mrs. O'Brien. At Bandon a large crowd had assembled, and ' when the train steamed in a scene of much excitement ' took place and cheers were repeatedly given for Mr. ' O'Brien. In reply to a question as to the charge on which he was arrested, Mr. O'Briee said the charge was of a vague and general nature, et things that occurred be- tween May and September, but that the real accusation had reference to Tipperary. No other incident occii--' ' wortny 013p.en's. arrival cmc. the train Yeachea the iermirills fowl ciiiiert Wert; raised by. the vast concourse of people who had assembled. Mr. O'Brien was placed an an outside car in the custody of District Inspector Smith, two armed policemen being seated on the other side. Preceding the car was a large body of mounted police, and following, it about fifty Hus- sars with drawn sabres. A ciarload of police followed the Hussars. Vast crowds lined Albert Quay and the South Mall, and their cheering was continuous as Mr. O'Briery passed. div.p: wasted, and the finest opportunities lost. Speak- ing broadly,the mass of the children at our elemen- tary schools are taken from school too soon, whilst the children of the middle and uppee,classes are kept at school too long. There may be over-pres- sure at times in our national schools, but there is not over-education. What is needed, and the need iS now being generally recognised, is that practical training which comes under the head of techni- cal education. We want workmen who know something of the "why and wherefore" of what they do; who display intelligence in receiving and carrying out instructions; and who have some aptitude for improving upon antiquated methods. There is a wide field, and, as Mr. GLADSTONE remarked the other day, there always will be, for artizans of this class. The over-education, such R 5 we have it in this country, apr lies to the young Laen who are trained to be " scholars," apart from consideration of the particular calling in life which they may be called upon to follow. The result too Often is that, when they enter the struggle for a livelihood, they find themselves left behind by men Who have been learning in the world's school the sort of work that is required of them, and are able to do it. Our higher education is classical and Cumbersome ; what we need is such reform as will make it practical and useful.

Germany CONFIRMATION has been received of and the what at first was regarded as an Slave Trade. incredible report, namely, that the German Administrator at Bagamoyo has published an official notice giving free liberty to every one for the purchase and sale of slaves in Bagamoyo and its vicinity. A Reuter's telegram says:—" The Proclamation is posted up both at Bagamoyo and Ear-es-Salaam, and is signed by the German Com- mandant. The slave brokers who were turned out Of Zanzibar have established themselves at Baga- raoyo, where they are doing a thriving trade. It is rumoured that the Sultan has telegraphed to Europe for assistance." It may be that the Ger- • man Commissioner has been acting in this matter on his own responsibility, and that the pro- clamation he has issued will not be sanctioned - by the Imperial Government. But whether this be so or not, Lord SALISBURY should lose no time Ml demanding an explanation from the German Government. Bagamoyo is on the east coast of Africa, opposite the island of Zanzibar; and it is, ae a matter of fact, part of the dominion of the Sultan of Zanzibar. Under the treaty just concluded with Germany, England assumes the Protectorate of Zanzibar proper, and Germany of the Bagamoyo portion of the mainland. It was at the request of the British Government that the Sultan issued a decree prohibiting slavery in his dominions ; and it would seem as if the German authorities were flouting this decree. It remains to be seen whether the decree can be flouted with impunity. Things have come to a pretty pass if the concessions made to Germany are to result in her thwarting us instead of helping us, as she is Pledged to do, to suppress the slave trade in East Africa. It is little to the purpose to urge that the , German proclamation does not strike at the pro- hibition of slave-hunting and of the export of slaves by sea. It is sufficient that it permits of slave-dealing in Bagamoyo, notwithstanding the fact that slave-dealing is prohibited by the Sultan of Zanzibar. The proclamation is a blow at the Sultan, and through the Sultan it becomes a blow , at England. It is just possible that the German Commissioner has some idea of currying favour with the slave-dealers, who are an influential body, but it is difficult to believe that the Imperial Government will sanction a reversal of its policy for a purpose so degrading. It is not long since England joined Germany in blockading the Zanzi- bar coast with the object of suppressing the slave trade; and, further than this, Germany is pledged, along with European powers, to assist inputting an end to the horrible traffic. It is satisfactory to ob- serve that the press of Germany repudiate the pro- clamation. The " Volkszeitung" says: "We hesi- tate to take for certain the news originating from English sources. The baseness and foolishness of such a decree would be equally great. The Commis- sioner would have played a wicked game with the honour of the German name." The " Vossische Zeitung " writes: "Such a decree would be the vio- lation of the general acts of the Congo Conference, and a denial of all that the German Government has solemnly declared to Europe and the Reichstag It would not only be a breach of international , obligation, but also from a political and moral point - of view its consequences would be incalculable." ' We are not disposed to say anything stronger than this, for we cannot but think that, under pressure I I at home and abroad, the objectionable proclama- tion will be withdrawn by the German Govern- , rnent.

The exposure of the Boulangist agitation is a story of "treasons, stratagems and spoils." Not only has "the bravo General" gone out, but he has gone like a badly-snuffed candle—leaving a dis- agreeable smell behind.

At Runcorn, two boys have been brought before the magistrates, and fined for ringing bells, thereby annoying a number of dressmakers. Years hence, the boys will most likely take to another form of ringing belles, and then the dressmakers will not be annoyed.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a Penalty of ki). and costs was inflicted upon a Pemberton fishdealer for offering unwholesome fish for sale in the Market Hall. This is something like a penalty; and yet it is little enough. People who adulterate or offer foul food for sale should be taught, through the breeches' pocket, that honesty Is the best policy.

Mr. I. S. Leadam is renewing his assault on the T9ry citadel of Altrincharn. His speech at Thel- wall on Saturday is, like all his speechas, thoughtful and argumentative—a complete contrast to the small talk of the verdant Disraeli. As the Liberals were less than 600 behind in 1886, out of a constituency of 10,000,there is a fair chance, with steady hard work, of winning the seat.

Lord Salisbury is about to visit Rossendale to give Lord Hartington a lift. He doubtless thinks that one good turn deserves another, and it is a inatter of course to say that if the Salisbury Ad- ; in.inistration hadn't been propped from the out- ! side by the leader of the Dissentient Liberals it would have collapsed long since. It is understood that the Premier will visit Rossendale about the Middle of November.

September has done something to redeem the character of the weather of 1890, which has been bad, very bad. Some are summers and some are riot, and this year it has been one of the " nots." But now— Through the gloaming broadens the harvest moon, While the fagged hind whistles his homeward tune, for there is a harvest, after all, and there is oppor- tunity as of old to gather the kindly fruits of the earth.

-- The Rev. J. M. Wilson, who preached the annual sermons, on Sunday, of the Warrington Parish Church, suggested that something should be done to diminish the amount of smoke in the town. Warrington is certainly a smoke-smitten place ;
and something should be done to mitigate the nuisance. Why not begin by summoning the worst offenders before the magistrates ? Is it that certain magistrates are amongst the worst offend- ers?

The Government have rendered a greater ser- vice than they intended by raising the licensing question and pointing to the necessity of reduc- mg the number of licenses. Several Licensing Courts have taken the Writ, and set about exercis- ing the powers which they undoubtedly possess to refuse renewals, where a house is not required, or where it is structurally unsuitable for the purpose of a public-house.

In some cases, as at Birmingham for instance, a special set has been made against what are known as "tied houses." It was certainly never intended that a monoply of this kind should be established. It converts the landlord into a mere agent of the brewer, and restricts competition in a way which cannot be said to be conducive to the production of "the best value for the money." A license is a monoply in itself without creating another by binding the landlord to the use of a particular tap.

But the soundest around of objection is, after all, the non-necessity of so many licensed houses, especially when they are huddled together in narrow streets and passages as in the centre of Warrington. It is one of the things thst instantly strikes a stranger, and the impression he gets is to the discredit of the town. Increase the facilities for drinking, and you increase drunkenness; and as the reverse of this holds good, it is to be hoped the magistrates will have the maxim in mind at the adjourned court on Tuesday next.

The circumstances of a fearful row and a fear- ful fight in a railway carriage were investigated, at the Altrincham Police Court, on Monday. It transpired that the three offenders were drunk when they entered the train at Lymm ; and one of the magistrates very properly suggested that some responsibility rested with the Railway Company for allowing drunken men to enter• the train. Granted that it sometimes is difficult to say when a man is drunk, there can surely be no difficulty when there are three men all drunk together.

A person of the name of Woods has found him- self very much in the wood through appealing against a sentence of a month's imprisonment for assault. The appeal is costing him so much that he would like to drop it, " do " his month, and have done with the matter; but he finds this cannot be done; the appeal must be proceeded with. He feels now pretty much as the darkey did who being lectured prior to being flogged exclaimed : "Massa, if you floggee, floggee; and if you talkee, talkee; but no floggee and talkee, too."

The strike and lockout at the Plate Glass Works of . Messrs. Pilkington Bros. Cowley Hill,. is exciting great interest at St. Helens ; and it would seem as if the firm have entered upon a struggle greater than they bargained for. It is obvious from the united trades demonstration which was held on Saturday, that workmen of all classes believe that the men out on strike are in the right, and there is every evidence of a determination to support them. This tendency to act in thorough concert is a hopeful sign for the future of labour. United they may stand; divided they will fall.

Lord Wolseley is not a teetotaller,as is commonly supposed ; but he is a strong temperance man, and believes in putting a strait jacket upon the drink trade, as will be seen from the following extract from a letter :—" When I see strong measures taken in England to prohibit the sale of poisons in the form of spirits of all sorts, then I shall believe in the new British Reformation. It is to me in our present state the most monstrous imposition and humbug to preach abroad what we dare not carry out at home."

The Volunteer has his pleasures, but he risks penalties. On Monday, at St. Helens, no less than thirteen Volunteers were fined two guineas each, and 6s. 6d. costs, "for wilfully neglecting to make themselves efficient, whereby the corps had lost the capitation grant." As they had not put in a single drill during the year, their conduct is inexcusable, though it can hardly be said to have deserved so heavy a fine. If they had resigned, as they might have done, the capitation grant would still have been lost. The authorities must beware, or they may find that heavy penalties lead to wholesale resignation.

The Labour Congress at Brussels has been con- cerning itself with the question of an extension of the franchise' as a preliminary to reducing the hours of labour. A resolution was come to, on Sunday, "not to vote at the next election for any candidate wlko did not support the principle of universal suffrage." We have not yet arrived at universal suffrage in this country, but we are so near it that the working classes have the power in their own hands of controlling Parliament—if they care to exercise it. They have a good deal to learn in Warrington, for instance, so long as they allow a brewer to rake in their hard earnings, and mis- represent them in Parliament.

--- The inquiry made by the Special Commissioner, on Wednesday, with a view to the re-arrangement of the wards in the Borough of Warrington,passed off very satisfactorily. It was quite as well that various proposals were made, to ensure the matter being considered on every side. Mr. Cresswell is thoroughly familiar with work of this kind,and evi- dently takes pains to make himself master of all the facts of the case. He may be relied upon to give a decision which, if not satisfactory to every- body, will be fair to the ratepayers as a whole. He has left it to the Town Council to decide, if they can, upon the names to be given to the wards. This is a tickle task. Uniformity and consistency should be aimed at; and the names should, if pos- sible, suggest the locality of each ward.

THE VISIT OF 31.1 R. JOHN MORLEY TO ST. HELENS. The executive of the St. Helens Liberal Associa- tion are rapidly completing the arrangements for the great demonstration to be held in that town on Monday, the Il9th inst. The Volunteer Hall has been secured for the gathering, which already gives promise of being one of the most successf al political demonstrations ever held in the town. It has been decided that Alderman Thomas Cook, J.P., chairman of the association, shall "preside, and in addition to an address from the Right Hon. John Morley, M.P.. the proceedings will include speeches by Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., for the Scotland Division, Liverpool; Mr. Ralph Neville; Q.C., M,P. for the Exchange Division, Liverpool; Mr. Lloyd George, M.P. for the Carnarvon Boroughs; Mr. W. R. Kennedy, Q.C., Liberal candidate for the borough : and Mr. Samuel Woods, miners' agent and Labour candidate for the Ince Division. The admission will be by ticket, in order to prevent an inconvenient crush inside the hall. NOW OPEN FOR THE SEASON.—Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at Mr. Chantry's. 13 Sankey-at., Warrington. Open every Friday from 3 to 9 p.m. Writing : Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and flowing style. Terms for the complete course, One Guinea. Book-keeping : Pupils are taught how to open. keep, balance, and close a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certificate for proficency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand. Pit- man's system. Pupils will ne received on Friday next, at any hour from 3to 9 p.m. No classes, the instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at Mr. Chantry's 13, Sankey-st., Warrington, or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Brown-st.. the Market, Man- chester.—Adrt.

A LIVELY WEDDING, SCENE. An extraordinary scene was witnessed in the neighbourhood of Eccleston-street, St. Helens. on Monday. A middle-aged mad employed as A coal- hawker and a widower, had decided to re-marry, but the new alliance did not meet with the appro- val of his children The ceremony was performed in a church on the outskirts of the borough on Monday, and on returning from the church the couple were received by a large crowd of people, who laughed and jeered. Street sweepings were thrown upon the couple, and rotten eggs were brought into requisition. One young fellow struck the bridegroom a blow in the face which disfigured him, while a young woman seized the bonnet of the bride and tore it up. The bride and bridegroom eventually got inside their house, and remained there. Charles Houghton, a brother of the bride- groom, was arrested on a charge of being drunk and disorderly. He was broughtoup, on Tuesday, at the Police Court and was fined 7s. 6d. and costs, or ten days.

ASTON SCHOOL BOARD. •, At a special meeting of this Board, on Saturday, Miss Blanche Smith, of Weston, was appointed assistant mis- tress of Aston (mixed) school, with a salary of £35 per annum. Miss Smith succeeds Miss Deakin, resigned.

FUNERAL SERMONS AT RUNCORN.' On Sunday evening at St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Runcorn, the Rer. S. Pulford Williams, the pastor preached a funeral sermon occasion by the death of Mr. Robert Evans and Miss Pattie Evans, two members of the

church. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Safficey-sL., Warrington.—Advt. SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT RUNCORN. On Friday Mr. Worsley, the cowner, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court on the body of Annie Limb, six months old, daughter of John Limb, waterman of 37, Lock-st., who was found dead in bed on Thursday morn- ing. Dr. Carrutliers said he had examined the child,and was of opinion that death was the result of a convulsive fit. There was no evidence of overlying.—The jury returned a verdict accordingly. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. BENEFIT OF BRIGGS, SENR., AT WIDNES. The annual benefit of Mr. James Briggs, the ground. man of Widnes Cricket Club, was held on ;.laturday after- .noon. The proceedings opened with a cricket match which attracted a good number of spectators. At five o'clock a football match between 15 of Widnes and T. R. Sutton's team was played before about 3,000 spectators. • A closely contested and exciting game resulted in a draw no points being scored. The players afterwards sat down to a sumptuous tea at the Railway and Commer- cial Hotel, a musical entertainment following. SHIP CANAL FOREMAN IN TROUBLE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Gut tridge, a respectably dressed man, vies charged with being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night. Mr. Percy Davies appeared on his behalf, and pleaded guilty. He was also charged with assaulting Mr. Cooper, the landlord of . Wilson's Hotel, but Mr. Cooper had with- drawn the charge. The prisoner was a foreman on the Ship Canal, a pontoon builder, and had a large family, and he had expressed.his sorrow for what had occurred. He blamed the drink for having misbehaved himself. He was fined 55., and costs Os. 4d., or seven days hard labour. MAIL CARTS for children.—Gakand, Ironmonger, Warring- ton and Earlestown.—Advt. A NASTY SCUFFLE AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE. Richard Bilton, a deaf mute, was brought before Run- corn magistrates, on Monday, charged with absconding from Dutton Workhouse, with clothing belonging to the Union.—Mr. A Linaker, salicitor, prosecuted, and said on Sunday afternoon the Master, Mr. Cunnah, had occa- sion to interfere with the prisoner takinr, food from the dining room, and a vary nasty scuffle toOk place, but the Master did not desire to make a noise about it. After- wards the man climbed over the wall of the house and absconded ; he was afterwards apprended in Runcorn. He was a violent man, and he thought he ought to be examined by a doctor in order to ascertain whether he was accountable for his actions. As the prisoner did not know the deaf and dumb alphabet, the charge could not be communicted to him, and lie was remanded for a week and in the meantime he will be examined by a doctor.

WIDNES.'

John Pechenkis, a Pole, ie-siding at 33, Cromwell-5t., was brought up in custody charged with being drunk and disorderly and travelling on the L. and N. W.R. without a ticket, on the 13th Inst., P.C. Gordon deposed that at half-past eleven on Saturday night he was called to the London and N. W. R. station, Widnes, where he saw the defendant drunk and creating a disturbance. Sergeant M'Gregor stated that at 11.45 p.m. on Saturday night he saw the prisoner drunk in the Police Station. He (witness) asked him for his railway ticket, and he produced an old Runcorn Bridge ticket. Mr. M'Connell, station master, said when the prisoner got off the train, he would not give them any information respecting himself, nor produce a ticket. Win. Stott, ticket collec- tor at the above station, said he knew the prisoner, and saw him get off the train on Saturday night. He tried to get past without a ticket, but witness stopped him. He asked him for his fare, but the prisoner refused to pay it, although he had money in his pocket. The pri- soner, for being drunk, was fined ss. and costs, and for the second offence 105. and 12s. costs, or seven days ; in all, Ll 13s. 6d.
A PENITENT YOUTH AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, George Wendt, 19 years of age, of 17, Cholmondeley-st., was brought up in custody charged with stealing a pipe and case from a shop in Widnes-road, on Sunday, the 14th inst., the property of Ralph Kerr, tobacconist.—Alice Kerr said she was a single woman, and resided with her brother in Widnes-road. About eight o'clock on Sunday night, the prisoner came into the shop with two of his companions. They purchased some ginger beer, and afterserving them she left the shop to go into the kitchen. On returning she missed tke pipe and case produced. After they had left the shop, she followed them down Widnes-road, and overtook them near the Police Station. When she asked the prisoner for the pipe, she saw him hand it to one of his companions. The pipe and case were worth 7s. 6d.— John Roberts, one of the prisoner's companions, said he saw Wendt take the pipe (produced) out of a case on the counter, while Miss Kerr was in the kitchen. Witness along with the prisoner were going back to Mr. Kerr's shop to return the pipe when they met Miss Kerr.—The Chairman said it was a sad thing to see a young fellow like the prisoner act as he had done. It was a very unfortunate beginning, and the Bench hardly knew , whether they were doing right in letting him go. If he would promise not to offend again they would dismiss the case.—The promise having been given, the prisoner was 'discharged. ELECTRo PLATED GOODS.—Garland's oldest established Ironmonger, Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday night, a meeting of the Conservatives of the North and South polling districts of Widnes Par- liamentary division, was held at the Conservative club, Victoria-road. Mr. W. J. Stewart, chairman of the division, presided, and in opening the proceedings said he was glad to see they were to have a competition, be- cause he liked to have a good fight. He, as a general, never liked to think that his forces despised their antago- nist, but now they knew who they had to fight, and Mr. Moss had a foeman worthy of his steel. They were not afraid of their foe, but it was necessary to have all their weapons ready, so as they might be able to give a good account of themselves. He was rather amused that im- mediately after Mr. Deacon had been adopted, the first public meeting lie was invited to attend was a meeting of Nationalists of Widnes but the Liberal candidate found it inconvenient to attend, and sent an apology, in consequence of which he seemed 0 have got in a diffi- culty. He (Mr. Stewart) had not the slightest doubt that his last act, as the first had been, would be to ten- der his apology to the electors of Widnes division for having put them to the ;trouble and expense of a con- test. He had told their member, Mr. Moss, that a pub- lic meeting ought to be held in each polling district once in each year, so that they might take counsel with one another and keep their forces together for the day of con- ffict.—The necessary committees were appointed, and , Mr. R. Lewis was appointed chairman of the North I district and Mr. G. l'ride chairman of the South dis- trict. THE FATALITY AT WIDNES FOUNDRY. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an inquest at Widnes Police Station, on the body of Thomas Rogerson, aged 14 years, eon of George Rogerson, of Gladstone-street, who was killed at Widnes Foundry on Wednesday. Mr. F. J. Poole, solicitor, and Mr. S. Robinson, anpeared on behalf of the company.— Joseph Atherton, Church-street, said he was a furnaco- man at the foundry. On Wednesday he was in charge of the engine which drives the gearing a the sheerlegs. The sheerlegs were employed to raise a heavy iron ball, weighing about 30 cwt., which when raised to its proper height was allowed to drop for the purpose of crushing and breaking old iron. Ile was assisted by a man named' James Bennett, who pulled the rope which controlled the ball. The ball dropped and a large cog wheel broke, I pieces of which were sent flying about the room. The deceased was struck with something and fell down. The deceased was not engaged at the machine, but had been watching for -a few minutes.—By the Coroner :It would be safer if there were something tokeep the cog wheel in its place. They never oiled the cog wheel. He ordered the deceased away,but he refused to go.—James Bennett corroborated.—Thomas Allan Bffilough, 50, Peelhouse- lane, Farnworth,engineer to the Widnes Alkali CompanF, said on Wednesday he was sent for to Widnes Foundry. He examined the broken wheel, and from what he could see the metal seemed of excellent quality. The broken edges did not suggest old cracks. The teeth of the small cog wheel or pinion were fractured at the edges, and he inferred that the pinion was out of gear, and that if it came in contact with the large wheel whilst revolving rapidly, it might cause the wheel to break. The jury retired to consider their verdict, and after an hour's absence, they returned a verdict of " Accidental death " and made a suggestion that a notice board be put up warning the workmen not to go near the place when on their way to other parts of the workshop. RUNCORN POLICE COURT. At this Court on Thursday, Harriett Baxter and Louisa Murray were each sentenced:to -14 days hard labour for disorderly conduct. James Miller, was fined 10s. and costs for hawking without a license. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. A quorum could not be formed on Wednesday when the monthly meeting should have been held. The meet- ing will therefore be held on Wednesday next. The issue of books during August was 1866 a decrease of 131.

NATIONAL SCHOOLS, EUNCORN. To a large audience of children and their parents, Mr. T. H. Annett gave a magic lantern entertainment in the National schools ,on Monday night. The subject— The Life of Christ—was explained by the Rev. G. H. Kingston. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES. Harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday, when the Rev. Arthur McGilmour, of Prescot, preached two sermons to good congregations. In the afternoon a children's service was held, and the Rev. J. Calvert delivered an appropriate address. On Monday evening a service of song was given by a choir of 50 voices, under the leadership of Mr. W. Roach.; and the accompanist was Mr. J. T. Jones. Major Waring read the narrative. The collections caused a satisfactory augmentation of the Church funds. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zi-aland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " Office, by Cunard, GUIOTI, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, " Examiner Office. Bewsey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. • HARVEST FESTI VA LS AT RUNCORN. .The annual harvest thanksgiving service, in connection with Holy Trinity Church, was held on Thursday even- ing. The sacred edifice had been charmingly decorated with fruits, .cereals, and plants, and was much admired by the large congregation that assembled. The preacher was the R. Archdeacon Blakentl, chaplain to the Queen, who delivered an appropriate sermon.—A good congregation also assembled at the Church Of St Michael and All Angels, in the same evening, when the annual harvest thanksgiving service was held. The Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett, 8.D., vicar of Widnes, was the preacher. The church was decorated with the fruits of the earth, with the customary taste and ability. The choir rendered speciallyselectecl music.

DEATH OF Mn. PIERPOI NT, OF RUNCORN. Mr. Robert J. Pierpoint ; tanner, Halton-road, died on Sunday last after a lingering illness. He had attained the advanced age of 77 years, 57 of which he had spent in Runcorn, where he was much respected. Being of a retiring disposition he took no part in public affairs in the town, and his funeral was conducted in a most un- ostentatious manner according to his expressed desire. He was interred in the burial ground attached to Bethesda Congregational Chapel, with which he was formerly connected. The coffin was carried on the shoulders of four workmen. His sons, Mi. B. Bastock Pierpoint, and Mr. Robert Pierpoint were the chief mourneis. By his will the deceased gentleman has left £lO to be distributed amongst the poor of the town. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. aW. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. BILLIARD MATCH.—RUNCORN V. NORTHWICH. , On Wednesday afternoon a number of the members of Runcorn Liberal Club visited the Gladstone Club, North- wich, for the purpose of engaging in a billiard match. The journey was made in traps and the drive was much enjoyed. The visitors were heartily welcomed by the Northwich wielders of the cue, who entertained them to an excellent tea: Ten games were played, and Runcorn succeeded in winning b'y the narrow margin of 83 points. The return match will be played on Wednesday week. Details : RUNCORN. NORTHWICH. PLEURO-PNEIIMONIA IN LANCASHIRE. - Yesterday morning it was reported at the County Offices, Preaton, that pleuro-pneumonia had broken out on the premises of James Winstanley, Bedford Mill, Leigh. Two animals in a herd of 13 have been attacked and will be killed to-day (Saturday). DISAPPEARANCE OP A WIDNES LANDLADY. The inhabitants of the nighbourhood of the Arch Hotel, West Bank, have had a fruitful source of gossip during theyast few days in the disappear- ance of Mrs. Carrighar, landlady of that hostelry. By a strange coincidence, a lodger named Hop- wood, who hails from the Lancashire tOwn of Bury, and is a married man, has not since been seen. Mrs. Carrighar has left two children in the charge of a man named Jones, of Bridge-street. At the Widnes Petty Sersions on Thursday. the license of the hotel was transferred to Mr. Machin, manager of the Mar- ket Hotel. MR..CONINGSBY DISRA.ELI delivered an address on Wednesday night. at a meeting in connection with the Withington Habita- tion of the Primrose League. Referring to the ob- struction in the House of Commons, and the conse- quent failure of Ministers to pass some of their measures, be said the first duty of the Government was to administer the law rather than to pass new legiSlation. He maintained that the present Govern- ment had done this in such a way as to produce confidence, and that the result had been commercial prosperity, which had been to the advantage of all BATHS, all kinds.—J. S. Garlands, Ironmonger. 51,:Bridge Street, Warrington. Branch—Barlestown.-41clet. MEMORIAL TO A LANCASHIRE RAILWAY CHAIRMAN.

On Wednesday, a bronze statuette, the work of .tir. F. J. Williamsgn, and inserted into one of the central columns of the entrance to the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Station, at Liverpool, was unveiled by Mr. R. T. Armitage, the chairman of the Company. It is a statuette of the late Mr. John Pearson, chairman of the railway, an ex-Mayor of Liverpool, and an ex-fligh Sheriff of Lancashire. During Mr. Pearson's term of office the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway made considerable progress. The ceremony attracted a large concourse of people. The Directors of the Company and other officials attended, amongst them being Sir D. Radcliffe and Messrs,. Heywood, Bright, William Tunstall, and John Ratasbottom, directors. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-3. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adrt. THE STRIKES IN AUSTRAL/A.

The Warrington Trades' Council have issued an appeal to the various branches of industry in War- rington, soliciting immediate support for their brethren who are at present locked out, in Austra- lia. The circular says:—Support, in this case! to be effective.. must be rendered with the greatest promptitude. The Council trust that the generous way in which our Colonial brethren responded, last year, to the appeal of the London dock labour- ers—forwarding a total contribution of .£38,000— will insure a liberal response to the appeal which is now made on their behalf. Freely as we have re- ceived, therefore, let us as freely give. The com- mittee will sit from sto 6o' clock, on Saturdays, at the Cocoa rooms, Horsemarket-st., to receive monies collected ;or forward same to secretary, W. Bullock, 10; Brackley-st., Warrington.

WINES SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tnesday. Mr. T, S. Timmins presided and there Were present the Rev. Dean Finegan, the Rev. Fr. Clarke, Messrs. C. E. Barlow, S. Quinn, Dr. O'Keeffe, Major Wareing, and a IL Denby (clerk.) DISTRICT' EDUCATION COMMITTEE. A report of the work of this Committee for the paSt 12! months was presented. There were 4,446 cases presented before the Committee as compared with 3,83 a in 1880 t. These represented 1,740 and 1,708 persons respectively. 58T persons applied for the payment of fees in 2,004: cases ;. as compared with 561 persons, and 1,542 cases.. The Committee recommended the payment of the fees in 1.806 cases, last year 1,522. There were 405 prosecutions before the magistrates and 364 were fined ss. Last year 431 were prosecuted and 417 fined. One boy was com- mitted to an industrial school and 15 to a truant school, and at the present time there were 10 children in truant schools and 3/ in industrial schools. Last year there were no children in truant schools, and there were-382 in industrial schools.—The report was adopted. SCI3DOE ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE .—This Committee re- commended the following appointments :---John Birken- head, certified assistant senior boys department, Simms Cross, at £lO a year. Thomas Philips, certified assistant, senior boys, Warrington-road, salary £741 Alice Woods, assista-nt, junior boys, Wet Bank, salary £35. Recom- mended that the following be appointed teachers at the central classes of pupil teachers, viz., Miss Harris, sewing ; Miss Robertson, domestic economy • and Miss Wood, composition and writing. Recommended that the best thanks of the Board be given to the Rev. J. Roger ' Jones, MA.,for conducting the examination of the Boards pupil teachers in Biblical knowledge for the year 1690. The minutes were passed on the motion of Dean Fine- gan.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee reported the payment of ac- counts amounting to £5112 13s. The receipts amounted to £lBO 9s. Id. Carried. THE SALARIES SCHEME. A letter was read from Mr. Showan head master at Simms Cross school, complaining that in the new schemes of salary equal justice was not done. Dean Finegan said the Committee had no wish to injure the teachers of any school, and the communication was referred to the 'School management Committee..

' WIDNES IRISH NATIONALISTS AND MR. • DEACON. At the usual weekly meeting of the Widnes Branchof the Irish National League, Dr. O'Keeffe' presided, and after mentioning that the ultimate success of the Home Rule cause was certain; said he had a particular object in being present at that meeting. They were aware that for some time past the Liberal Association of the Widnes Division had been en- gaged in selecting a person to contest the division in the Liberal interest at the forthcoming general election, and he was proud to say that their efforts had resulted in the selection of a gentleman who was well-known to all of them, namely, Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., of the firm of Messrs. Gaskell,Deacon,and Company. He need not tell them that Mr. Deacon was in favour of Home Rule, and was pledged to support the Home Rule policy of Mr. Gladstone. Be was also in favour of free education, and also compensation to publicans in certain extreme cases. The Pories would do all they could to return Mr. Moss, but he was confident that their efforts. in that direction would fail. It was therefore the duty of every Irishman and Liberal in Widnes to see that his name was on the register. Be felt certain that no Irishman would be- grudge losing a day's work to see that he was placed upon the register, and thus help to return Mr. Deacon' at the head of the poll, with a triumphant majority. The fol- lowing resolution was then unanimously adopted, on the motion of Mr. Horan, sec•mded lop Mr. 114ach "That we, the members of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League, pledge ourselves to support by every means in our power the candidature of Mr. Deacon at the forthcoming election ; and in order to place him at the head of the poll we hereby call upon every Irishman in Widnes who can claim a vote to do so at the Revision Court on the 30th inst."

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST RUNCORN POLICEMEN. Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Dr. Steele, at Run- corn Petty Sessiuns, on Monday, Lawrence Costello, a police sergeant stationed at Sutton, and William Fryer, a police constable of the same place, were summoned for having assaulted Joseph Foscley, on the sth September. Foscley was summoned for having been drunk at the same time. Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, appeared for Foscley, and the police were represented by Mr. Cartwright, of Chester.—Mr. Davies wished to charge the officers with being drunk, but after discussion the case was proceeded with as it stood.— From the statement of the advocate, it appeared that , Foscley was a labourer, and lived next door to the Weaver Tavern, Frodsham Bridge, which is kept by his sister-in-law, Mrs. Edge, and since he left the Ship Canal works, three weeks ago, he had assisted her in the management of the business. On the Friday night in question, Charles Chesworth, Foscley's uncle, whom he had not seen for 18 years, called in the house, and at closing time he took him into his house to have supper. They had beans and bacon, and a glass of beer each,and that was all the drink they had. They were quite sober. A little after eleven o'clock Foscley left to take Ches- worth across the Marsh to Rock Savage. When they were near the mill, they passed the sergeant and con- stable,whc,after they had gone about 20 yards,returned, and ran roughly against them. Fryer then searched Chesworth, planing his hand in his watch pocket, in such a manner that Chesworth asked him if he wanted to rob him. Costello at the same time was searching Foscley, and in doing so struck him about the body. At last' Costello placed his hand at the back of Foscley's neck and gave him a push, and then Fryer thrust him in the back with the point of a stick. He afterwards struck him on the shoulder blade,and he said "I think you have done enough." Costello replied "give it the —." and Fryer gave him a blow with the stick behind the ear and inflicted a wound which bled freely. Chesworth went on towards Rock Savage and Foscley ran home. His wife went down to the mill and asked the officers why they had been abusing her husband,but they denied that they had done so, and followed her home. The Sergeant said they had a warrant against Foscley and could take him at any time, Foseley told them to leave his house, but the sergeant would not until he said " please." Mr. Davies commented upon the difficulty he had in getting I witnesses' as respectable people were afraid of swearing against the sergeant.—Foscley cor- roborated this statement. In cross-examination lie ad- wit,tted that he had been myicteci of.....arne trespass, and. that there wag a Waiiii-it 51,fdtlit him for an assault. Confirmatory evidence was given by ChesseOrth, Sarah lidge, Mrs. Foscley, and W. Jackson.—Alfred Redford, a young man, stated that at half-past six on the day named, he saw Sergeant Costello playing bowls with Mr. Turley , at the Norton Arms Hotel Green, Halton. He was get- ting "nicely on "and could not walk straight. He went in search of P.C. Fryer to report him.—Mr. Cartwright,in his speech for the defence, said police constables had onerous duties to perform, and in the exercise of those duties they earned among the lower class of the people, bitter and undying hatred. If the allegations in this case were true it would jeopardise the char- acters and position of the officers. He contended that the officers had no motive for such ridiculous con- duct as that described, and argued that the evidence of Foscley, who was a convicted poacher, was not to be relied upon. Then, too, Sergeant Costello was to give evidence in a case charging Mrs. Edge with a breach of her license,and she would not be actuated by the best feelings towards him .—The defence of the officers was a complete denial of the charge.—P.S. Costello deposed that he had been in the force 13 years, and 11 months as sergeant. He spoke of the meeting with •Foscley and Chesworth, and he searched the former in the ordinary way, because he was a well-known poacher. Foscley was drunk, and cursing and swearing, and wit- ness told him he should report him. There was no violence used whatever, Subsequently Mrs. Foscley came and inquired why Fryer had "laid on her hus- band." Witness informed her that he could not have done so, as he had not been out of his sight since nine , o'clock. He went to the house to see what the complaint was, and found Foscley had a slight scratch behind the ear. Witness offered to go with Foscley to the doctors, but he said he would go in the morning. Foscley, was sitting on the chair and was swearing all the time witness was in the house. Neither he or Fryer were drunk. He was on the Bowling (keen for about half- an-hour, but he was not playing a game, Mr. Turley was showing him how the game vcre played. He was in uniform,but was not on duty. He had nothing to drink ~ there. He had never had I.nythingstrenger than ginger beer in a public-house.—ln cross-essmination witness. denied the evidence of the prosecution point by point. He was not in the habit of going into farmhouses for drink,nor of drinking in McWaters' house.—George Ward,' relieving officer, Runcorn, said the sergeant when on the ' green was perfectly sober, as was P.C. Fryer. He did not see either of the officers in the Norton Arms.—Geo. Turley said he was teaching Costello the game. He did not see him have anything to drink. P.C. Fryer said lie had never touched , intoxicating liquor during the whole of the day. With I reference to the meeting at the mill, he searched Ches- worth because he was in comnany with Foscley. He did not use any violence, nor did he search his watch pocket. He denied that he struck Foscley with a stick or anything else. Foscley was drunk. Allen Lovell, lock tenter, William Hazlett, foreman miller, and Peter Heyes gave evidence that the officers were perfectly sober, and conducted the search without violence. No assault was committed. Foscley was under the influence of drink. The magistrates,who were engaged nearly six hours in hearing the case, dismissed the whole of the summonses.

HanvEsr TnamisoiviNo SERVICES.—On Sunday, ser- mons were preached in the United MeOedist. Free Church, Frodsham, by the Rev. H. Fothergill, pastor, afternoon and evening. The decorations were of a choice character, and the church presented quite a charming appearance. Large congregations attended the services, but particularly the one held in the evening, when the church was filled. On Monday eveninga public meeting was held in connection with the festival.. when Mr. B. , Parker, Helshy, presided, and addresses were giien by the Revs. H. Fothergill and P. Pizey, a.t4 other gentle- men. Mairrliaos or Mins RIGBY.—On Wednesday morning a marriage, in which much interest was taken,: was solemnized at the Pariah Church. The bridegroom ins Mr. Josiah Wyatt Lane, of Brighton, and the bride Miss K. & Rigby, daughter of Mr. James Rigby, sen. of Belle Monte. The bride, who was charmingly attired, and who carried a splendid bouquet, was given away, by, her father, the bridesmaids being the Misses Jane and Alice Linaker, Mr. B. A. The church: was well filed with the friends of the happy couple, who, subSeqUently went to Bournemouth, where the honeymoon will be spent. The presents were numerous and costly. DRAINAGE BOARD MEETING.—A meeting 'of the rate- payers within the Frodsham and Ffelsby Drainage Board district was held last evening, in the Town Hall, Frodsham, which waS presided over by Mr. Henry Beswick, returning officer. The meeting having been called for the purpose of electing new members of the Board for the ensuing twelve months, the list of persons qualified to serve as members was read, when the follow- ing were unanimously appointed :—Owners Messrs. William Hayes, Ashton Hayes; and. Arthur H. Telbot, Dlettort Lodge. Occupiers Messrs. James Andrews, Frtdshann ; Ralph Bate, Netherton • Wm. Booth, Frods- ham; Henry Beswick, Barrow ; Thomas Davies, , Frodsham ; John Eititton,Woodhouses ; Joseph Ellams, Helsby ; John Priestner, Frodsham; James Percival, Godscroft ; Thomas Ellarns, Helsby ; Joseph Smith, . Netherton; Geo. Eakins, Helsby ; and David Savage, Helsby, the whole of the above-named gentlemen being re-appointed with the exception of Mr. Talbot, who takes the place of Mr. E. A. Wright, J.P., Castle Park, . Frodsham, a member of the Board since its formation. Mr. Wright's retirement is much regretted by those in whose interest he has laboured for the past ten years.

SHEEP STEALING.—PRISONERS COMMITTED FOR TRIAL. Yesterday (Friday), at Frodsham Police Court, before Mr. Charles Reynolds, Thomas Jackson, George Jackson sour., Alexander Jackson, and Samuel Harvey, labourers, and Margaret Jackson, wife of George were charged

! with having between the 13th and 15th inst., stolen a Scotch weather sheep, value £2, the property of John Priestner, farmer and butcher, Main-sr., Frodsham. On Saturday afternoon prosecutor had 77 sheep on Frodsham Marsh, and on Monday at noon he found there was one missing. He gave information to the police and next morning he was sent for to the police station and shown the bead of the sheep, which was marked, that he had missed. About a fortnight ago he missed a sheep in the same way, and for five or six years sheep stealing had been a common occurrence in the neighbourhood.—After 1 bearing evidence, his worship committed the prisoners for trial at the Quarter Sessions, and agreed to admit them to bail in £lO each and two sureties of £lO Each. •

div.p: PENKETII.

Cuuncir MISSION. On Wednesday evening the harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above mission. The serv- ices were conducted by the Rector of Warrington, Canon Cross being prevented from attending by family bereavement. There was a full congrega- tion ; collection £l2. The interior was very taste- fully decorated. • A Bo Y RUN OVER. On Saturday, as the one o'clock !bus from Penketh to Warrington started to leave the village, a boy named Singleton, about six years old, ran after it, with the intention of riding on the step. Finding he could not catch it he. gave up the, attempt, and, stopped in the middle of the road. As he did so the trap of Mr. Joseph Humphreys, of Cuerdley Cross, was passing, and, seeing the boy in the way, the occupants shouted to him, but he did not appear to , realize his danger, and before the trap could be drawn up, the boy was knocked down and mu over, the wheels going over his legs just above the ankles. He was immediately conveyed home, and medical assistance was obtained. It was found that no bones were broken, but one of the boy's leo was severely bruised. SINGULAR INCIDENT AT FIDLERS FERRY

• STATION. A singular incident occurred at Fiddlers Ferry Station, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. R. Fisher, a: local coal dealer, having coal in the siding, had loaded his cart, and was about to leave the yard, when he discovered the gates locked, and he was refused egress. The peculiar part of the affair con- I sists in the fact that, the officials having let Fisher in, knowing how near was the time for closing the yard, then refused to let him out. What they in- tended to do with the horse until Monday morning is hard to say. Fisher, finding the predicament he was in, hastened to Warrington to interview the district goods manager, and came back armed with instructions that he was not to be interfered with by the station officials in this way. Mr. Fisher, we , understand, quite expects that compensation will be made to him for his loss in having two horses besides men standing idle for two hours and i half while he went to Warrington.

THE RECREATION SCHEME. On Tuesday eveningli large and influntial meet- ing of the public of Penketh was held in the Wes- leyan day schools, to further consider the formation of a Limited Liability Co. for recreative and build- ing purposes. Mr. C. E. Parker occupied the chair, and gave a very clear and concise sketch of the objects of the company as stated in our last week's report of the first meeting. Mr. Parker invited questions and the invitation was readily accepted, and a lively and interest- ing discussion took place, questions being asked and suitably answered with regard to the acreage required, which was propoAed at 22 statute acres, amount of capital required to float the scheme, water supply for baths, age of shareholders, pur- chase of land and price, &c. The following gentle- men took part in the discussion :—Messrs. R. Garnett, J. C. Routledge, E. Cross, H. S. Jones, G. D. Bryant, R. Boardman, J, Maipleyt and J. T: cinmer, salt Many matters orpublic interest cropped. ttp,one of these being a gas and water supply for Penketh, and a feeling was expressed that someone should undertake to supply the village with the same, as there was apparently difficulties in the way as far as Warrington was concerned. The very sore ques- tion of the present recreation ground was touched upon. Mr. J. T. Gumniereall stated he had had an interview with the lord of the manor, Mr. Hughes, and he (Mr. Hughes) had said in effect that he would consult his solicitors 'and see what could be done in the case. At present it appears that the land cannot be disposed of by the owners, nor can the sod be turned to make the ground suitable for cricket or bowling. It was thought the voice of the meeting should be taken as regards the Park Co. and Mr. Gummersall moved the following resolution: 'That this meeting has listened to toe plan sketched out by Mr. Parker for the formation of a public recre- ation ground, Szc., for Penketh and heartily advo- cates the further prosecution of the scheme." The formation of a committee and a vote oithanks to the I Chairman brought the meeting to a close..

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

That although the Tories of Widnes Division may not be afraid of Mr. Deacon, the Liberal candidate, it is clear from Mr. Stewart's remarks, on Wednes- day night, that they think they have a tremendotis struggle before them. That hitherto it has not been thought necessary for Mr. Moss to visit each polling district once a year, or even to visit the chief town in the divi- sion in that space of time, but Mr. Stewart has awakened to the fact that Mr. Moss ougl.t to see his constituents more frequently than up to the pre- sent has been considered essential to his success. That a weak attempt was made to. extract -capital from Mr. Deacon's inability to attend the meeting of local Irish nationalists, and Mr. Stewart is a• little " too previous "in his prophecy. That perhaps—who knows? Mr. Moss may have the unpleasant task of making his bow and retiring once again into private life. That Mr. Deacon has addressed a meeting of the Council of the Liberal Association and his views were received with the warmest approbation. That Home Rule and Free Education are two prominent articles in Mr. Deacon's political creed, and lie will without doubt have the solid vote of the Liberal party and the Irish party in the Division. That it is assuring to have it on the authority of the respected secretary of theßuncorn Burial Board that there is accommodation in the Cemetery for the present generation of Runcomians, and genera- tions yet unborn. That as the Cemetery has been opened for 30 years and for ninety years yet Will fulfil its I.urpose the ratepayers of that day amply did their duty .in the provision they made, and as one of the members observed by the time more land might be needed, cremation might be universally in vogue, and the ratepayers would not require a Cemetery, , but urns for the dust of their departed relatives. That sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. That a policeman's life is not a happy one when constabulary duty's to be done, and the case which occupied the Runcorn Bench of magistrates for nearly six hours on Monday afforded proof of the truth of the saying. That the evidence was so contradictory that the Bench had only one course open to them and dis- missed both summonses. That Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys has followed up his victory at the poll for members of the Board of Commissioners by leading a bride to the altar, and he will now become " one of us " more completely than before. The wide circle who have the pleasure of his acquaintance, will join in wishing the newly married couple happiness and long life.
MARRIAGE OF MR. E. 'WYNNE:, HUMPHREYS, OF RUNCORN.

At St. John's Church, 1.. ongsigh t, Manchester, on Wednesday, 'Miss Ellen Taylor, only daughter of Ur. Samuel Taylor, maili*clurer, of Victoria Park Manchester, was married to Mt. E. Wynne Hum- phreys, solicitor,of tank Charhhera, Itancorn,and the" event possessed considerable interest to the people of Runcorn, amongst whom Mr. Humphreys had taken a most useful and prominent position since he commenced to practice his profession in the town. The ceremony took place at half-past nine, and was performed by the Rev. C. P. Roberts, M.A., the Rector of the parish. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in an ivory cash- mere dress, with train, and trim med with orange blossom ; and also wore a wreath and veil fastened with a pearl crescent, the gift of the bridegroom. The bride was at- tended by her cousin Miss Emily Dyson, of Huddersfield, who was dressed in cream crepon, with white hawthorn hat, and adorning her throat w.rts a gold brooch the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. Frank Whitworth of Manches- ter, officiated as the best man. After the service, the guests, who consisted of the respective families of the bride and bridegroom, adjourned to Mr. Taylor's resi- denco, where breakfast was provided. The menu was as follows : Soups : Capon, macedoine; fish: salmon, soles en mayonnaise; entree: cutlets and peas •, joints: lamb— mint sauce roast fowls, tongue, roast ducklings, boiled chickens, ;lam, roast beef; game: grouse; dressed lobster; Pate de Foie Gras; sweets: macedoine jellies, vanilla creams, compote of apricots, cheese cakes, almond pastry; ices: vanilla cream, strawberry cream; dessert : pines, grapes, peaches, filberts, etc. The usual toasts were proposed and responded to. Later in the day Mr. and Mrs. Humphreys departed for Holyhead en route for Dublin, Killarney, and the west of Ireland where the honeymoon will be spent. The list of presents were very numerous and costly and the following is a partial list:— Mr. Taylor, cheque, sewing machine, &c. Mrs. Taylor, breakfast service, &c. THE CHEMICAL UNION.

, • The opponents to the launching of :the Chemical Union will, no doubt, besorry to hear that the com- bination is practically accomplished. Many have been hoping that their wordy warfare would have prevented the proposed cotnbination, but like all others who enter too zealously into the work they have in hand, they have So far over-reached their point as to show the general public the strength of the alkali makers' position. The fact is, the Alkali Union has a very strong position, and there is no reason why the public should not look quite as favourably upon the proposed combination as they did upon the Salt Union. If anything, the chemical trade generally possesses more fea- tures of interest than the manufacture of salt alone. As we go to press, the Constructive Committee of the Chemical Union are reported to be holding a meeting of alkali manufacturers at the North- Western Hotel in Liverpool, for the purpose of ex- plaining the present position, and of having their actions confirmed by the trade.—Chemical Trade Totowa. The meeting spoken of above passed off very suc- cessfully, and it was stated the manufacturers themselves are prepared to underwrite the whole ot the purchase money it need be.
