div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

ASSAULT ON • BIaCrTHBR. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, John McGuire, a young man, was charged with drunkenness, and with having committed an assault upon his brother. It was stated that the defendant struck his brother severely, but as the latter did not appear to give evidence against him, a fine of ss. and costs only was imposed.

ASSAULT ON A MoTurin. On Thursday, at tke Warrington Police court, a young man named John Troy was charged with having as- saulted his mother, on the 15th instant., by striking her. He complained of his mother's conduct, but admitted having assaulted her. She did not wish to press the case, but the magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs.

NEGIJICT OF FAMILY. On Saturday the Warrington magistrates had before them a man named Frank Miller, a puddler, who was charged with deserting his child in February, 1889. He was sent to prison for three months, with hard labour. He had cost the guardians about ET, including £3, the expenses of bringing him from Stockton-on-Tees, where he was arrested on warrant.

div.head: DRINK AND VIOLENCH,
div.p: DRINK AND VIOLENCH,

At the Warring;;;-Folic;-Court, on Thursday, George Connolly was charged in custody with having, on the previous night,been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, and with having assaulted Sergeant Jones and Con- stable Bell. The officers stopped the defendant, where- upon he kicked them and was taken into custody. It was his 25th appearance. He was now fined 10s, and costs for being drunk, and 20s. and costs for the assault. AN UNCORROBORATED CHARGE OF TEMPT. On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, dames Rickett, Annie Daley, or Rickett, and Mary fikully were charged by a fish hawker named Patrick Dovey with having, on the night before, knocked him down in Academy-street, and stolen from him a purse contain- ,p6r les, 3d. The prisoners loudly proclaimed their innocence, and as there was no evidence to corroborate t he statement of the complainant, they were discharged. The magisti&tes said that they believed Dovey had been robbed, but the evidence as against the prisoners was not sufficiently strOng to watt a conviction.

TRAVELLING ON THE RAILWAY WITHOUT TICKETS. This offence was charged against Margaret Fallon and Chas. Cooper, at the Warrington Police Court, on Tues- day, and they were each fined 10s. and costs. On the arrival of a late train on Monday night, at Arpley, from Manchester, the female prisoner, who was drunk, failed to produce a ticket, but asserted that at Oxford-rd. she had given the money for her fare to a porter. The other prisoner, Cooper. said that on Monday afternoon he was at Ditton, and got too much drink. Ile booked to Widnes, fell asleep, and was carried to Manchester, whence the officials sent him back as far as Warrington, telling him to walk the remainder of the distance to Widnes.

BAD FISH IN THE MARKET. A Wigan fish dealer, named Clayton, was summoned to appear before the Warrington magistrates on Monday. to answer a charge of having exposed for sale unwhole- some fish in the Market Shed on Saturday, the 6th inst. The defendant did not appear, and the case was heard in his absence. Inspector Norman said that on Saturday night he seized 321bs. of fish on the defendant's stall. It was in a very decomposed condition. The defendant when he (witness) took the fish away used disgraceful language, and threatened to cut him to pieces with a large knife which he was brandishing.—Clayton was fined 10s. and costs for using profane language, and £2 and costs for offering the fish for sale. A DISHONEST SERVANT. Selina Rowlands, a domestie servant, was brought before the Warrington magistrates on Tuesday, on two charges of theft. She was in the service of Mr. and Mrs. Ravenscroft, Friar's-green, when £2 was missed from a box belonging to a lodger. On this discovery being made, Ravenscroft made a search,and then missed a purse, containing 4s. 6d., and nne or two miscellaneous articles. Prisoner having left her employment suddenly, suspicion rested upon her, and she was apprehended. She now pleaded guilty, and it was stated that she was incorrigi- ble, and had brought a great deal of trouble upon her .mother, a widow, who lives in Winwick-road. When arrested she was wearing new clothes, and had a new umbrella. She was sent to prison fer three months, with hard labour_

STEALING A 'THEATRICAL MANAGER'S HAT. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a man giving the name of James Hopkins was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday evening, and with stealing from Thomas Thorn, at the Theatre Royal, a black felt hat, value 2s. Bd. The defendant was engaged on Monday week to load a lorry with actors' property, and, after being paid, was told to come again on Saturday night. He turned up then the worse for liquor, and after performing some slight duties he was paid and told to go away. He re- fused,and assaulted the property man, but the police coming up he went away. Later on he returned and jumped on Mr. Thorn's back,throwing that gentleman to the ground. He picked up Mr. Thorn's hat and then ran away, but was apprehended an hour later by Police Con- stable Davies. Prisoner was committed to jail for one month, with hard labour. A PHELIC-HOOSE DISTIIIIIMICCH.—ASSA.IILT ON A LANDLORD.
itirned

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, two men named Patrick Burke and Edward Kay, the former an old offender, were charged with being drunk and refus- ing to quit the licensed premises of the Horse and Jockey Inn, on Friday, and with assaniting Peers Brimelow, the landlord, and Thomas Bate, his assistant. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, prosecuted, and said the two prisoners 'kicked up a fearful row on Friday, and he should ask the Bench to deal severely with them. Kay was a fish dealer in Winwick-rd., and was a customer at the public-'house ; but he had been warned by the land- lord not to bring any such characters there as the other prisoner. On Friday afternoon the two men entered the house, but the barmaid refused to serve them, and they went on the bowling ground, and there wilfully smashed a glass. Bate, the assistant, remonstrated with Burke, who thereupon knocked him down. The landlord was fetched, and'he ordered them away, but they attempted to assault him. In a few minutes the men left, return- ing two hours later, asking again to be served with beer. They were again refused, and then they assaulted Bate, knocking hits on the floor and kicking him. Kay, seeing that Mr. Brimelow was going to the barman's assistance, struck him in the face, and Burke afterwards assaulted him in the kitehan. The magistrates committed Burke to gaol for three months with hard labour. Kay, who made his first appearance, was let off with a fine of 20s. and oosts, altogether £2 Bs. 6d.
MINOR, CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

DISTURBING TSB PlLLCB.—iimn Cunningham, for creat- ing a breach of the peace by being disorderly in Butter- Market-street on the 2nd September, was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for 14 days. Bavien OF TIM BTELAWS.—Tbomas Carty, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to take fire on the 10th September, was fined is. °ASCE= SANGUAGH.—Mary McGuire was summoned for using obscene language on Friar's-green on the Hth inst., and was fined 2s. 6d. P.C. Wade proved the case. I Di us CBARGE.—James Moran, for having been drunk in charge of a horse and cart in Scotland-road,' was fined ss. ande4sts.—John Bradshaw, for a similar offence in Bridge-street, on Saturday morning, was fined a like SUM. TOSSING.—Two ouths named respectively Thomas Hawkins and Michael Healey, were summoned for tossing for money on Sunday afternoon in Howley-fields. Both the defendants pleaded guilty.—P.C.'s Jones and Critch- /ey proved the case, and the defendants were each fined 2s• f3d.
TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett and Mr. E. M. Crosfield.

Scnoor. Avraxrarms Cass.—Several persons were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fines were imposed. Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, proved the cases. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Mr. John Fairclou gh DIIIINIKENNESS.—John Connolly and Mary Riley were each fined 10s. and costs for this offence. Catherine Browne and Mary Ainsworth were fined ss. and costa for I a similar offence.

Them—Elizabeth Brimelow, charwoman, was fined 10s. and costs for stealing from a wardrobe itt the dwelling-house of Mr. Gee, Thelwall-lane, Latchford, where she was employed. THURSDAY :—Before Major Litton and Major Pickmere. BRUNKENNESS.—For this offence Margaret Donaldson was sent to prison fora week, and Sarah O'Brien was cautioned and allowed to go on promising to leave the
town. FSLIDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison. _
and Dr. Gornall.
DammENNEss.—Elizabeth Hawkins, charged with hav- ing been drunk in Wilson Patten-st., on the night before, was cautioned and dismissed.

A PALTRY CASE.—Frank Leigh was summoned for hav- ing assaulted Mary Ann Forrest, who, in her turn was summoned for assaulting Martha Leigh. In connection with the same case El za Smallwood was summoned for using threats towards Mary Ann Forrest, and the latter was charged with threatening Mrs. Smallwood. The parties quarrelled about a farthing cane. Mary, Ann Forrest was fined ss. and costs, and the other cases were dismissed. THREATS.—Patrick Shaughnessy was bound over to be of good behaviour, he having used threats towards Alice Carney.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Withington and Mr. James Tinsley. THE DOGS' ORDER.—The following persons were fined Is. and costs for allowing their dogs to be at large, un- muzzled :—John Jones, Orford ; Mary Massey, Martins- croft; the Rev. J. J. Langham, Padgate ; and George Sudlow, Houghton. DRIINICENNESS.—For this offence Joseph Wright, Mark Magann, James Coyne, and James lace, were each fined ss. and costs.
FURIOUS DRIYING.—James Woolley was fined 10s. and costs for furiously driving on the highway. THE EDUCATION ACT.—Several persons were fined for neglecting to send their children regularly to school.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Z. Armitage and Mr. Cecil F. Parr. DatrwicENNEss.—A labourer living at Winwick, named Henry Webb, was charged with being drunk at Croft on the 13th inst., and was ordered to pay the costs. P.C. McMullin proved the case.—Martin Gibbon was brought up on a warrant charged with being drunk at Grappen- hall on the 23rd September, 1888, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. Constable Millington proved the case.

DRUNKENNESS. —For this offence Brian Eaves, Martha Flannery, Michael Glynn, John McCabe, Brian Redmond, and John McDonald, were each fined ss. and costs. Catherine Lynch made her 33rd appearance, and was fined 10s. and costs.

BREACHES OF THE PNACE.—For this offence Mary Ann I Daley, Elizabeth Ryan, Winifred Carney, Thos. Roberts, and Bridget Oats were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months. Prrat AND Toss.—Edward Shone, Luton-st., and Patrick Finn, Eleanor-st., were each fined Is. and costs for playing pitch and toss in Luton-st., on the 6th inst. A STRAY HoasE, —A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon WM. Hewitt, of Mill-field-rd., for allowing his horse to stray in Lugsdale-rd. BOYS AND FIRBVIORKS.—WiIIiam Glynn, Nelson-st., a boy, was summoned for discharging fireworks in Water- lee-road on the 6th inst.—P.C. Gordon said the defend- ant was throwing the fireworks in people's faces as they passed along.—The father said it was wrong that shop- keepei s should sell fireworks to boys.—On the defendant promising not to offend again, he wasdischarged on pay- ing costs. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—Edward Jones, of 26, Bridge-st., was summoned for assaulting Alfred Bowden on the 14th inst. Mr. Knowles appeared for the complainant. It was alleged that the defendant called Mrs. Bowden names, and when her husband interfered struck him a violent blow. Mrs. Bowden in cross-examination admitted that she had spit at Jones.—The defendant said he had anted under great provocation,and as he promised not to offend again, the case was dismissed.

RUNCORN PETIT SESSIONS. MONDAT.—Before Mr. Hy. Reynolds and Dr. Steel. PERMISSION TO SELL.—On the application of Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, John Massey was granted permission to sell at the Albion Inn, Nelson-st., under the license held by C. Erinshaw. DRUNK AND DISORDBRLY.—For this offence S. Jones, Maurice Kelly, J. Burke, and J. Butterworth were each fined ss. and costs. BELL RINGING nv GRHINWAY-RD.—Frank Lindley and ' Jos. Clarke boys, were summoned for annoying the in- habitant.* of Greenway-rd., by tinging the bells of cer- tain houses on the 9th inst. P.S. Gosling proved the case, and said the defendants had a piece of string at- tached to the bell handle and stood across the road. Whenever anyone passed, they allowed the string to lie on the ground. Many complaints had been made. Superintendent Large said bell ringing had become a great nuisance in the neighbourhood. The defendants were ordered to pay 4s. 6d. costs. REFUSING TO QUIT.—J. Jones and J. Percival, labour- ers, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and refusing to quit the Rose and Crown Inn. For a like offence committed at the Quarry Hotel, Weston, A. Kilgrass was fined ss. and costs. A CARELESS DRIVBE.—J. Bowers, a young man, was fined 6d. and costs for riding on a waggon without reins. _ .
_ BREAM; OP TUB Paacs.—For fighting together at Weston, on the 6th inst., J. Kilcraft and M. Lae were each bound over to keep the peace for six months.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note tint reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington. not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
ST. MILEINS OLD BOYS v. Rurrcontr Rues. "A."—The St. Helens Old Boys opened their season with a match against Runcorn Recs. " A," and the game ended in a draw of two minors each.
Scrvon v. FRODSHAM.—(AIIiance Match.)—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday, in beautiful weather. When time was called, Sutton had won by 2 —2-3 to 1-o—l or, 25 points to 7.

WARRINGTON A v. LAIIASTIIIL A.—The opening match of the season for these teams was fought at Lancaster on Saturday, the Warringtonians for the first time journey- ing to the ancient county town of Lancashire. The day proved beautifully fine, but intensely hot. A good mus- ter of spectators assembled to see how the homesters would fare with the" champions,' and both teams were applaudeden entering the enclosure, the sides being composed as follows :—Warrington : Full back, Boscow ; three-cararter backs, Daniels, Heesom, and Webster; half backs, Lawless and Mather; forwards, Davies (captain), Beard., Povey, Littlewood, Neild, Rowe, Holmes, Isher- wood, and Thornley. Lancaster: Full back, Hartley three-quarter backs, Stevenson, Goodman, and Boak ; half backs, Gardener and Denby; forwards' Carter, Jones, Watson, Punchard, High, Fisher, Lofthouse, Barber, and Pinch. Fisher had the better of the tossing argument with Davies, and was thus enabled to take advantage of a powerful sun. Isherwood commenced operations, and after a series of long kicking, Stevenson CAIRO away with a rush until pulled up by Webster at the quarter flag. Lawless retaliated with a similar run and pass to Thoraley, and play was contested at midfield. The visitors were again beaten back, and after a smart bit of passing, Danby crossed the line near the corner flag, the place failing. The home team had still some- what the best of matters, until a dribble, headed by Littlewood, Rowe, and Isherwood, transferred the game to neutral territory, and the position was further en- hanced through Holmes following up a kick of Mather's and flooring Stevenson at his own quarter flag. From a pass by Heesom, Webster ran strongly to the line, and in the loose play which ensued the ball was kicked across to Daniels, who secured an equalizing try, far out, Webster making a good bid for goal. Directly after this, a splendid bit of passing amongst Lawless, Heesom, and Daniels resulted in the full back being tackled in close proximity to the goal line. A bad pass, however, completely lost the ground gained, the home forwards getting away to the centre line. Boscow soon retrieved the lost position, and then Daniels had a shy at goal. The distance was too great, but putting his men on side, Lawless picked up, passed to Webster, who in turn threw to Davies, the last-named dashing over the line, the place again failing. Some lively play by the home forwards ensued on the restart, who succeeded in clear- ing their lines of impending danger. The relief was but temporary, for Neild charging a kick caused play to be located in the home stronghold, and from a pack Mather dodged over. Following the drop out Warrington kept up a fierce attack until another bad pass gave Lancaster a foothold, which completely altered aspects, and Boak taking advantage et a miskick, secured a try, the score at half-time being three tries to two. Very soon after restarting a grand bit of passing between Neild, Davies and Povey, who in turn threw out splendidly to the left, was witnessed, but the pass was mulled and a rare chance lost. Boak retaliated with a pOW etfUl run until checked by Daniels and Boscow. Davies, Beard, Isher- wood, and Thornley soon regained the lost ground, and directly afterwards Daniels was very conspicuous by another grand tackle. Still Lancaster were having somewhat the best of the argument, and but for the cool and safe play of Boscow, would in all probability have scored. At length the ball was taken to centre by the good following up of Holmes and Isherwood. This was also supplemented by a rattling dribble from the feet of Povey, and a similar one following from Holmes, a considerable advantage was gained. An unusually got try followed to Boscow's credit. The opposing full back kicked to the last-named, who was :immediately ' tackled offside. Boscow appealed for offside, but no whistle being blown, he ran on and secured a try, from which Heesom kicked a goal. Although Boak scored on the call of time from the home team, the remaining play was completely spoiled by the offside tactics of the Lancaster men, the game ending Warrington 1-3-0 to

After Nevins and Turner had exchanged kiosks with the Lancaster backs, Eyres intercepted a pass intended for Cowell, and running to Lambert his career was blocked, but Berry (a most promising forward) was in attendanoe, and eagerly snapping up the well- meant pass, a grant twy was the result, Turner placing a goal. This reserve had evidently stimu- lated the Northerners, for on the re-start we found them invading Warrington territory. The effort I was only momentary, to; a grand run by Barnes raised the enthusiasm to a high pitch, the ball being transferred ,to within a few yards from the pavilion goal line. Law- less had a free kick, and Berry being on the alert charged Lamberts kick, the ball rolling dead. A passing move- ment by the homesters was next witnessed, but nothing came of it, Garth, Flartley, and Winder each showing up prominently with useful work. A spell of exchange kicking followed, and then Lambert pulled Antrobus up when scoring seemed a certainty. Evntually the oval was punted in touch near the Lancaster quarter flag, and Massey taking advantage of the lagging which his opponents indulged in, bounced the oval in play, and raced over the line, planting the leather behind the posts, Barnes placing a goal. Cowell made his mark soon after the kick off in dangerous proximity to the Warrington goal, but Nevins was a barrier, and from the charge Jolley, Readies, Ashton, and Berry came away with a dribble, and being aided by a quick passing movement of the backs took play near the line, when half-time was called with the score—Warrington 2-0-3, Lancaster 0-0-0. Gibson re-started, Antrobus replying. A fine opening was presented Hartley, but Evans was as safe as ever, and only a minor rewarded the visitors' effort. This -vas the only time that the visitors were really dangerous, for from now to the call of time, the Warringtonians had matters as they pleased. Though little combination existed among the forwards, the backs made up for the deficiency, and scarcely did it fall into their hands but what ground was made. An unfortu- nate accident happened to Massey at this period of the game, a sprained ankle necessitating hi retire- ment. This is to be regretted, as it is feared his services will not be available for the match against Swinton next Saturday. A grand pass from Barnes to Lawless enabled the latter to run the leather to the line, Lambert even- tually sending the oval dead. Evans was called upon to defend his charge, which he did with commendable promptitude and from a pass by Bandies to Barnes the last-named finally passed to Lawless, who scored, Turner failing at the place. Again Warrington pressed, and Barnes, running grandly, again passed to Lawless, who wriggled his way through' the opposing defence, and placed the second try to his credit. Bandies and Jolley each crossed the border, but failed to have the points allowed, and it was left to Barnes again to do the trick. After receiving the oval from the half backs he again passed to Lawless, who ran through the thick of his opponents and quickly secured his third try, Barnes this time placing a goal. The game now dragged somewhat, but towards the close Turner got clear away from a line eut, but success did not await his effort, and the whistle brought the game to a conclusion, the score standing— Warrington 3-24, Lancaster 0-0-1. Teams: Warrington, Evans, back; Massey (captain), Barnes, and Lawless, tnree-quarters ; Antrobus and Bate, half backs; Fair Turner, Randles, Berry, Nevins, Ashton, E. Dillon' Jolley, Eyres, and Donohue, forwards. Lancaster: Lambert, back; Hartley, Cowell, and Bleasdale, three-quarters ; Parkinson and Garth, halfbacks; Gilson, Smith, Winder, Beaumont, Wynne, Douthwaite, Fawcett, Miller, 3nd Redhead, forwards. Referee, Mr. Crooks, Manchester.

NOTES ON GA.MFA AND ATHLETICS. CRICKET. There can be no doubt that not only actually but also relatively we are immeasurably strong,er in our cricket than when the Australians first visited us in 1878. The mere record, therefore, of matches lost and won is no fair test of the merits of the present Australian team as com- pared with those of former teams. Yet the figures are somewhat startling. The team now with us, during a season when the pitches have been frequently in favour of their two renowned bowlers, have so far lost fifteen matches, won thirteen, and drawn eight. Taking eleven a-side matches only, the 1878 team won nine, lost four, and drew four; the 1880 team won five, lost 2, and drew four; the 1882 team (probably the strongest of all) won twenty-three, lost four, and drew eleven; the 1884 team won eighteen, lost seven, and drew seven; the 1888 team won nine, lost seven, and drew twenty-two; the 1888 team won nineteen, bet fourteen, and drew seven. It is also worth noticing that the brilliant cricketers who came over in 1882 did not lose a single county match, and those of 1884 only lost one.

On .`_;aturday afternoon at Hastings, amid a scene of considerable excitement and enthusiasm the South gained a hard-earned victory over the North by nine runs. The close of Friday's cricket gave every promise of an inter- esting finish, as the North, with an innings to play, wanted 175 runs to win. The weather was again of the most charming description, and the first match of the annual festival at Hastings may be regarded as a com- plete success. The chances of the game varied in a remarkable manner. At the outset, despite some admir- able batting by Cinian, the bowlers held the upper hand, and the sixth wicket went down at 81, when the South- ern team looked to hold the best of the game. Then, however, Attewell joined Albert Ward, and the two men made matters look altogether different. When he had scored three Attewell was missed by the wicket keeper standing back, and the mistake might have cost the South the game. While they were together Attewell and Ward put on 50 runs, and then Lohmann dismissed Attewell and Feel with successive balls. The score at luncheon tivoe stood at 131 for eight wickets. During the last half hour a most plucky and spirited attempt was made to save the game, and but for an error of judgment in running the efforts might have been suc- cessful. As it was the innings closed for 185, and left the South victorious, asalready stated, by nine runs. Ward's excellent 41 included seven fours and two twos.

The Hastings Cricket Festival, which has been favoured with splendid weather and has resulted in a finan- cial success, concluded on Wednesday with the defeat of the Australians by the South of England eleven by ten wickets.
LIBERAL MEETING AT THE LWALL
SPEECH BY MR. LEADAM. Mr. I. S. Leadam, the Liberal candidate for the Altrincham Parliamentary Division, addressed a meeting of the .electors of Thelwall in a field near
the Ship Canal huts on Saturday afternoon. Mr. Leadam, who had travelled from London to attend

, the meeting, arrived at Bank Quay Station, War- rington, between two and three o'clock, and he drove in a wagonette to Thelwall, accompanied by Mr. J. A. Swanwick ;chairman of the Lymm Polling District), Mr. John Swanwick, Mrs. Swanwick, and
Mr. W. E. Welford. From LatChford he was escorted

to the field by the Lymm Nonconformist Brass Band, which played among other pieces one entitled " Gladstone shall be our leader." The proceedings in the field commenced abut fire o'clock. Mr. J. A. Swanwick was in the chair.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said they were lucky that afternoon with regard to the state of the weather, and he hoped their luck would stick to them till the close of the poll at the next Parliamentary election in that division. (Applause.) In some respects it was a matter for regret that they could not meet in a more centralplace in the village of Thelwall, but that was not the fault of the Liberal Com- mittee. A more suitable place in The!wall was denied to them because the Tories were afraid of them. The Tories were afraid to let Mr. Leadam talk to the Thelwall

people, and they were also afraid, as was generally the case, of public discussion. The schoolroom in Thelwall was closed to them, and to all political parties. The moral was that the Liberals ought to make this one of the points of agitation—that all schools maintained by the public money should be thrown open to every political party. (Hear, hear). A smaller room had been proposed by their, unfortunately, Liberal Unionist friend, but still their old friend, Mr. Long. They thanked him for his kindness in the matter, although he knew that if they had consented to use the room they (the Liberals) would have had to say a great deal Mr. Long could not agree with. It was more satisfactory to be able to speak of Mr. Long in that wav,because as a rule the Liberal Unionists were greater Tories than the Tories themselves. (Hear, hear' and laughter.) But that was not the case with Mr. Long. (Applause). The present time was in some respects a historical one. Thelwall was a big place 800 or 1,000 years ago. It had been comparatively quiet ever since, but there was now every indication that it would become a place of marked importance on account of the cutting of the Ship Canal. They hoped it would bring many voters among them, who, in course of time, would be able to share with them in the triumph of having a good Liberal representative for the division. (Applause.) Thelwall had always presented a difficulty to the Liberal party for a certain reason. They did not lack Liberal voters. Indeed, there were many of them in the village. but they had been so long dominated by the wealthy Tory landlords, who to some extent "lorded it "over them, that they could not be as outspoken as they wished to be. He hoped, however, that time would alter that condition of things. If the Liberals would only make up their minds to face their wealthy Tory neighbours, and say " we are going to say and do what welike," they would find that the danger they now feared was a very imaginary one after all. and they would soon be perfectly free electors, and such as the law intended them to be. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGH MANNING moved the first resolution, which was as follows :—" That this meeting expresses its earnest desire for the early and complete success of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule policy, the more so as it is convinced that only after the settlement of the great Irish question can we hope to remedy the many English grievances which are crying out for speedy and radical cure." (Applause.) He said that any question which was purely and distinctly Irish, and in which nothing national was involved, was a question of Home Rule. If any policy was proposed by Mr. Gladstone which in- volved an infringement of a national question he must not be expected to support him, though he had done so for 36 years. If the Liberal party who advocated Home Rule for Ireland meant, as the Conservatives said they did, the dismemberment of the empire, there was a sharp method of dealing with them, and that was to have them up for high treason. He added that the Irish question blocked the way, and the sooner it was disposed of the better. (Applause.) Mr. LHADAM, who was warmly received on rising to address the meeting, said this occasion, as had been ob- served, was a historical one, as it was the first opportunity he had had of being introduced to those voters who had come to make Thelwall and neighbourhood their home. The Liberals were more pleased to see the new comers than were their friends of the Conservative side. He was happy to hear that of the new corners, who were accus- tomed to independent action, and to having an oppor- tunity-of meeting together and discussing political ques- tions without being susceptible to intimidation on the part of those whom they might think their superiors 19 out of 20 belonged to the Liberal party. (Applause.) Dealing with Irish questions, Mr. Leadam said the Irish tenants were not allowed to enter into their trades union. He dared say that those present knew that as long as the Tory party could help it they were not allowed to have trades unions ; they owed their right of combination to the Liberal party. (Applause.) The Tories would not allow the Irish tenants the right of trades unionists, and Mr. Balfour, who denied everything, denied that pri- vilege. When the Coercion Act was introduced the Liberal party moved an amendment to allow Irish ten- ants the same rights that trade unionists possessed in , England, but it was rejected by the Tory party; and I therefore it was incontestably the case that Irish tenants I were not allowed the rights of trades unionists. Not only so, but in trade union disputes, the services of a I British jury were engaged in England, but in Ireland the people were not allowed trade unionist rights, but were liable to be had up on a charge of criminal conspiracy before resident magistrates people who had been appointed by Mr. Balfour, and who were promoted according to the degree of zeal they had manifested against the popular cause, people who were hand in glove with the landlord—and these were the men who were appointed as magistrates. (Cries of " Shame.") While the combinations of the tenants were repressed with the bayonets and bludgeons of the police, the com- binations of the landlords were quite another thing. There was a combination of the landlords of a scandalous kind, under the leadership of Mr. Smith Barry. What did he do? He saw a neighbouring landlord about to Sell his property upon terms which had been agreed upon with his tenants. Mr. Smith Barry, thinking that if the landlord sold his property upon those terms, that ' the value of his own land would be deteriorated, formed a combination, but Mr. Balfour did not break his (Mr. Smith Barry's) head. because he was a Tory. Mr. Smith Barry formed a combination among the landlords to pre- vent the agreement being carried out, and for that purpose brought together a number of rich men who got hold of the estate. That was the sort of thing that went on ; Indeed, the Irish tenant was in a very hopeless position when the landlord came to him and said "I request you to purchase your land from me under the Ashbourne Act." He had no one to whom to appeal ? If he sent for his member of Parliament, and a meeting was called, it was broken up, and the people were sent to prison. If he combined with his fellow tenants the same thing happened, and the landlord dictated the terms upon which he had to purchase the land, and the English tax- payers found the money. The other day a meeting of tenantry in Kildare was held. He did not know whether the heads of the people were broken or not, but it was likely they were. The tenantry ventured to meet, and they said they had been compelled to purchase their land at such a rate they could not afford to go on paying the instalments of the purchase money, so that he (Mr. Leadam) and others present, who had been made the landlords of the tenants in Kildare, as British taxpayers, would have the satisfaction of handing out of their pockets large sums of money to the Irish landlords—. I more money than the land was worth. They would find they would not get their money back; because the land being worth less than had been paid for it, the tenants were unable to keep up their instalments. The British taxpayers would, therefore,have to pay the piper. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. MILFORD supported the resolution, which VMS put to the meeting and unanimously agreed to. The song "Clear the way" having been sung to the one of" Mold the Fort," Mr. Szatvox moved "That this meeting heartily aanks Mr. Leadam for his preeenceandspeech." Mr. Join.; PRICH koneof the workmen on the Ship Canal) seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. !JUDAH, in reply, said he was glad to find that in Thelwall, which had not been looked upon as one of the most promising parts of the division, a good sound Liberalism existed, as active and as healthy as one could wish to see anywhere. He believed it would spread and make itself felt in the division before the next election came. (Applause.) Another song having been heartily Sung, accompanied by the band, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Swan- wick for presiding, on the motion of Mr. Leadam seconded by Mr. O'Reilly, and the proceedings were brought to a conclusion.

- -- - Referring to the match between Runcorn and Salford, the writer of the' football notes in the Manchester " Guardian " says that Runcorn always prove an attrac- tion in the Manchester district, and they had a very cordial welcome. Coming as they did without two such sterling players as Wainwright and Brazenclale, they sur- prised the spectators by more than holding their own, winning a capital game by a try only. This was beauti- fully obtained by that clever three-quarter Crompton in the first half, the way in which he dodged his antagonists being quite worthy of his reputation. Runcorn were hard pressed at times, but their defence was very safe, and Salford had to accept the inevitable. H. Drury, the Eccles half back, and W. Anderten, of Barton, who was among the forwards, were hardly up to the Salford stan- dard, but they may of course improve in a week or two. Drury, ab all events, should prove an acquisition.

Swinton are opening their season in grand form and Warrington will have to put their best foot first on Saturday if they wish to stop the rush of the " lions." Last Saturday the Swintoniaus eimply rollicked round Mossley, which.however, by the way„is just now a much weaker team than it has been for some seasons back. We are told that Valentine, Winterbottom, and Marsh had practically their own way, the new three-quarter giving great satisfaction. Valentine not only crossed the Mossley lines several times, but placed four of the goals. The goal that was dropped by Marsh, surrounded though ha was by the opposing "host," was a masterpiece. Eumby was very clever at half back, his passing to the three-quarters being capital.

The'. wirepullers " opened their season in a velrY satisfactory manner on Saturday, when they completely upset the representatives of the ancient town of Lancas. ter. Though not quite so combiaed as they will get to be later on, the Warringtonians showed some fine play especially in the passit.g. Barnes does not appear among the list of scorers, but perhaps he did more than any other individual player to contribute. He played a three-quarter game of the highest class, and his passing to Lawless at the wing was accimate and well-timed.

div.head: RUNCORN V. SALFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. SALFORD.

These teams met on Saturday at Salford, and the game commenced by W. Hughes kiciting off in the direction of the racecourse goal. Anderton returned, and smart play by Salford carried hostilities into the visitors' quarter. Houghton cleverly relieved, and Faulkner and W. Hughes, by a grand dribble, rushed the ball to the Salford line. A slight relief was gained, but a penalty kick being awarde to Runcorn, the ball was placed for Crompton, but the ball going wide and a man off-side the wearers of the green didn't get much value out Of the episode. From the scrimmage the ball was passed very smartly by W. Hughes to Cawley, who got right up to the home line before Drury foregathered with him. It was an awkward spot, and the man-to-man conflict that ensued ended in Salford conceding a minor. Following the drop-out, Runcorn kept up a fierce attack, and but for the splendid tackling of Drury would have made greater headway. Barrett kicked well to Houghton who coolly returned, but Kent, in endeavouring to show his abilities in the punching line, mulled the leather, and got slightly mulled himself by half a dozen Runcorn forwards. Faulkner again distinguished himself, and the game gradually worked towards the Salford stronghold. A free kick to Salford was a welcome relief, and caused the leather to be taken to midfield. Drury improved matters for his side by a daring dribble, but his efforts received no support from his colleagues, for the Runcorn full back cleverly getting possession, walked past several opponents, and then put in a fine kick that neutralized all the advantage. Then a lively bit of play ensued, in which the ball was passed and re- passed with a smartness and dexterity that delighted the beholders. Broady making a beautiful pass to Cromp- ton, gave that dangerous player a chance, which he splendidly availed himself of, and, running with grand judgment, got away with only H. Cook in attendance. A fine sprint ensued,in which the Cheshire man came off victorious,for he managed to ground the leather on the magic rut near the corner flag. The kick at goal failed. After this shaking up, the Salford men livened themselves a little, and Myles, getting a good pass front Barratt,put , in a run, in which his destiny seemed to be the Runcorn goal; but unfortunately he met Crompton on the way, and the result of the meeting was that both were knocked down, some few minutes elapsing before Crompton could get on his legs. Then Barrett punted prettily, and while Cowley was capturing the oval Barrett captured him, and the nimble Drury, coming up in the nick of time, got the leather to the visitors' line.. The Runcorn men cleared the danger, and took the warfare to midfield. Another slight attack by Salford was cut short by the call of half-time, and the score stood in favour of the visitors by one try and a minor to nil. The second half commenced by Eagles making is mark from Broady' s return, and placing the ball Mr Wattle, who, however, failed to negotiate the premier point, though the effort was strong and well directed. Myles got a pass from Barratt, but was too well looked after by Faulkner and Gayter to get danger- ous. The game now began to be of a more even character. Twice Walsh made splendid long passes to Cook, and in neither case did the wing man make any ground. He was too faulty in his picking up, and too hesitatmg as to what he should do when he had the ball. The style of play that:was now developing may be pleasantly des- cribed as keen and vigorous, with the honours equally divided. Both teams were playing for all they were worth, and occasionally their temper got the better of their judgment. The last ten minutes of the game was as fierce and exciting as any portion of it. Salford re- peatedly made efforts to break through the stubborn defence of their opponents without success, and the final phase of the game was reached without any alteration of the score. Thus the victorious Runcormans emerged from the contest with the tangible trophy of one try and one minor point to nil, and no doubt the pleasant satis- faction of being able to beat one of their most noted opponents on their own stronghold. The teams were as follows :—Salford : W. Manwaring, back; F. Myles, A. Barrett, and H. Cook, three-quarters; S. Walsh, and H. Drury, half backs; H. Eagles, T. Kent, T. King, J. H. Tune. T. Craven, J. Birch. J. E. Shaw, W. Anderton and J. *Tittle, forwards. Runcorn : S. Houghton, hack ; T. Davies, I. Crompton, and H. Cawley, three-quarters; H. Hughes and W. Evans, half backs; W. Hughes, P. Riley, 'W. Faulkner. J. Gayter, It. Dolan, W. Rigby. W. Broady, F. Hancock, and J. Davies, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LANCASTER.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LANCASTER.

The inauguration of the footbaU season in the War- rington &Arid took place on Saturday afternoon, in charming weather. Everything that was possible to make the opening day a success was oomplete. The team setdown to meet the Warringtonians was Lan- caster, a club in the minds of many not of the first water, but if we nasty judge from their results of last season, they were fitting representatives to perform the no small task af opening the seven months' campaign of football in this district. The weather throughout the day was more in kee.ping with the summer pastime of etas could be plainly noticed in the plays after cricket,about a quarter of an hour's pla, when in the first scrimmage formed they represented a steaming mass. Soon after the advertised time to kick off a sheer an- nounced the fact that Warrington had entered the arena, headed by their popular captain, J. T. Massey. A pleas- ing fact was that many of the old and tried faces who lead done battle for the " wirepullers "almost since their infancy were still donning the primrose and blue. Lan- caster soon followed the Warringtanians, and operations at owe commenced by Fair Turner kicking off towards the pavilion goal. Bleasdale responded, and from the first scrimmage formed Bate, Nevins, and Lawless passed well, the homesters gaining a foothold in the visiting twenty-five. Donohue was foremost in a rush, which terminated in a minor, but this latter point was only the forerunner to a brilliant and unselfish piece of work,

A fourth edition has just been published of " - Orient Line Guide," edited for the managers of the Line by Mr. W. J. Loftie, 8.A., F.S.A., author of "A historY of London," &c. The work is handsomely printed and bound, and is published by Messrs. Sampson, Lewe, and Co. The chapters for travellers by sea and land are • brightly written, with facts and statistics of all kinds brought down to date. The work is fully and admirably illustrated, and there are no less than thirty maps and charts, besides views of ships, and plans of ships. To the traveller by the Line, the guide is invaluable, but apart from this, it is exceedingly interesting to the general - reader. It contains a mass ot valuable information which is not otherwise readily accessible. In the " Great Writers"' series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have "The Life of Nathaniel Haw"- thorne," Pram the pen of Mr. Moncure de Conway. div.head: BULKA AND THE WILD BOAR.
div.p: BULKA AND THE WILD BOAR.

BY COUNT TOLSTOL I had a bull dog, and his name was Bulks. He was perfectly black, except for the paws of his fore- legs, which were white. All bull dogs have the lower jaw longer than the upper, and the upper tooth set into the lower; but in the case of Bulka the lower jaw was pushed so far forward that the finger could be inserted between the upper and lower teeth.

Bulka had a broad face, big eyes, black and bril- liant. And his teeth and white tusks were always uncovered. He was like a negro. Bulks was not ugly, and he would not bite; but he was very powerful and tenacious. Whenever he took hold of anything, he set his teeth together and hung on like a rag, and it was impossible to make him let go; he was like a pair of pinchers. One time in the Caucasus we went boar-hunting, and Bulka ran to go with me. As soon as the boar- hounds got to work, Bulka dashed off in the direc- tion of their music and disappeared in the woods. This was in the mouth of November: a that time the wild boars and pigs are usually very Pot. In the forests of the Caucasus, frequented by wild boars, grew all manner of fruits—wild grapes, cones, apples, pears, blackberries, acorns, and rose- apples. And when all these fruits get ripe, and the frost loosens them, the wild swine feed on them and fatten.

At this time of the year the wild boar becomes so fat that he cannot run far when pursued by the dogs. When they have chased him for two hours. he strikes into a thicket and comes to bay there. Then the hunters run to the place where he Is at bay and shoot him. By the barking of the dogs one can tell whether the boar has taken to cover or is still running. If he is running, then the dogs bark with a yelp, as though some one were beating them but if he has taken to covert, then they bay with a; long howl, as though at a man. In this expedition I had been running a long time through the forest, but without once coming across the track of a boar. At last I heard the protracted howl and whine of the hounds, and I turned my steps in that direction .

f was already near the boar. I could hear a crash- ing in the thicket. This was made by the boar pur- sued by the dogs. But I could tell by their barking that they had not yet brought him to bay, but were only chasing mound him. . . . . .
S-uddenlil heard something rushing behind me, and looking around, I saw Bulka: He had evident- .
ly lost track of the boar-hounds in the forest, and had become confused ; but now he had heard their baying, and also, like myself, was in full tilt in their direction.
He was running across a clearing through the tall grass, and all I could see of him was his black head, and hie tongue lolling out between his white teeth.

• I called him, but he did not look around; he ' passed by me, and dashed into the thicket. I hurried after him, but the farther I went, the denser became the underbrush. The branches ' knocked off my ha f and whipped my face; the thorns of the sloe-tree clutched my coat. By this time I was very near the .barking dogs, but I could not see anything. Suddenly I heard the dogs barking louder ; -there was a loud crash, and the boar, which was trying to break his way through, began to squeal. And this made me think that now Bulka had reached the scene and was attacking him. I put forth all my strength, and made my way through the underbrush to the spot. Here, in the very thickest of the woods, I caught a glimpse of a spotted boar-hound. He was barking and howling without stirring from one spot. Three paces from him I saw something black struggling. When I came nearer I perceived that it was the boar, and I heard Bulka whining piteously. The boar was grunting and charging the hound, which, with his tail between his legs, was backing away from him. I had a fair shot at the side and the head of the boar. I aimed at his side and fired : I could see that my shot took effect. The boar uttered a squeal, and turning from me dashed into the thicket. The dog ran barking and yelping on his trail. I broke my way through the thicket after them. Suddenly I heard and saw something under my very feet. It was Bulka. He was lying on his side and whining. Under him was a pool of blood. I said to myself, "My dog is ruined"; but now I had something else to attend to, and I rushed on. Soon I saw the boar. The dogs were attacking him from behind, and he was snapping first to one side, then to the other. When the boar saw me, he made a dash at me. I fired for the second time. with the gun almost tcuching him, so that his bristles were actually singed. The boar gave one last grunt, stumbled, and fell with all his weight upon the ground. When I reached him, he was already dead; only here and there his body twitched, or puffed up a little. But the dogs, with bristling hair, were tearing at his bell) and his legs, and others were licking the blood from where he was wounded. That reminded me of Bulka, and I hastened back to find him. He crawled to meet me, and groaned. I went to him, knelt down, and examined his wound. His belly was torn open, and a whole mass of his bowels protruded and lay upon the dry leaves. When my comrades joined me, we replaced Bulka's intestines, and sewed up his belly. While we were sewing up his belly and puncturing the skin, lie kept licking my hand. They fastened the boar to a horse's tail, so as to bring it from the woods, and we put Bulks on a horse's back, and thus we brought him home. Bulka was an invalid for six weeks, but he got well at last.

div.head: REASON WHY
div.p: THE REASON WHY

Why is it that some people can scarcely venture out of doors during damp and foggy weather P It is because than owing either to a naturally delicate constitution or the neglect of proper precaution in time, they are liable at the least exposure to draughts, winds, or damp, to catch a cold which will develop() into a cough. Influenza, Asthma, Bronchitis, Inflammation, or even Consumption!

Why is it that others either can not or dare not enjoy the pleasures on the table, that partaking of necessary food is impossible, or the free indulgence of their taste results in horror which the bravest shrink from ? It is because they are troubled with Indigestion in some form or other, whether it goes under the name of Dyspepsia, Flatulence, Bilious, Head-ache, Loss of Appetite, or any other form of that malady.

War is it that others again are dispirited, nervous, melancholy, always look upon the dark side, and regard everything through the coloured spectacles of a morbid imagination? It is because they suffer from a disordered Liver, which brings nervous headache, sleeplessness, jaundice, bile, low spirits, confirmed melancholy, and other horror in its train.

MURDERING HIS MOTHER'S SWEETHEART. SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT PLUMSTEAD.

In the early hours of Saturday morning, Walter James Lyons, aged 20, a machinist in the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich, living at 32, Conway-road. Plumstead, went home and found his mother (a widow) had gone to bed and left the house in darkness. Suspecting something Wrong he procured a light, and on entering his mother's • l'ooni found there with her a quarter-master sergeant in Itle Artillery, named Stewart, stationed at Woolwich uarracks. A violent altercation took place between the 8211, mother, and Stewart. The two latter got up, left ' 141 e house, and walked into Griffin-road, a street adjoin- ing. They did not return to the house, so the son went otlt about half-past one o'clock in the morning to look for them. He found them together in Griffin-road. Another violent altercation ensued, resulting in young Lyons Aabbing Stewart in the chest with a butcher's knife, which he brought from his home. Thu knife penetrated nine inches and entered the heart. Stewart fell dead on the snot. Mr. Reavell, principal foreman in the Royal Laboratory, who was returning home late, saw the knife glitter by the gaslight, and went to the spot and procured hell). The son was apprehended by Sergeant French, Who took him to Woolwich Police Station, where he > was charged with murdering Stewart. He made a Statement that his motive for the deed was strong disapproval of Stewart's conduct. The knife was secured, - and the body of the murdered man conveyed to the Parish mortuary. It is said the widow and the sergeant Were to have been married an Saturday. On Saturday afternoon Lyons was charged at the tVoolwich Police Court with wilful murder. The prisoner, Who is a slim-built and sullen-looking young fellow, mowed but little emotion, and stood throughout the earing, which only occupied about ten minutes, with NS eyes fixed on the floor. When asked whether he had any reply to the charges made against him, he raised his !yes for a moment and said, "No, sir." At the close Of Tile hearing a man in the rear of the court asked permis- sion to speak on behalf of the prisoner, but he was not heard. he further hearing of the case was deferred until Priday.

INQUEST AND VERDICT. An inquest was opened at Woolwich Workhouse on Tuesday on the body of John Stewart, quartermaster- sergeant, 51st Battery Royal Artillery, who was killed by W, alter James Lyons, at Plumstead, on Saturday morn- Edwin Phillimore, painter, said that last week he was Staving at 32, Conway-road, Plumstead, the residence of krs. Lyons. He retired to bed at 10.40, and at 12 30 he Was disturbed. He heard Walter Lyons say, "I will not gO out of the room." His mother said he would have to gO, and then the accused screamed his loudest that he Would not go out of the room until the man went out of the house, and that if he did not go he would dash his brains out with the hammer. An altercation followed, and the son appeared to get very angry at the man say- ing he could kill Lyons with one blow. The son then called his mother foul names, and she replied that they Were to get married on the morrow. The son asked why ahe could not wait until to-morrow, and she said "I Shall please myself about that." The deceased and the Woman then left the house. Witness heard shouting and acrearos from the street, and, rushing out, found the deceased lying on the ground. Two policemen came up, and the accused handed them the knife he had used. He also handed them the pocket knife, saying, "You may a,a 'well have this, for if I had not done it with one I should with the other. Take me ; I know my doom." , ,rie refused to speak to his mother, telling her she ought ‘0 be ashamed of herself. In answer to questions, witness said he had seen the ,accused drunk only once. He had heard the accused tell tis mother that he had been told to look after her and the officers. He believed the crime was the result of the gnarrel, and was not premeditated. Ellen Lyons, widow of James Lyons, a fitter in the arsenal, was allowed to be seated while giving her evi- dence. She said she lived at 32,Conway-road, Plumstead. Iler son Walter James lived with her. He was twenty- years of age. Another son lived with her, aged fifteen, and there were two lodgers. She slept down- stairs. She became acquainted with deceased last Fri- day afternoon, at Woolwich Garrison Sports, and he remained in her company all the afternoon. He accom- Panied her home at about midnight. She first saw her aao Walter when he came into the bedroom, at about one o'clock, saying, " What is the meaning of this ? " ,I,le said he would not have this sort of thing in the "use. Stewart said "Are you master, or is your mother taistress, here ?" Walter said he would put Stewart out Of the house. Stewart said he was not going to be rrightened by a brat like him, and remarked," I'll fight 3 better man than you ; I've fought in battle." Then Stewart got up and dressed. The accused went into the kitchen, and came back with a small hammer,and in the struggle the hammer got broke. The hammer was taken from the deceased. She told her son that they were going to be married by the registrar next day. Walter Was out of temper, and told Stewart to go. The latter Nvas twice the sizeof the boy. Stewart went to the door, and said he did not know which way to go, and she accompanied him to the corner of the street, and stood talking to him. Walter followed, and said, "What are •'You doing here ?" She feared a fight, and held Walter, Who threw her away, and she fell. The men then struggled, and she saw Stewart stagger and fall. She Put her arm under his head, and he gave a sigh and ,!Xpired. She noticed nothing in her son's hand, but sheard him say in the struggle, 'Go away ; I have got a 3nife," Her son had been drinking heavily. She identified the knife produced, which she used as a bread knife. Her son was subject to violent fits of passion,and Often would not listen to reason. Her husband's brother was in Harming Heath Asylum, and her husband's mother was at Darneth, both suffering from insanity. By the Jury: Stewart said he had money to marry her 1"9 license if there was not time to be married by banns before he went to India. There was no familiarity be- nd the fence between Stewart and herself except Prank Brunn, of 73, Conway-road, Plumstead, stated that he heard the quarrel in the road. He heard the accused say, " I will do it, mother. I said I would if I taught you again. One of you will get killed, or else I Shall get killed myself." The sergeant said, "Don't stab Your mother; stab me." Lyons went back a few paces, drew a knife from his breast pocket, rushed at the ser- geant, and stabbed him in the left chest. The sergeant reeled and fell, and Mrs. Lyons threw herself on the body. • Robert James Johnstone, of 59, Station-road, Plum- stead, deposed that hearing screams he went to the spot. rte heard the accused say, ". I told her I would the first ,tirae I caught her, and I caught her in the very act be- °lnd those boards." He saw the accused hold a knife ,tIP, and put out his hand to stop the blow, but it was too late Police-Sergeant Rolph deposed to arresting the accused, Who gave up the knife, and said, "I know my doom." 'rhe prisoner had been drinking, but knew perfectly well What he was about. • Inspector French put in a statement voluntarily made ;7 the prisoner at the police station. It described the , quarrel as previously detailed, and the prisoner added that finding his mother so long gone, he went down to- Wards Griffin-road without his boots. Hearing a slight rourmurin,g he looked through the fence. He then de- ,seribed what he saw. He told the man the best thing ne could do was to be off. He and the man then got into the road, and walked to the junction with Conway- , Vad. There the man said, " You have not got the neart to do it." " I said nothing (added prisoner), but Stabbed him there and then in the chest with the bread knife." Among other formal evidence, Sergeant Simpson de- , Posed that the deceased was not married. The Coroner, in summing up, expressed his regret that - an accused person was not permitted to attend a coroner's eoUrt to hear evidence against him, and pointed out that ' a marl must not vindicate propriety at the point of the knife. The jury, after deliberating forty minutes, returned a 'verdict of "Wilful murder" against Lyons, but added a ' rider expressing their belief that he had received great Provocation. EXTRAORDINARY SCENE AT THE INTERMENT. The remains of Quartermaster Sergeant Stewart, the Victim of the Plumstead tragedy, were buried with mili- tary honours in Woolwich Cemetery, on Wednesday afternoon. There was a great crowd, estimated at fully ,• twenty thousand persons, present. After some thousands o, ad been admitted to the cemetery the gates were closed, ont the arrival of the funeral cortege necessitating re- . °Pening' the crowd overpowered the police and several snore thousands rushed in. Women were thrown down • l•nd crushed' and the constable was injured. Young Yons who stabbed Stewart, is in Holloway Goal. On Oesday he inquired about his mother, and expressed the OPe that her health had not suffered from the shock. . .aaving seen the report of the inquest, he said that many nf the circumstances spoken of had passed from his ; pemory, and he was much disappointed at the verdict of jury, which he had hoped would have been man- ' The trial is expected to take place at the ; `-ettral Criminal Court during the second week in I?ct9ber. His fellow-workmen at Woolwich Arsenal are al-sing a fund to engage counsel for his defence.
AN IRISH ELOPEMENT.

A remarkable elopement is reported from the Curragh Inilltary camp, in Ireland. On Sunday morning an officer 1) high rank from the Curragh camp drove to a neigh- boring railway station in search of his daughter, who ;tWhas missing,. On making inquiries there he fund that Young lady had left by the mail train for a southern 4.:3.R1 company with a young man. He awaited the lival of the next train, and proceded on her track. arrival in the city in question he went to the different Ir,els, but could find no trace of the young lady until the train leaving next morning, when the couple were confronted by the young lady's father. A very painful ieelle ensued, but it ended in her forcibly being placed a carriage en route for home. div.p: UNITED TRADES DEMONSTRATION AT ST. HELENS.
THREATENED GREAT STRIKE.

A great trades demonstration in support of the strike hands and lockouts from the Cowley-hill Plate Glass Works of Messrs. Pilkington Bros., was held on Saturday afternoon. The weather was very favourable, and the proceedings were successful in every respect. The members of the various trades assembled at their respective headquarters and marched to Bickerstaffe-st., Fletcher's coachhouse, where they waited in one procession, the principal marshals of which were Messrs John Bradbury (plate-glass workers), Thomas Glover (miners), Robert Hunter (bottle makers), and William Tay- lor (joiners, bricksetters, and carpenters). About 2,000 men took part, each branch of industry being headed by its trade banner. First in order came the plate-glass workers, including the strike hands and, lockouts, who were attired in their white linen, and they were headed by the Roughdale's Brass Band. Next came the bricklayers, stonemasons, engineers, joiners, and miners. Following these were the bottlemakers, who had engaged the services of the Viaduct Institute (Earlestown) Brass Band. The flint-glass workers and coopers brought up the rear, the coopers being headed by the St. Helens Borough Band. The leading thoroughfares of the town were paraded, and the sidewalks were thronged with eager spectators. Happily, everything passed off quietly and orderly, and there was not the slightest mishap to mar the proceedings. In the evening an enthusiastic public meeting was held in the Volunteer Hall, capable of holding about 2,000 people. There was a crowded audience. Councillor John Forster presided, and he was supported by Councillor T. R. Threlfall, secretary of the Southport Trades Council; Messrs. S. Woods, miner's agent, Wigan, and labour candidate for the Ince Division; John Bradbury (presi- dent of the United Plate Glass Workers' Society), Robert Hunter (secretary of the Lancashire Glass Bottle Makers' Society), Thomas Glover (miner's agent, St. Helens), P. J. King (president of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union), J. Prescott (secretary, Plate Glass Workers' Society), and H. L. Riley, &c.—The Chairman, who was well received, referred to the strike at Messrs. Pilking- ton's works, which had been in progress for about three months, and said he thought it was time something was done to prevent the waste of labour and the waste of , money that had been going on. Looking at the question 'as an outsider, and at the figures which had been sub- mitted to him, he felt there was a considerable justifica- tion for the steps which had been taken. He contrasted the work and wages at Messrs. Pilkington's with other works in the town,and said that the difference was saved by the firm of Pilkington Bros., at the expense of the physical exertion and the wear and tear of the systems of the men who were employed there. (Cheers.) The men accordingly demanded that extra men should be employed and their duties lightened, and he expressed a hope that no employers, no matter how hard they might be in other respects, would ever " mark " a man simply because he had the courage of his convictions, and stood up by his fellow workman, who was asking for that which was justice and right. The demonstration that afternoon had been for the express purpose of awakening the sympathy and co-operation of the public, and he hoped that meeting would be carried onin a conciliatory fashion—that the men would hold out the olive branch of fairness and right, and that Messrs. Pilkington would see the figures as ordinary outside critics saw them, and endeavour at a very early date to bring about a settlement of the dispute. (Cheers.) He then announced, with regret, that Mr. Tom Mann, of London, who had been expected to attend, had wired that he was unable to do so.— Mr. John Bradbury moved "That this meeting, repre- senting the various trades of St. Helens, begs to express, in the most emphatic manner, its disapproval of the want of courtesy shown by Messrs. Pilkington Brothers to their old employes now on strike, and resolves that their hands now on strike, along with those locked out, are deserving both of the moral and material support of their fellow townsmen, and pledges itself to do all in its power for their support." He alluded to the visit paid by Messrs. Fenwick and Woods to the firm of Pilkington Brothers, and said the men had tried to do all they could to bring about an amicable arrangement, and the men at Cowley Hill could give the lie direct to the asiertion that they had been dragged out by the men from other works. The men at Messrs. Pilkington's ought to be placed on an equal footing with those else- where; and if they now submitted to the masters' terms it meant that reductions would take place at other works. It behoved every workman to assist those engaged in the struggle, who already had the help and sympathy of the public of St. Helens. Be complimented the men upon their quiet and peaceful cenduct during the strike, and said it reflected the utmost credit upon them when con- trasted with what had occurred at Southampton. (Cheers.) —Mr. Robert Hunter, in seconding the resolution, said that the executive of the Glass Bottle Makers' Society had unanimously decided to support the men on strike from Messrs. Pilkington's works. Messrs. Pilkington were greater tyrants and oppressors of the working classes than any other firm in the town, and there was an urgent necessity for every workman to help the men who were struggling against the oppressors of trade unionism. (Cheers. )—Councillor Threlfall, of Southport, supported the resolution, and said he was surprised that the extremely reasonable, just, and wise demands put forward by the glassworkers had been so contemptuously rejected. He was all the more astonished because the name of Pilkington had stood synonimous with a good deal of courtesy, uprightness, and fairplay. The only exception to that feeling he had found in St. Helens. In these days of glorious labour advancement it was surpris- ing that in St. Helens any firm should endeavour to return to the old antiquated system of trying to break up the union by getting their hands to sign a certain docu- ment, for the men were now able to snap their fingers, tear up the paper, and throw it in the fire. (Cheers.)The men were making the struggle a question or the liberty of labour, and every trades unionist in the employ of Messrs. Pilkington ought to be brought out in orderLo assist. (Loud cheers.) The miners of the district miglit back up the strikers in a very effective fashion ; and if that was done, Messrs. Pilkington' who had not hitherto listened to reason, might possibly find their pockets were being permanently touched. (Cheers.)— Mr. Samuel Woods also supported the resolution. Ile said the men engaged in that struggle had an honourable and just cause on their side, and as they were being sup- ported by other trades the victory would be theirs. (Ap- plause.) If that struggle with Messrs. Pilkington was becoming one of tactics and diplomacy as to which could hold out the longest, or which had the greatest power, he said it was only a common act of retaliation that the men should work with those weapons which would bring them the victory. (Cheers.) What were those weapons ? He understood that Messrs. Pilkington owned glassworks and collieries, and the men employed therein were going to make their cause a common one, and all would put their shoulders to the wheel in the most effective manner to bring about a speedy victory. If there did not seem to be any signs of surrender from Messrs. Pilkington, then the whole of their men would be asked to co-operate and to stop the whole of the works belonging to the firm: (Loud cheers.) If the men were determined to continua the battle, and he believed they were determined, he should be one of the foremost to obtain not only moral but material support to bring them a noble victory. The day was gone by for employers to crush out organisa- tions, and if Messrs. Pilkington declined to receive another independent deputation he should assist in bringing out other workmen and stopping the whole of the works until they obtained their • rights. (Loud cheers.) The resolution was then carried. Mr. Thomas Glover afterwards moved "That consider- ing the growth of trade societies in St. Helens, the time has now arrived when we should organise a trades council, and the meeting pledges itself to use all efforts to inaugurate a trades council as early as possible." He considered the unity of all trades would be the best thing for the working classes, and he thought the time had arrived when a trade council should be formed in St. Helens. (Applause). He referred to the strike of the plate-glass workers, and said if it was deemed advisable to bring out the colliers employed by the firm he should do his best to obtain support in other quarters. (Cheers.) Mr. J Sephton (Flint (ilassworkers' Society) seconded the resolution, and said he was quite sure a good strong trades council was wanted in St. Helens. (Applause.) Mr. J. P. King supported the resolution, and said the demonstration that day reminded him of the scriptural story of the beating of drums and the flourishing of trumpets before the walls of Jericho fell down, and he hoped their proceedings that day would have the same effect upon Messrs. Pilkington. (Laughter and applause.) If workmen were in earnest and decided to follow the advice tendered to them, they should set themselves to the task of organisation at once. If they were strongly organised, they could snap their fingers at the men who were trying to cheat them out of their rights. With re- gard to the proposed trades council, 5,000 chemical and copper workers would be ready to support it, and he trusted it would be a great success. Votes of thanks to the chairman and speakers conclud- ed the meeting.

div.head: MR. SPURGEON ON PULPIT ORATORY
div.p: MR. SPURGEON ON PULPIT ORATORY

On Tuesday evening Mr. Spurgeon delivered the (in- augural address to the students at the Hackney College, West Hampstead upon the occasion of the opening of the eighty-eighth annual session of the institution,which has for its object the training of young men for the Oongre- gational ministry. Mr. Spurgeon who was suffering from a bad cold, said the ordinary sermon should always be evangelistic, and the " exhortation" should not ,be kept until the close, by which time the sinners got drowsy. They should avoid affectation in preaching, and the tone and manner of voice which seemed to indicate that the preacher might say with the Pharisee, "Lord, I thank Thee that Jam not as other men are." Let them beware also of dealing with subjects that were too deep for them, in the manner of some preachers who professed to know exactly when the Lord would come, and began taking in their coals by the scuttle. He had never known of a soul being saved by a diScussion on "The Ten Toes of the Image.

Sir,—l thought the quiet of the Lord's flay being dis- turbed by the Salvation Army ,lotovith their drumming, bad enough; but,when I hear of music in the Park,— sacred so called for fear of giving offence. together with a series of concerts at the Public Hall for the sake of the "almighty dollar," I think its time next for the theatre to begin and see what morals it can create on that day. Instead of one day out of the seven being kept sacred. I think it time fee our clergy to speak out, and laymen likewise, else what are we coming t&? Empty places of worship, forsooth ! Vests Sze.,
