div.head: MORE MESIC AT NEWTON.
div.p: MORE MESIC AT NEWTON.

Sir,—The lovers of music in Newton-le-Willows have great reasons for rejoicing at their prospects for the coming festive season. 'They have for many years had their" Choral Society:" and now yet another is announced, "The Newton Musical Society." 'Critics might say that there is a Write of plagiarism here, but that's ruk It has, however, been rumoured, that—to use a phrase much too common—some of the leading spirits of the infant society have been " morltig heaven and earth" to beguile members Of the "choral" away, so as to strengthen their own ranks. But I can't believe th.s, and want more evidence. Yell see, their president is a man of sterling integrity, andwould wash his hands of them altogetherif be knew' " shady tricks" were re- sorted to. Still it is said. some few have "taken their hook "en their own responsibility ; but they are what may be called the least to be relied on, and in the words of the iramortdiKelo, " they never will be missed." The new Society, It is further said (and I hope it is true, for Itio like good music) are about to undertake Berlioz's " Faust:" Mendelssdhn's "Elijah," and last, not least, Beethoven's "Choral Symphony." Unthinking people might say in this connection, that "Fools rush in, where angels fearto tread"; but in making that remark, they would be "-speaking without the book," and in ignorance of Whom they have happily secured Tor their conductor. Those " Works of the Great Masters" re- quire a -man of file very widest experience to steers body of chorallista through ; • and haven't they got him ? Besides, the 'musical acumen of the singers themselves always Ilightens the conductor's onerous duties, and thrice fortunate is the new Society in this respect. But, ." All's well that ends well." and. I wish them, with all my heart "a happy issue out of all their—" struggles. LOBGEEANG. Earlestcrwn., Sept. 19th, 1890.

div.head: rEksTING RIINCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: rEksTING RIINCORN OFFICIALS.

- see from your-report of the proceecYrns of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, that the said body have been feasting, at the ratepayers' expense, the officials who were employed at the recent election of Commissioners. Judging from the amount of the hotel bill (saidto include nothing but food) £5 145.., the feast- ing must have been done on a most sumptuous scale, as the number of officials-employed were only seven, which gives an average of over 16s. per head. True, the Chair- man said it was provided for the officers and those taking part in the election, but the only person who took partbeside the officers was the presiding officer, and even by including that gentleman at the "feast the cost would be reduced by only 2s. a head. The candi- dates paid forthemselves at the rate of 7s. each—or just one-half What it took to`Seed the officials—a fact which requires some explanation. Did the officials consume double the quantity ? I observe the Chairmon states the officers were at the booth from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., but these hours are very much shorter than those at Municipal, County Council, or Parliamentary Election.s, at which the officials have to make provision for themselves ; and I think the officials in the present case ought to have done the same., ,especi- ally as their salaries were paid to them for the day. in addition to a special fee which plenty of men would bo glad to receive for a week's work. I agree with the Chairman that "it was a. rather humiliating position for -the officers to wait there with their hats tinder their arms for some candidate -to ask them to have something to, eat after their day's labour ;" but I was not aware untiLnow that it was the habit of the Board's servants to do sUch a thing, and I am sorry to hear it. thave hitherto held a higher opinion of them, , and would still prefer to believe that there is some manly -41- independence left in them, and that if left to themselves, • ' they would elect to go their ,own way, and enjoy them- selves on their easily earned money in a manner-more suited to their respective positions.—Yours RATEPAYER.

, EQUITABLE .Le,CAL RATING. Sir,—Can any of yonr ;numerous readers inform me under what authority has arisen the custom of exempt- ing unlet shops and houses from the payment of local rates. As far as I can ascertain the law remains -that all house and shop property Shell be assessed for rates on the basis of a rental that any occupier might be reasonably expected to pay, and I cannot learn that any authority exists for exempting the landlord '(as temporary occupier of ,unlet property) from the , demand for su.,-11 rates. The advantages availableio;present ratepayers from a system of such ,continuous localtrating—the great re- duction of their rates that would , promptly ensue—the lowering of mite by landlords anziuus to transfer the • ratepaying privilege from themselves to suitable tenants. the check that would be put upon the irresponsible . recklessness of the speculative 'builder (who would think more than twice 'before "running up" a small matter i of 200 or 300 houses if be knew that an their comoleti•on he would have to pay the local 'rates as well as the ,ground rent) must he my apology for wiaing to you and .seeking the opinion.of your readers .on this importaart

-Subject . , Permit me to add that two orgatisatiors have recent- ly been formed to deal with similoir .quest Eons affecting the relations between landlord awl tenant.—(l.) The ." Tenant Tradesmen's; National 'Union" (eerhose mem- bership already extends beyond London -to most of the irapertant towns of England—from 'Newcastle to Southampton). Advecates Fair Bent .and Fixity of Tenure for shopkeepers, so long as agreed.eovenants are duly performed—the right of the tenant alene to the goodwill ,which he has created or purobased—and to the value ofese permanent improvements made by him— ▪ and the payment by the landlord of a fair share of rates .for local anprovements,—(2.) The "Working Man's Home Union which numbers in London alone 20,000 .members,and is ripe for extension throueboutothe whole .of England--e-aims at the prompt. reductien at rents, -thorough &saltation, tenmeable repair and reasenable comfort in the houses and lodgings of the •elasses—alsoat conferring farther power on Councils for the erection of cheap and suitable werk- men's dwellings near the centres of emplaTinent—at ;securine proper provision Wing made for disturbed families before o'..elearances " .are carried ant—and at promoting cheaper and a.deepLate rail and tram •ear .2.ocommodation far working-men going to and from tbeir 'work. No fee -or payment for membership is required by 4thsr!Usion.—l still gladly forward any number .ofj Membership Forms 'that may be ',squired on application) to me at International College, Finehley-rd., Ilampeteado ;Lopdon.--Mith very sincere thanks, your obedienti servant, AMES .HAYMAN, President of the Unions!, 'THE .ORIETIN LICENSE AT MARLESTOWN. Sir,-4 hope the ratepayers are all en the alert with regard to the appfication fer the provisienal transfer of the license of the "Griffin Etaxi." Whoa seen in all its bearings, it will be rightly deemed op extraordinary application, and that it can be legitirnatO rejected on several grounds. Let the ratepayers remember first of all that one objection which would be fatai in many cams would practically only incur a loss of time in this. To prove misdemeanour or misconduct on the part of thie par- ticular licensee will not secure the suspension of the license. This house is held smiler the vicious system a tied houses, and, along with pother /Limy il4
watfling- the,Cointy
same street, is owned by a Brewing Company so that such an offence will only obtain the dismissal of the servant, while the license itself will thus be easily

saved. One objection to the proposal is that the feeling of the whole nation is decidedly against any changes like the one suggested, which simply amounts to the abolition of an insignificent house and the establishment of another in its stead on a most important site. The present Con- servative Government have twice brought in bills osten- sibly intended to facilitate the reduction in the number ' of public-houses, plainly admitting that the number is already too large. Such an application should therefore I be promptly refused when even ordinary renewals are being stopped. The members of the L. & N.-W. Recreation Grounds should also have a special voice in this matter with regard to the choice of the new site. Surely after exact- ing such an amount of money for the beautifying of those grounds the Company's Directors will respect a petition from them against a scheme to fix a public- house on alny part of the grounds. Then again, the days of the present unsatisfactory licensing system are numbered, and I believethat under any new system the Griffin would be among the first in Earlestown to receive notice to quit. There is nothing whatever to favour its continuance on or near the spot where it now stands. The people whom it was at first licensed to serve have been removed years ago. At that time..-several rows of houses clustered there, but these haveall been demolished, and the works extended over the Whole ground leaving the Griffin standing alone in a peniectly solitary situation. On the south side of the street where it stands there is not a single cottage for about the length of a quarter of a mile, namely 200 yards to the west, and the same distance to the east, where the next building but one is another public-hcuse. On the opposite side of the street there is not a cottage for a 100 yards eastward, and 50 westward, making nearly a furlong, the space being occupied by reserved grounds. The utterly isolated position of the Griffin reminds me of the restricted distance required for a 'cemetery, and I do not see any reason at all wily it should not be allowed tostarve on its own present 'funereal pile. I hope the cause will be put in the hands of an able lawyer. Thanks be to the present Government that profession is now well versed in the licensing question. I trust also that the various ministers of religion will com- bine to do their best, as I have ne doubt that the most impartial among them will admit the justice of the op- position. Hoping that the action will be successful so that the magistrates will banish this Griffin to the mytho- logical limbo of all other Griffins and hobgoblins, I am, yours truly, Earlestcwn.
J. H. PROFIT.

div.head: PITY POOR RUNCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: PITY POOR RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

Sir,—No doubt I was only one of many ratepayers I who were greatly edified by the discussion which took I place at the last meeting of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, respecting the expenses of the recent election, and lam rather surprised that you did not head the subject " Pity the Poor Gfficials." What a sorrowfial picture was that presented by Mr. Taylor I ust fancy, seven sleek well paid, fashionably dressed officials stand- ing "with their hats under their arms," and a pleading expression on their faces, waiting to be asked to have something to eat. " Poor 3e," with which theatre goers will be acquainted, is a fool to this harrowing state of affairs. Seven officials and a returning officer of ample proportions and generous •disposition, perspiring in a small room from 9 a.m.. to '5 p.m., with a brief interval snatched to pay a visit to the Market Inspector's Office, to get a snack—(aristocratically called lunch)—of roast chicken, ham, and other common food, in order to merely keep the lamp of life alight to enable them to record the votes of theinexacting paymasters, the rate- payers,-and then reduced at the finish to the humiliating necessity of asking in the dumb show described by Mr. Taylor, for something to eat ! Surely this will harrow the soul of the wealthy taxpayers. But, thank heaven, these hard worked gentlemen are now to be placed beyond such straits, and the successful candidate will no longer have his joy alloyed by such a sight, and the un- successful candidates will be bereft of these sympathisers lin his misery—for with the yearning for the flesh-pets of Runcorn satisfied, their rubicund countenances will only mock the defeated. This important town of Runcorn will not in the future havetlts fair escutcheon dimmed by a picture of hungeringservants. There is only one thing wanting by those wito settle the bill. A copy of the menu should be given to those pre- servers of the liberties of the ratepayers—the reporters —so that we may know that our servants were amply provided for, and were not left to feed on the husks of a banquet prepared for their more fortunate brethren in the rare of life. The cost of lunch and dinner was stated at £5 14s. Was this sufficient for the purpose? For so small a sum could they have been supplied with the delicacies of the seasonF Could salmon, grouse, duck, chicken' lamb, beef, and the "usual trimmings" as Samuel Weller would have said, have been provided for such a paltry outlay of public money, which is well known rarely goes so far as that from a private purse. That sum divided amongst Seven officials is only 16s. 3d. a head, and I am afraid they were only regaled with the roast beef of England and potatoes and cabbage, with a little rict pudding to follow, and Adam's ale to wash the

lot down. It has been hinted to me that for 16s. each a much better meal than that could be prepared. I friend "in the know" says a latourer in a chemical works has to keep a little wife and a big family on 16s. a week, and that no matter whether he stood with his hat under his arm, OT stood on his head with his hat on his feet, his master would not ask him to have soraething to eat at the end of his day's labour of ten hmem. He would have to provide his own table with the delicacies of the season or*, forty ribbed steak, just as he ;leased, and he would have to help te;keep these poor officials in the bargain. And, adds my friend, considering that these officials received a guinea each for eight hours work, why should they not do ditto? "Oh," I aeplied, "You do not recognise the frtness of things. What could a Law Clerk receiving £llO a. year (with extras), a Secretary with LEBO a year, a Surveyor with ?XX) a year, an Assistant Overseer with £250 a year, a Collec- tor and Librarian with £125 a year, and a Nuisance Inspector with rim a year--do with a forty ribbed steak? These are men of intellect, and need aore nourishing food than a man Who earns his living by the sweat of his brow and the wasting of his muscular tissue. Brain requires a tremendous anocunt of sustaining, and we as ratepayers must be prepared to de our duty." my friend was not prepared to corriute this logic. but he ;put me a poser as a firriaber. He agked me if I knew lihat, since the bill for this dinner had been passed by the Board, the candidates and mernbers who partook of the meal had been asked by the Secaetary for seven shilling each—their share of this feed. Ash was ignorant of this, I thought I would just mentioa tittto you, Mr. Editor. Perhaps you can enlighten 'me. if should be sorry to think that the officiFtla had not had their 16s. worth a)f roast beef.—Yours, in doubt, VICK SWIVELLEII.

div.head: FATALITIES ON THE ~RHIP CANAL
div.p: FATALITIES ON THE ~RHIP CANAL

Mr. J. F. Price, deguty county .coroner, held an •inquest on Thursday ,concerning the death of John ;Thomas Peacock. Deceased had resided in and about Manchester since last Mara. 40n Monday he -7went on the Ship Canal at Flixtecato -seek work, and was knocked down by.a wagon which was being ,shunted from behind. He died &tom shock and hemorrhage. A verdict of accidental death was 'returned.

-------- On Thursday night, a2Dout ten o'elock„, a workman .named Owen Ellis, aged IQ, who had been to Lymm on ibuziness, was making his way across a boat-to a dredger, ,onqsahich he was working, ,and which iis,cutting the ship eanal.across the river, when a splash was'lleard by the nislaesaverkmen, who went to his assistance. Ile was not to ,be seen. The river was dragged andthe •body found ten minutes afterwards. The deceased was .2 seaman, and•liveelat Gregwood Farm, the ',Talley near lfolyhead. Mr_ :Worsley, coroner, held an inquiry regarding the death paterday, when a verdict of " .aceidentally drowned" was returned.

div.head: IiEN3SION AT GRA.PPENHALL
div.p: IiEN3SION AT GRA.PPENHALL
THE ASSISTANT OVERSEER TO BE MO CAREFUL

On Tkarsday a revision of tb.e voters' lists for ;tire townships of Grappenhall, Appleton, and the extru municipal.partssof Latchford, was held by Mr.C. Lloyd, at Crappenhall. as possible under the circumstances. He then went on to say that it had been his practice to request a committee of the Town Council to supply him with plans and pre- pare a scheme for his assistance and guidance, but it must be aistinctly understood he was not bdund to accept that scheme, and in very few cases:he had accepted the scheme without modifications. He then invited the most ample expression of opinion by those present, the ' express object of that inquiry being not to stifle discus- sion,but to encourage it. If they were not able to arrive . at an opinion that day he was prepared to adjourn that I meeting for 48 hours, so as to give those who had not been heard an opportunity of coming forward. He added that he would make a note of Alderman Burgess's objec-

tion. Alderman Bunosss said he would be glad if the Com- missioner would do so. It had come to his ears that his name was not the only one omitted ; otherwise it was very possible that it would not be reported that morning that the scheme was carried by five. The COMMISSIONER: Has the Committee's report been before the Council. The Towx CLERK: It has not; there has not been a meeting of the Council since. The COMMISSIONER:: IS it not usual for & question of this importance to be submitted to the Commit ? The TowN CLERK:: There was not time. The COMMISSIONER said that he could not take the scheme to be submitted as the expression of opinion of the Council, but he tOnk it as an expression of opinion of the General Purposes Committee,in whom he supposed the Council had confidence, and so far it would have

weight. In answer to a question, the TOWN 'CLERK said he had I only receivedone notice of objection to the scheme of the ' General Purposes Committee,and thatwas signed by Mr. A Browne on behalf of several members of the Town Council. Mr. A. RacwNE said he represented the whole of the members for the North-west and North-east Wards, with the exception of one. The TOWN CLERK then referred to the Corporation scheme, and said that the present number on the burgess roll was E',234. The ComussioNert said he couldsee no objection to the proposals with regard to number nine, or Latchford Ward, but he must honestly tell them that number eight puzzled him very much. The TOWN CLERK said they were desirous to maintain, as far as practicable, old boundaries. In number seven and eight wards the rateable value was almost equal. The COMMISSIONER said that when he came to consider the rateable value in number eight ward, he found that there were two railway stations, which probably repre- sented a very considerable part of that rateable value. Was there any evidence of the possible increase of popu- lation in the ward. The TOWN CLERK: No, sir. Alderman WRIGHT There is a very material increase going on now. Councillor ROBERTS: I think we shall disagree on that. h e COMMISSIONER said they had got a rateable value of X 157,910 in Warrington, which if they divided by nine they would get an average ratable value for each ward, but he could not possibly distribute the wards according to rateable value, because they knew that the value of the centre of a town was always out of all proportion with the outlying parts. Rateable value was, therefore, nut a satisfactory criterion, and he scarcely ever paid any attention to it. The number of electors was a very material question, and 930 was the normal average for each ward, but in the scheme submitted to him number 7 ward contained 1,260 ' burgesses, while number 8 con- tained only 539. That was a disparity which, at first sight, would strike anybody. In number 7 ward there would be 410 burgesses for every representative, while in No. 8, every 180 would have a representative. The Commissioner also referred to. the difference between number 4 ward with 636 voters, and number 6 with 1,214 voters. He should like to know what reason there was for giving such extraordinary preference, sothat certain parts would have the same influence in the Council as other parts with three times the number of burgesses. He would suggest that part'of No. 2 ward, near Mill-lane, be added to number 8 ward by making Mill-lane a boun-

dary. Alderman WRIGHT said he thoroughly approved of that suggestion. He thought that the South-west ward,owing to its enormous rateable value, was a most important ward, and, besides, immediately outside the borough boundary, along Liverpool-road, they had a population of not less than 300 between the borough limits, and what they considered the most natural boundary, Sankey Brook. There was no doubt that, from a sanitary point of view. they should have to go in for that extension. The COMMISSIONER: I must not take notice of that. I am bound to suppose that the legislature is always right. (Laughter.) Mr. A. BROWNS said that if the Commissioner would look at the notice of the objection he had served, he would notice that his figures would bring out an almost equal number for the different districts. Mr. Browne then went on to refer to his objections to the Corporation plan as set forth in the minority scheme given above. In dealing with number 8 Ward, the COMMISSIONER asked whereabout the new docks would be and if they would not lead to an aggregation of population in the, neighbourhood. It was pointed out to him by Mr. BROWNE and Councillor ROBERTS, that the approaches from the South-West Ward to the site of the docks under the railway bridge, were very bad and not likely to be Improved. The COMMISSIONER thought even a railway bridge should not be allowed to interfere with the growth of a town. • Councillor HEATON argued that the making of the docks,and the construction of the new road ..cross Arpley Meadows, would tend to increase the population of the South-West Ward. Ile also referred te'the rate at which building was going on en the vacant land in the neigh- bourhoed of Museum street. He opposed Mr. Browne's suggestion to add that part of the South-East Ward bordered by Buttermarket street, Academy street, and Mersey street, to the South-West Ward. He said it was the same as taking a piece out of the centre of a side of bacon. , Alderman WRIGHT and Councillor BOLTON also opposed the alterations of the Corporation Scheme proposed by Mr. Browne. Councillor BOLTON particularly opposed the taking away of a part of the South-East Ward, and he thought the people would decidedly prefer to be left where they were. The 00mMissIONER : Do you consider you represent them? Councillor BOLTON : I do. .The COMMISSIONER: Have you had any meeting. Councillor BOLTON: No; but I have spoken to them casually. The COMMISSIONER: Well, but they could not know what Mr. Browne's proposal was. I don't want you to lead us astray as to whether you represent anybody er not. Would your election be affected if we took away that por- tion of the ward? Councillor BOLTON: If you were to cut it up in half-a- , dozen pieces I think they would return me. (Laughter.) The COMMISSIONER : Well, I don't want to deprive the Council of your services. (Laughter.) Perhaps there are some Irish voters in that part of the ward. Are you an Irishman? Councillor BOLTON: I should not like to be. (Laughter.) The COMMISSIONER asked if the Irish were represented there, buthe was informed that they were not. Alderman CHANDLEY supported the Committee's plan, and said that one of the most important reasons for recommending the plan was that it gave such excellent boundary lines. He was sorry that the Commissioner had spoken rather disrespectfully of old boundaries-- The COMM,ISSIONER said he did not speak disrespectfully of anything. What he said was that when lie found the intesestsof the population of a place necessitated change he did not 8.113 w his mind to be influenced by the anti- quity of aborder. Thatwas a different proposition. Alderman CHANDLEy said the Committee had been unanimously in favour of well-defined boundaries, and , they thought irdesirable as far as possible to maintain old well-known boundaries. With regard to number 8 ward they could have no objection to the proposal with regard to the western portion, but they should much prefer Bridge-et. for the eastern• boundary. They also pre- ferred to adhere to the proposal with regard to number 6. The CPISTAISSIBNER : What do you think of the disparity of nUtuber4, which will practically have double represen- tation is the Council. Alderman GIIANDLEY : I do not see we can remedy that. The COMMISSIONER : You think it inherent in the nature of things. Number. 4 is not only far below in the number of .burgesses, but its rateable value is the lowest in the wholeborough. Alderman ,CHANDLItY said he had no strong feeling in the matter if it were thought advisable to increase that ward. The COMMISSIONER : Mr. Browne proposes to remedy what is on the .faCe of it a rematskable and abnormal inequality both cfratealde value and of population, and I want to know any answer you can give to justify dne , in maintaining such a state of things. Alderman Onannutr.: have no objection at all. •Hear, hear.) The Comattssronan No argument in favour of the .present state of thins. ;I Alderman CILVISLCMY,: No. The Commissociage am obliged to con ;it is very ,candid of you. ler. IV. Dtoor.E, as a.property owner inttlie South-east; ward, supported Mr. Browne's proposals. As to Arpley! ,doelaz, the great questise was whether they would be ; .made or not. The COMMISSIONER lthey are bound to carry thorn out. Mr. RIGGLE : They are aot shaping yet. Councillor H. Roanirrs said that he was a member of the General Purposes Committse, and they were divided by five to four on the scheme scbmitted by the Town Clerk. Four of them entirely dizsented, and they supported the alternative scheme submitted by Idr. Browne. In submitting that alternative seheme they did so as largely as possible with an eye to equal electoral districts—in area and In electorate. With re- gard to wards 5 and 6, as proposed to be altered by their selieme, he thought that the Commissioner would find that there wto an amount of valuable land, suit- able for building, In those two divisions, which was pretty nearly equal. Coming to number seven as altered by their scheme they would leave 936 voters in it, and a large proportimsof uncovered land for building,. Ear taking away the gasestorks they took a portion that was impasaibla abouifi he enlarged, because it Wne

already entirely covered over. Mr. Roberts also ob- jected, but said he would not press it strongly, to the inclusion in No. 8 of the proportion proposed to be eliminated from N 0.2 It would bring in a number of voters to whom it would be a great inconvenience to

poll. Mr. BROWNE, referring to the rateable value of No. 8 district, said that it was accounted for by the inclusion of the railway works, and by the fact that there were two or three large works in that particular district. They indirectly had a representation already by the fact that the workpeople employed there resided in different parts of the borough, and took their part in different wards. He did not wish undue value to be given to the rateability, seeing that it was represented by the work- people in different parts of the borough. Alderman HARRISON said his great objection was to part with the portion of No. 7 that abuts on No. 8. Arpley fields would be materially altered by the construe- , tion of the Ship Canal, which would completely drain the fields and render the land suitable for building purposes. Thus No. 8 would be materially increased in population. They respected old boundaries and old landmarks, and they would very much prefer that the portion referred to remain with No. 7. The plan had passed the ordeal of the Parliamentary Committee, and the General Purposes

Committee. The COMMISSIONER: I pay all respect to that, but honestly confess that four to five is what you may call a highly respectable minority. Alderman Hatuusox said that the Parliamentary Com- mittee was entirely unanimous, and it was one of the most important Committees of the Council. There was a strong opinion in the town and in the Council that No. 7 ward should remain as at present. The COMMISSIONER: Do I understand, apart from the 11 gentlemen represented by Mr. Browne, that the Com- mittee and the Council are of the same mind in wishing the ward to remain as before Alderman HARRISON I have not the slightest reason for doubting it. Councillor J. SHAW GREEN said that he was present when the plan was put before the General Purposes Com- mittee, and it seemed to him that the Parliamentary Committee had taken a 'flying leap at the town, and had simply taken certain streets as being old boundaries. One of the five who voted in the majority at that meet- ing said he did so because the plan had been passed by the Parliamentary Committee. He (Councillor J. Shaw Green) thought that equality of representation was of more importance than the antiquity of boundaries. I Mr. KIERNAN said that he should like the Commissioner to give as much sway to an unofficial opinion like his own, as to those of members of the Council. He would like the wards to be more equalised, in the manner indica- ted by Mr. Browne, as he believed it would be a more equitable representation. Mr. Kiernan here referred to the opinions held by a lare number of Irishmen in the town, and was understood to add that he knew the feel- ings of almost every Irishmaniin England—(laughter)— and he might say that he was a representative of the majority of Irishmen in Ireland itself. The COMMISSIONER: You should have been in Parlia- ment, I think. Mr. KIERNAN : I had a chance to do that, Mr. Commis- sioner, but I refused. I thought I could be of more use in the rank and file. The COMMISSIONER: Have the Irishmen in England condescended to discuss this question. Mr. KIT RNAN : They have not. The COAMISSIONEU said that if, after the inquiry. Mr. Kiernan would obtain for him some expressions of opinion, he would see that they were considered. It was the interests of the public that were at stake. Councillor FLOOD remarked that in reference to No. 3 district, in which he resided, a statement had been made that a large portion of the population who worked in that district would go over into No. 4 district. That was not correct, for four-fifths of those who worked in No. 3 district also resided in it. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH thought that it was un- necessary to add the gas-works portion to No. 8, and al- so pointed out that there would be suitable land for building at Arpley. The COMMISSIONER: There is a means of increasing the population of No. Bin the direction where I think the increase will take place—towards the new docks. I will visit the place and will take care that everything shall be explained to me. Councillor IlercinNsoN said that as a tenant in No. 7 district for 35 years, he had great objections to having the portion removed to No. 8 ward. He felt certain nearly everyone would object to the ward being reduced. Mr. Bli6wNE said that the only objection the other side seemed to have to his new scheme was that they wished to stick- to the old boundaries. The COMMISSIONER: The great objection is the addi- tion of the Gas-works portion to No. 8. We are agreed regarding No. 1, and objections to No. 4 were not very emphatic. In regard to the addition of the Western boundary of No. 8, they agreed to that. Mr.liaowNE ; I do not offer any strong objection. Alderman Wnionr : I hope you will understand that thereis a very strong objection to Nos. 5 and 6 being al- tered. , The' COMMISSIONER: I understand that you prefer the present scheme. THE RETURNING OFFICERS. TheCommissionnu intimated that the next business was the assignment of Aldermen as returning. officers. There were at present five Aldermen acting as returning officers, and the Act of Parliament directed him to state to which of the Wards the Aldermen would be assigned. The Tows CLERK said that it had been agreed that the returning officers should be 'assigned as follows No. 1 Ward, Alderman Davies; 2, Alderman Crosfie/d ; 3, Alderman Holmes; 4, Alderman Ilsrrison ; 5, Alder- man £utton •, 6, Alderman Wright; 7, Alderman Fran- comb:;'B, Alderman Burgess; 9, Alderman Chandley. NAMING THE WARDS. The following list was proposed as the names by which the various wards shoulu in future he known :- 1, Town Hall ward; 2, White Cross ward; 3, Bewsey ward; 4, Orford ward; 5, St. John's ward ; 6, Cen- tral ward ; 7, South-east ward; 8, South-west ward, and 0, Latchford ward. A conversational discusison followed on the suggestions, and the Commissioner ex- pressed himself stongly in disfavour of naming No. 6 the Central Ward. It was also pointed out by the Com- missioner that in many towns wards were named after some person of celebrity who had been connected with the town, and asked if that could not be done in War- rington. Ide did not, from practical experience, favour calling wards by points of compass. Suggestions were then made that •wards might be named after Lord Winroarleigh, the late Mr. George Crosfield, and the late Mr. W. Beamont, and Mr. Kiernan suggested that the South-west ward be called after the old St. Austen's friary. 'Ultimately the matter was left over for further discussion, the Commissioners asking the Committee who had had the matter in hand to forward him a definite resolution in time for his decision. He should be happy to fardin with their suggestions. THE ASSIGNMENT OF COUNCILLORS.

The COMMISSIONRIt intimated that he was bound as far as possible to retain Councillors as near as possible to the districts they .at present represented. Observing those lines. it seemed better to leave it to them to decide, but bathe event of any division of opinion occurring, he would &tide the question. Ultimately the Councillors were allotted to the various wards as follows—those named first in order retiring the first year. those second in order the second, and those third in order the third. Names printed in italics indicate the councillors whose term expires in November next. No 1 Ward, Councillors J. Pairelough, W. Pierpoint, and R. Heaton ; 2, Coun- cillors H. Roberts. E. Greenall, and F. Monks ; 3, Coun- cillors I. Show Green,'T. Flood, and S. J. Beaman • 4, Councillors Jenkins, and F. A. Roberts ; 5, Councillors G. Blackhurst, J. Garner, and J. Platt ;6, Councillors J. H. Fleaning, T. Hutchinson, and R. T. Fairclough ;7, Councillors N. B. 'Percival, W. Bolton, and J. Cannel' ; 8, Councillors T. Hepherd, L. Voisey, and J. Muir; and 9, Councilors J. Athton, J. Taylor, and W. Tinsley. In regard to 1T0.•4 ward, which was only allotted two coun- cillors, it should be explained that that is owing to there being a vacancy in the representation of that ward con- sequent on -the resignation of Mr. Marsh. The gentle- man who may be returned for the vacancy will go to No. 4 ward.

The ComatissioNEß said that when he made out his award, he should send a duplicate to the Town-Clerk, and the original to the Secretary of State, and it would then await the sanction of the Queen in Council. As there would probably not be a Council held until after the next muniCipal election had taken place, his award would be for all iatents and purposes the law, subject to any amendmout•that might be made therein. The inquiry wes then closed, a vote of thanks being passed to the Commissioner on the proposition (el Mr. A. Iluowlix, seconded by Aldermaa WRIGHT.

TOFU: MURDER AND SUICIDE IN AMERICA. A terrible tragedy is reported from Portsmouth, New Hampshire, U.S.A. A man named Hein, a cooper, who was rendered desperate by the desertion of bin wife and the belief that his eldest daughter, agedls, laad got into bad company, attacked all his daughters, three in num- ber, killing the eldest and the youngest, and fatally wounding the other. After murdering his children he rushed into the street, where a mob had gathered eager to lynch hitit. He, however, evaded the people, and foind the man with whom he believed his wan And daughter had eloped, and fired two shota, wounding the man fatally in the back. div.head: EXTENSION OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE EXTENSION OF WARRINGTON.

THE RE-ARRANGEMENT OF THE WARDS. On Wednesday morning Mr. C. N. Crosswell, who has been appointed a Commissioner by the Home Secretary for the purposes of the Warrington Exten-, don and Water Act, held a public inquiry at the Town Hall, Warrington," to consider a scheme to , be proposed for the delimitation of the nine wards I into which the extended Borough is directed to be divided; for the apportionment of the existing COCTl- cillors among the said wards; fcr the assigntnent of Aldermen as Returning Officers; and for the making of such other provisions as raay be necessary or proper in consequence of the extension e the Borough and of the division and alteration of the wards." All persons were islvited to attendiand any burgess or other inhabitant affected by the scheme was entitled to make objections to it, or submit alternative schemes for the consideration of the Commissioner. Amongst those present at the in- quiry were the Mayor (Rderrean France-3mb), Alder- men Burgess, Chandlery, Harrison, and Wright; Councillors Roberts, Fiend, Blackhurst,'Shaw Green, Muir, Percival, Hepherd, Bolton, Garner, Ashton, Heaton, Hutchinson, lead J. Fairclough-; Messrs. A. Browne, W. Roberts, C. J. Holmes, Kiernan, Clayton (Liberal agent), Hatripson (Conservative agent), Mitchell, Diggle ; J. L. Whittle (town clerk), Dr. Gornall (medical eCcer), Longdin ,(borough sur- veyor), Chorley (borough treasurer), Fairhurst "collector), &c.
R!VAL SCHEMES. Two schemes of're-arrangement ,of the wards were submitted to the Commissioner. One had been adopted

at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Corporation, by a majority of five to four of the mem- bers present. Tien other scheme was one approved by the minority of the Committee, and it was supported be- fore the Commissioner by Mr. A. Browne, Who repre- sented eleven mcmbers Of the Town Council. It was also supported by Councillor E. Roberts. The two schetres were as follow. :—No. 1 Ward.—Com-

mittees scheme, estimated 974 burgesses ; from Market- gate, along Horsemarket and .Winwick streets to Tan- ner's=lane, theme along Tantaer's-lane, Froghall-lane, and Priestley-street to Green street, and thence along Green. street, Liverpool-road, and Sankey-street, to Market-gate. —minority's 'scheme, estimated burgesses 974; from Market-gate, .'along Horsettaarket-street to Tanner's-lane, thence along southerly side of Tanner's-lane to Bewsey- road, thence to Bewsey Rridgeland then along the Lon- don and North-Western Railway to Bank Quay Bridge, and from thence to Market-gate. No. 2 Ward.-Committee's-schnme, estimated burgesses 9361; fromijunction of Froghall-lane with Bewsey-road towards Bewsey-road and Lodge-lane to borough boun- dary, along sane to Sankey brook, where the boundary leaves the brook, continue along the borough boundary to Liverpool-road, along same to Green-street, thence to the junction of the latter ',with Priestley-street, and along Priestley-street and Troghall-lane to the point of .commencern ent. —Minority's scheme, estimated burgesses 986; from Bank Quay Bridge, along Liverpool-road to Sankey 'Bridges to borough boundary, along same to Lodge-lane, thence, by Bewsey-road to Bewsey Bridge, along the London and North-Western Railway to Bank Quay Tiridge. No. nirard.—Cbminittee's scheme,estimated burgesses 21.6.; from end of Tanner's-lane along Winwick-street and road, to Longford Bridge, along borough boundary to Lodge-lane, along the same and Bewsey-road to Tan- ner's-lane, and along the same to point of commence- ment. —The minority agree to this scheme. No. 'Ward.—Committee's scheme,estimated burgesses i 336 : from end of Pinnees-brow, along same and Orford- lane to end of Orford-avenue, along same to Gorsey-lane and along same to the borough boundary to Longford Bridge, and along Winwick-road and street to starting point —Minority's scheme, estimated burgesses 649; from the Rodney, along Winwick-road •to boundary, along the same to Cheshire Lines Railway, along the railway to Marsh House-lane, and back to the Rodney. N 0.5 Ward.—Gommittee's scheme, estimated burgess- es 81.6 i; from Railway Station Bridge, to Winwick-st., along the railway to the boundary, continuing same to Gorsey-lane, along Gorsey-lane to Orford-avenue, thence through Orlord-avenue and lane, Pinners-brow, and Winwitik-st. to said railway bridge.—Minority's scheme, estimated burgesseS 1057 ; from bottom of Pinners-brow, along Orford-laue and Marsh House-lane to Cheshire Lines Railway, along the line to the top of Orford-st., along the said street to 'Buttertnarket-st.,to Market-gate, from there through llorsemarket and Winwick-streets to starting point. No. 6 Ward.—Committee's scheme, estimated burgess- es 1,214 ; from Market-gate through Buttermarket, Irhun, and Church streets, Church-place, Manchester-rd. to borough boundary and Bouch Bridge, along Boundary- ' to Cheshire Lines, along the railway to Winwick-st., and From thence to" Market-gate—Minority's scheme, estim- ated burgesses; 1,080. This delimitation to be carried with elimination of the portion proposed to be added by
the minority to,No. 5 Ward. , No. 7 Ward.---Committee's scheme, estimated burgess-

-„. . es L. 260.; from Warrington Bridge 'along the river to Latchford Weir and • the borough boundary, along the boundary to Bondy 'Bridge, thence through Manchester-„ rd., Church-place and street, Irlam and Buttermarket= streets to Matket-gate, and through Bridge-st. to War- ' rington Bridge,--Minority's scheme, estimated burgess- es 935. This•delimitation should stand, but the follow- ing portions be eliminated :—From Market-gate down to Buttermarket-St., and along Academy-st to Mersev-st., and along Mersey-st. to Bridge Foot, and up Bridge-st. to Mersey-gate.. No. '8 Ward-'-Committee's scheme, estimated burgesses 539; from Ilatket-gate along Sankey-st and Liverpool- road to borough boundary, along the same to the Mersey at Atherten'e-Quay, along the river to Warrington Bridge, thence-along Bridge-st. to Market-gate.— Min- ority's scheme, estimated burgesses 872: This to stand as it is, witfirthe addition of the portion taken from No.
7. No. 9 Ward.-1-Committee's scheme, estimated burgess- es, 893 ;that portion of the borough in the township of Latchford. agreed to by the minority.
THE NEW WARD BOUNDARIES.

- - The CorreIBSZONER, in opening the Court, said they were doubtless aware of an Act of Parliament, passed , within the last session of Parliament for certain purposes, and it was under the clauses of that Act he was there that day. lie was there to hold an inquiry into ques- tions whicla were of importance to the future well-being of that town, anti of which due notice had, he assumed, been given on the walls of the town and in the local journals. Ey way of formally opera= the inquiry and of establiehing •hi s right to preside he would read the commission of her' Majesty's Secretary ef State which gave him Jurisdiction. He then read the commission. and mentioned that his award was to be given before the 30th September. The TOWN lIIROX • neXt read the notice of the inquiry that had been posted in the town and advertised in the local newspapers. answer to the Commissioner, the TOWN Crivals said the estimated population of the borough after the extension would be about 51,000. At the last cenensetwasea,4sB. The population was increa- sing rapidly. The original area of the borrugh was 1,442 acres, but the area of the extended borough would be about 1,921 acres. The rateable value of the borough before extension was £150,000, after ex-tension it would be £157,000. The borough was incorporated under the Municipal Corporations 'Act in 1847 ; the division of the Iherough was the sasne now as then, and ; the number ' of representatives on the Council was the same, nine aldermen and 27 conacillers. 'The Commessiserneavaid he had ',to divide the borough into nine wards instead of Aw,' as at present, and he had to give equal representation beach ward. div.head: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RIXTON.
div.p: DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RIXTON.

On Thursday evening about nine o'clock a des- tructive tire broke out in the stackyard of the Nursery farm, Hixton, the tenant, of which is Mr. H. H. Brooks. A messenger was at once despatched in great haste to Warrington for the fire brigade. The brigade turned out quickly but on arriving at Ltixton it was found that the hose was not of sufficient length, the nearest water being 200yds. away from the fimsnd the engine could not, there- ft we, be brought into service. Five large stacks, a corn shed, and a. valuable thrashing machine were , destroyed, and the fire had not been completely ex- tinguished yesterday afternoon. The damage to the I produce is estimated at about £3OO and the machine which belonged to Mr. Smith, of Eccles, was valued at another .£3OO. Both machine and produce were insured in the Yorkshire Fire Office. The fire is sup- posed to have been caused by a spark from the thrashing engine.

1 A collision occurred on Thursday between two goods trains near Clowel, on the Waterford and Limerick 1 Railway. Many 'waggons were broken, and the line was blocked forsonsehours. The drivers and guards escaped injury.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. EAUDE.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. EAUDE.
Sarah

We regret to announce the death of Mrs. Eaude, which took place at Bruche House, Man- chester-road, on Monday. She was the widow of the late Mr. Thomas Eaude who, for many years. was organist at the Parish Church. She too was an active and zealous worker in connection with the Parish Church. The funeral took place on Thursday and was attended by a considerable number of sympathising friends. The service was conducted by the Rector and the Rev. Mr. Timmins who had .been in constant attendance on deceased during her illness. The surpliced choir of the Parish Church was also present and sang suitable hymns, one io going from the Church to the grave and one at the' 1 graveside.

BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACT AT WARRINGTON. Yesterday, at the Warrington Police Court, the. Tanners-lane, Tanning Company, Limited, were summoned under the Factory and Workshops Act of 1878 for having failed to send notice to the - Government Inspector of an accident that had occurred at their works. Mr. James Jones, factorY inspector, said that he was in 1% artington on the 12th August, and met a man whose hand ws,s bandaged. On inquiry he found that the man bad been hurt a fortnight before at the works of the defendant company, and that the matter had not been reported. He did not wish, he added, to aggravate the case, but simply desired that manii- facturers should know that it was their duty to at once report matters of this kind. Mr. Atkin, whn appeared on behalf of the Company, said that the, offence had been committed through ignorance, LOT the Bench imposed a nominal penalty of ss. an costs. modern

At the annual licensing sessions for the Aston District, Birmingham, the Chairman of the Bench, Mr. Hill, made an important announcement of their views on the subject of tied houses. Mr. Hill said there was a matter of con- siderable importance which had been under the notice of the magistrates that morning—i. e., whether some reduc- tion in the number of licensed houses in the Aston district Ahould not be made. It was felt by the justices that the number was in excess of the requirements of the neigh- bourhood, and they intended to consider whether they should do anything that year, but the holders of the licenses might depend upon it that the matter would ,be dealt with next year. A great change had taken place of late as to the manner in which licensed houses were conducted. It was undoubtedly the intention of the Legislature that licenses should be granted to a vic- tualler trading for himself at his own profit, and although he might be tied to sell a certain brewer's liquors, he was still the responsible landlord and holder of the license. The practice, however, was very differ- ent now, and in the great majority of cases the landlord of the house was. simply the servant of the brewer or spirit merchant, and was liable to instant dismissal for any infringement of duty. These men, the bench under- stood, were paid small salaries, or a commission on the trade done, and consequently were not really responsible for the conduct of the house or the safety of the license. Under the circumstanceS, the magistrates would consider next year whether they should not refuse the license to these people, and grant it to none but the bona fide owner of the house. He would assure every license holder that the subject referred to, and also the question of reducing the number of houses, would be dealt with at the next annual licensing session.

James WDonald, an ex-convict, was remanded by the Bolton county magistrates on Thursday, on a charge of being concerned in the death of a fellow workman named Thomas Mather, of Egerton, or Saturday last. The men were drinking together, and Dl'Donald was the last rsan seen in company with Mather, whose body, much bruised, was found in the reservoir on Monday. A post- mortem examination is being made. • A Lloyd's telegram from Sydney states that the British steamer Namoi took fire in port, but the fire has been extinguished.

Yesterday's Cricket: Eleven of England 107 for five wickets. A nobleman has committed suicide in Berlin through betting losses. Four lives have been lost in Berlin through a fire in a dwelling house. It is estimated that it will cost £14,000 to repair the damage done by fire to the Spanish Alhambra. LOSS OF A STEAMER AND CREW. A Lloyd's agent at Hiogo reported on Friday the total loss of the steamer Musashi Maru, belonging to the Mituz Bishi Mail Steamship Company, off Cochin. All the crew were drowned oxcept one Japanese. DEATH OF DION BOUCICAULT. A telegram from New 1/ ork yesterday morning states: —Mr. Dion Boucicault, the play writer and actor, died here on Thursday night, after a lingering illness. The immediate cause of death was pneumonia. CYCLONE IN lOWA.-12 LIVES LOST. NNW' YOR' K FRIDAY MORNING.—A cyclone of great violence burst over lowa State yesterday, doing great damage everywhere. At the town of Manning, twelve persons were killed and forty injured. Further news is expected hourly of fresh disasters. COLLISION AND LOSS OF LIFE. A Lloyd's agent at Cardiff telegraphs that the steamer Colina, of West Hartlepool, arrived yesterday, badly damaged after a collision off Bull Point with the Marie Brocklemann brig, of Drogheda. The captain and three of the crew of the latter vessel were drowned. The re- mainder of the crew were landed at Cardiff. THE IRISH ARRESTS. The arrests of Messrs. ninon and O'Brien have not interfered with the arrangement for the American mis- sion. It is probable that Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., and Mr. J. J. O'Kelly, M.P., will start for the United States on October Ist. Mr. Parnell has been telegraphed for, and within a few days a meeting of the prominent mem- bers of the Irish party will be held in London. FOUNDERING OF A TURKISH WAR VESSEL. FIVE HUNDRED MEN DROWNED. The following is from Lloyd's shipping agency : " Lloyd's agent at Hiogo telegraphs, under date 19th September, as follows: The Turkish man-of-war Erto- groul foundered at sea. Five hundred of the crew are drowned, including Osman and Ali. The Ertogroul was a wooden frigate-built cruiser of 2,344 tons displacemmit, built in 1863, and carrying 41 guns of small calibre. Osman Pasha, who was one of those drowned, had, says the " Pall Mall Gazette" been sent on an official visit to the Mikadp, and his ship has been for some time in Japanese waters.. The gallant General is best known i in connection with the defence of Plevna.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. - The market is not vigorous, nor is there more than a very moderate trade going through. Cotton is tame and a shade weaker. The day's business is covered by an estimate of 7.000 bales, and Ameri- can prices are barely supported. Yarns are steady at about Tuesday's rates, and there is a quiet trade doing, but nothing of great weight. Good printers and finishing goods are steady with a quiet trade. Burnley sorts still leave much to be desired. Home houses are quiet.
